name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska legislative task force hears overwhelming public support for more investment in schools
description: Alaskans from across the state weighed in on lawmaker proposals to boost K-12 schools during nearly 10 hours of public comment on Thursday. They addressed an initial draft of recommendations from a joint legislative task force on education funding. The task force released its draft report this week where it recommended increasing state education funding […]
text:
School buses park outside the playground of Xóots Elementary School in Sitka on Oct. 6, 2025 (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Alaskans from across the state weighed in on lawmaker proposals to boost K-12 schools during nearly 10 hours of public comment on Thursday. They addressed an initial draft of recommendations from a joint legislative task force on education funding.
The task force released its draft report this week where it recommended increasing state education funding with inflation, funding school facilities and instruction separately, addressing a massive backlog in maintenance and contracting an adequacy study to evaluate the state’s spending levels.
 
Written public comments to the task force on education funding are due by December 8 and can be emailed to TFEF@akleg.gov or edfundtaskforce@akleg.gov
Over the next two months, the draft report will be further refined, designed, and finalized prior to being officially submitted by the first day of the 2027 legislative session.

Anchorage Democratic Sen. Löki Tobin, co-chair of the task force, opened the all-day hearing by saying the study will alleviate the political battles over state spending per student, known as the base student allocation. 
“We need this information to ensure that we put the right resources into the right components for our school system,” she said. “But we do not have that independent analysis that is absolutely critical to funding our education system.” 
In the meantime, the task force members asked for public input on a state definition for “adequate education.” They also introduced short, mid and long-term recommendations related to school maintenance, the legislative budgeting process, teacher recruitment and retention, transportation and others. Public comment is open until Dec. 8. 
Tobin said that it will be her focus as she was reappointed to chair the Senate Education Committee for the next two years.
Dozens of Alaska parents, students, teachers, principals, superintendents and education advocates testified in person in Anchorage, Fairbanks, Juneau and Kenai — as well as over the phone — urging support for state investment in education.     

Susan Nedza, superintendent of the Hoonah City School District, testifies before the task force on education funding in Juneau on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Susan Nedza, superintendent of the Hoonah City School District in Southeast Alaska, spoke in person in Juneau. 
“If the recommendations in this report reach reality, school staff will be able to focus efforts on our true purpose: students,” she said. “The focus now is on the stress and constant priority of stretching and finding funds to cover the bare basics instead of the well-being of students in our care.”
Many testifiers expressed support for investment in teachers and staff — to reduce vacancies, high turnover and growing class sizes — and much-needed school building repairs. They also pointed to the need for further investment in school nutrition programs, special education services, Alaska Native languages, the Alaska Reads Act, extracurricular opportunities and pathways to careers. 
Some expressed concern that families’ choice to enroll in homeschool programs should be protected, and that the state should not enact any changes to homeschool programs or current standards. 
School officials spoke to skyrocketing costs for heating buildings and keeping facilities operational, and said repairs go years without attention. They expressed support for the task force’s recommendation of a separate funding stream for school facilities costs aside from instructional dollars. 
“Facility funding, rising energy costs and improving conditions for our classrooms, keeping a roof intact or heating the building during the Alaskan winter should never require cutting teachers, class offerings or student support or student activities,” said Jason Weber, superintendent of Valdez City Schools. Many districts across the state have had to make such cuts in recent years. 
Support for education funding bill comes as Alaska districts grapple with ongoing deficits

“Roughly 70% of our school’s budget is related to maintenance,” said Rhonda Pitka, vice president of the Tanana Chiefs Conference and chief of the Village of Beaver in the Yukon Flats. She said they struggle to hire and keep maintenance workers to complete repairs. “This is a critical issue, and it affects the safety and usability of school facilities,” she said. 
Pitka and several officials testified that the rising operational costs also hurt school districts’ ability to offer competitive wages to hire and retain teachers. 
“Overcrowded kindergarten classrooms with high needs — this is tough to have a classroom full of young learners with limited support and lack of teacher aides,” she said. “We face difficulty hiring and retaining teachers in our areas, especially our special education aides, because of the low wages and the benefit issues with the state.”
Grant Guy, principal of Wood River Elementary School in Fairbanks, spoke to how the teacher shortage is burning out teachers in his district. He said that’s particularly acute for special education teachers and paraprofessionals. 
“The amount of time, energy, and cost to train those individuals are immense, and oftentimes by the time they start learning what they need to do to help students de-escalate from situations, they are so burnt out that they go and find positions that pay them more for much less stress,” he said.     

Christine Johnson, a Juneau resident and mother of four, testifies to the task force on education funding on the importance of supporting special education services on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Christine Johnson, a mother of four in Juneau, spoke to the struggle to receive special education support for her child, when the district lacked staff and funding.
“Special education is not an optional program. It is an essential part of providing an adequate public education,” she said. “When a student needs speech therapy, occupational therapy, behavioral support, assistive technology, specialized instruction, or additional support, those needs do not disappear because a district can’t afford the staff or resources to provide them.” 
Many testifiers expressed support for an increase to the state’s per student funding formula and said it would create more stability for districts if the Legislature approved education funding earlier in the year — one of the task force’s top recommendations.
“Make funding stable, timely, and consistent,” said Jason Hlasney, superintendent of the Lower Kuskokwim School District, which serves 22 rural schools across 22,000 miles. He said students need opportunities that foster hope.
“This fall, I asked our students and communities what they hope for. Students asked for welding, carpentry, mechanics, aviation, among other careers. They want to be college and career ready, and they dream of becoming nurses, dentists, hunting guides, and all the various things,” he said. “They ask for more Alaska Native teachers. Our students need learning that connects to real work close to home, from teachers who stay long enough to know every child.”    

Four wheelers and bicycles sit outside the Anna Tobeluk Memorial School on a frosty morning in Nunapitchuk. October 12, 2023. (Photo by Claire Stremple/Alaska Beacon)
 

Nedza, the superintendent in Hoonah, was among those who expressed concern that budget cuts for school nutrition programs are hurting students, and she said they should be part of what is considered adequate funding.
“Some schools have stopped providing meals, provide only some meals, charge students or rely on an increasingly limited general fund to cover this cost,” she said, and added Hoonah’s costs have increased so that the district spends roughly $100,000 on the lunch program each year. 
“Nutritious school meals and universal free meal programs are directly linked to better student attendance, improved focus and higher academic achievement,” she said. “At least nine states already have universal free meals at school, and Alaska needs to follow suit.”
Concerns raised around potential changes to homeschool programs
Several parents, students and advocates testified in support of homeschooling options, called correspondence programs, which vary across the state. Several parents told lawmakers homeschooling is a better fit for their educational and family needs. 
Kendal Kruse, a mother of five in Palmer and a member of the Matanuska-Susitna School Board, gave personal testimony opposing any changes to homeschool policies that she said would force students into neighborhood schools.
“One in five kids is using a correspondence school in Alaska. That is a huge percentage of our student population, for us to be highly concerned about repealing or reducing the access to these programs for students that need them, and I think that’s a huge mistake,” she said.
Kruse and others expressed concern about language in the task force’s draft report recommending districts investigate ways to incorporate homeschool students into neighborhood schools, which cited research that said “in-person learning significantly outperforms online and distance learning.”
Several parents also took issue with the task force recommendation to review statutes to ensure homeschool students are being provided an adequate education, noting that current law allows broad exemptions from “statewide content standards, proficiency assessments, and fiscal audits.” 
But Wasilla elementary school teacher Kathleen Yerbich spoke in favor of state testing for all homeschooled students, as she sees students in her classroom who have fallen behind after years of homeschooling. “This is the part no one talks about,” she said. 
“Some parents readily admit that the job was harder than they anticipated. Their kid didn’t want to do the assignment. They were too busy with sports to do all that was required, and so on. We are placing the parents’ right to choose above educating our children. I believe that all children should be tested yearly to see how they are doing,” Yerbich said. 
“All kids deserve an excellent education. They deserve a chance to learn to the best of their abilities and to be challenged to the next level. The elementary years go by quickly. It is unfair to children for the state of Alaska not to be diligent in making sure they are learning,” she said.
Following the hearing Thursday, task force member and Juneau Democratic Sen. Jesse Kiehl said the task force will likely revise some of the language in the recommendations to address homeschool families’ concerns. 
“We’re looking at opening more opportunities for school districts to offer those families more choices, not fewer,” he said. “And at the same time to make sure that parents have the tools to know if their kids are making progress, and so I think that we can reword that and hopefully put some of those fears to bed.”
Raising the BSA with inflation
School officials and advocates are urging an increase to per student funding next year. They say the BSA should increase  at least $1,011 per student — a roughly 15% bump that would cost the state $254.6 million.     

Lisa Parady, executive director of the Alaska Council of School Administrators, testifies before the legislative task force on education funding in Juneau on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Lisa Parady, executive director of the Alaska Council of School Administrators, testified Thursday that the figure was calculated with the state legislative finance division to account for inflation since 2017. The organization is also calling for investment in school facilities, and to restore a defined-benefit pension system for public service employees, including teachers. 
While the large majority of testifiers urged more state spending on schools, some — like Josh Church of Fairbanks, who recently ran for lieutenant governor as Republican Dave Bronson’s running mate — urged legislators to look at educational requirements and outcomes instead of more state spending. 
“We need to look at, not how do we protect the education system in the state, but how do we produce the best results for the kids of this state. So the answer to this is not always more money, more money,” he said. “The solution for more money, additional pensions, whatever it might be — we’ve been chasing that rabbit for years and years, and more money does not solve a problem if you don’t get to the underlying causes.”
Kiehl said the incoming Legislature will be working with presumptive Gov.-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins on the budget, the task force recommendations and first priorities for funding education. 
Kiehl, who also co-chairs the Senate Finance Committee, said his first priority would be addressing the BSA so that districts have predictable funding. “If we can take that off the table before the rest of the budget process, school boards around the state will have a chance to focus on education policy instead of rewriting the budget eight times,” he said.
Alaska is seeing high state oil revenues due to the surge in oil prices driven by the U.S. war on Iran, and Kiehl said schools are a top priority. 
“The business of the Legislature is the business of “no” and figuring out which things to say no to, and where we have to say yes for Alaska’s future, we’re going to say yes in schools,” he said. “Exactly how much? Exactly when? That’s the hard work that starts in January.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Slotkin ‘seriously’ considering presidential bid, says decision could come soon
description: U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she is giving serious thought to making a run for president in 2028, as Democrats debate the party’s future leadership following the midterm elections. “I’m looking at it seriously, but I haven’t made any decisions, whether it’s me or somebody else,” the Michigan Democrat said Friday at the “What’s Next” […]
text:
DENVER, COLORADO - NOVEMBER 13: Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) speaks during the What's Next summit at Mission Ballroom on November 13, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. Following the midterm elections, prominent Democrats and political insiders are gathered for the three-day event to evaluate election results, debate party strategy, and discuss potential 2028 presidential contenders. (Photo by Mark Makela/Getty Images)U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she is giving serious thought to making a run for president in 2028, as Democrats debate the party’s future leadership following the midterm elections.
“I’m looking at it seriously, but I haven’t made any decisions, whether it’s me or somebody else,” the Michigan Democrat said Friday at the “What’s Next” conference in Denver, hosted by the group Majority Democrats.
Slotkin said she wants to be part of a new generation of Democratic leaders who approach governing differently, adding that the timeline for deciding whether to enter the race would likely be shorter than six months.
“I think it’s shorter than that,” she said.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Her comments came as Democrats contemplated a governing agenda after the “blue tsunami” in the midterm election delivered control of both the U.S. House and Senate. Slotkin said the party’s next generation of leaders must focus less on internal disputes over ideology and more on providing economic relief for Americans.
“The message that was sent so extremely clear on election night was that people are desperate to know whether there’s going to be an American middle class in this country and whether they’re going to be able to be in it,” Slotkin said.
She argued that any Democrat who continues infighting over whether they should embrace moderate or progressive policies “has lost the plot.” 
Slotkin pointed to her relationship with fellow Michigan Democrat, U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, as an example of how lawmakers with different perspectives can find common ground, noting that the pair campaigned together despite their disagreements.
“We have more in common, whether you’re a moderate or a progressive, than we do separating us,” Slotkin said.
She said Democrats should be able to work with colleagues who support policies such as Medicare for All, even if they disagree about the best approach to fixing the healthcare system.
‘I’m popping a flare’: Slotkin says Trump is using ‘same playbook as every authoritarian in history’

“The truth is everyone could agree on the fact that our healthcare system is broken,” Slotkin said. “We may have differences on how we want to fix it, but the value that underlies that is that the people are desperate for us to fix healthcare.”
Slotkin also reiterated her opposition to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer returning as Senate majority leader. El-Sayed has affirmed his support for U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who entered the race last week. While Slotkin didn’t say if she supported Van Hollen, she told reporters that she would have more to say about the leadership contest later this week.
Slotkin’s remarks at the conference came as she also addressed a renewed confrontation with the Trump administration. Slotkin said she received notice from the Department of Justice on Thursday that it was again threatening an investigation and possible criminal indictment over her public statements.
The senator said the latest development followed comments by Trump calling for legal action against her.
Slotkin referenced an earlier effort to pursue criminal charges against her in February, following her participation in a video with other Democratic lawmakers discussing the obligation of military and intelligence personnel to refuse unlawful orders.
She characterized the administration’s actions as an attempt to criminalize political opposition.
“This says more about him than it does about me,” she added. “And I’m happy to have him demonstrate to the world that freedom of speech is something he wants to criminally indict.”

title: Gateway Cities and the market-rate housing debate
description: This week on The Codcast, CommonWealth Beacon reporter Hallie Claflin is joined by Aaron Vega, president and CEO of the Western Massachusetts Economic Development Council, and Rachel Heller, executive director of the Massachusetts Housing Partnership, to discuss a wide-ranging debate over development and housing affordability that has landed smack dab in the[...]
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOST: Hallie Claflin
Guests: Aaron Vega, president and CEO of the Western Massachusetts Economic Development Council; Rachel Heller, executive director of the Massachusetts Housing Partnership








IF THERE’S ONE THING advocates, officials, residents, and experts can all agree on, it’s that Massachusetts’s Gateway Cities need more housing. A lot of it.  
What kind of housing needs to be built? That’s typically where the agreement ends.  
This week on The Codcast, CommonWealth Beacon reporter Hallie Claflin is joined by Aaron Vega, president and CEO of the Western Massachusetts Economic Development Council, and Rachel Heller, executive director of the Massachusetts Housing Partnership, to discuss a wide-ranging debate over development and housing affordability that has landed smack dab in the middle of nearly every low-income city in the Commonwealth. 
In the state’s 26 former industrial cities — where many residents live in neighborhoods with highly concentrated poverty and median household incomes sit well below the state’s average — housing costs are rising, supply is well below demand, and vacancy rates remain low, meaning competition is too high to stabilize prices. New developments, as well as their proponents, are often met with resistance and backlash, either because the projects lack affordability, are branded as “luxury” housing, or because of gentrification concerns. 
But many leaders and experts push back, arguing that what these cities need most is a mix of housing — including market-rate units — that will attract businesses, jobs, and higher incomes that could spur economic development.  
“Ideally, we wouldn’t be subsidizing market-rate housing. In an ideal world, the market would be the market, and housing could be built,” Heller said. “But we don’t have that market in Massachusetts, so we are seeing people struggle across income levels.” 
In this episode, Claflin, Heller, and Vega discuss why the state subsidizes market-rate housing (4:25), what the Housing Development Incentive Program has accomplished in the Gateway Cities (11:48), and how market-rate housing can help create mixed-income communities (22:36).

name: Mississippi Today
title: Insurance commissioner mulls one-time grants as more Mississippians drop health coverage
description: Mike Chaney, the incumbent Republican insurance commissioner, speaks during Mississippi Economic Council's 2023 Hobnob at the Mississippi Coliseum in Jackson, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 26, 2023.
text:
Insurance Commissioner Mike Chaney is considering a proposal he says could help Mississippians struggling to afford health coverage.
Chaney told Mississippi Today his office is weighing a proposal to provide one-time grants of about $250 to help low-income people without health insurance pay for healthcare expenses. The program would be funded through the Mississippi Comprehensive Health Insurance Risk Pool Association, the state’s long-dormant insurer of last resort. 
The grants could be used to buy a health insurance plan, offset an emergency room bill, see a primary care physician or pay for a flu shot.
“This is not about socialism,” Chaney said. “It’s about keeping people out of the ER and keeping them healthy so you have a healthy workforce.”
Chaney’s proposition underscores the challenges of many low-income Mississippians struggling to afford healthcare costs. Mississippi has been hit particularly hard by the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act tax subsidies last December. Those tax credits had made health insurance more affordable for tens of thousands of Mississippians. The impact has been especially severe because Mississippi lawmakers have for over a decade opted not to expand Medicaid, leaving many low-income residents with limited coverage options. 
In Washington, D.C., House Democrats have said restoring the enhanced premium tax credits is a top priority for the new Congress, which is set to convene Jan. 3. But meanwhile, people are selecting plans for 2027. Open enrollment began Nov. 1 and will continue through Jan. 15. 
Chaney estimates the proposed grants would total $4 million to $5 million and reach about 20,000 people — roughly a tenth of the people who have dropped marketplace coverage in the past year. He said he is working to make the funding available as early as December — but he doesn’t want to dissuade people from purchasing health insurance coverage.
Mississippi’s Comprehensive High Risk Pool Association was created in 1991 to provide healthcare coverage to people who were denied insurance. Financed with mandatory contributions from private insurance companies, it stopped issuing policies after the ACA barred insurance companies from denying coverage to people with pre-existing conditions. The association has more than $22 million in assets, according to 2024 tax filings.
This is not the first time Chaney has proposed using the remaining funds to help people struggling to pay for healthcare. Earlier this year, Chaney proposed using the association to create a customer portal for short-term health plans.
He told Mississippi Today he abandoned the idea because the premiums offered by insurers for the short-term plans, which were designed to bridge a temporary gap in coverage and do not meet federal requirements for comprehensive health insurance under the Affordable Care Act, were too high. 
“I kicked that bucket down the road a long way,” Chaney said.
Matthew Fiedler, interim director of the Center on Health Policy at the Brookings Institution, said small grants cannot substitute for health insurance, because insurance is designed to help people pay large healthcare bills. 
“The amount of money we’re talking about here would only be sufficient to cover people with very minor healthcare needs,” Fiedler said. 
Chaney said though the grants would be small, the program’s intention is to give people money for essential healthcare visits and reduce the amount of care hospitals provide to people who can not pay. 
“If you keep them out of the hospital, you save a hell of a lot more money in the long run than you would if you just did nothing,” Chaney said. 
But low-income people struggling to afford healthcare may be more likely to use the funds to cover urgent healthcare needs as opposed to preventive care, said Sabrina Corlette, a research professor and co-director of the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University.
“When you’re living paycheck to paycheck, there will be emergent needs and preventive care might not be one of those,” Corlette said. 
The plan could also have unintended consequences for hospitals. 
Richard Roberson, president and CEO of the Mississippi Hospital Association, said he has concerns about the financial consequences for facilities that participate in a joint federal-state program for hospitals that serve a disproportionately high number of low-income, uninsured and Medicaid patients. Qualifying hospitals receive supplemental payments to offset uncompensated care costs. 
“We just want to make sure that doesn’t compromise or jeopardize hospitals’ ability to get reimbursed,” Roberson said. 
Corlette and Fiedler both said Mississippi could instead consider expanding Medicaid — a policy decision that is up to the state Legislature, not the insurance commissioner — to expand access to healthcare and bring more federal funding to struggling hospitals.
The Legislature came close to passing Medicaid expansion during the 2024 session, but the effort ultimately died in conference committee negotiations. Lawmakers have been largely silent on the issue since then. 
Other states have established supplemental subsidies to help offset the loss of enhanced tax credits. This approach can be cost-effective because it allows people to continue accessing existing federal assistance for marketplace health plans, Fiedler said. However, this approach relies on the state operating its own health insurance marketplace, which Mississippi does not do.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: Most school levies failed, which prompts a review of how we fund schools
description: The recent election sent a contradictory message about Minnesota public education. About 73% of voters approved a constitutional amendment increasing payouts from the state’s Permanent School Fund, which generates revenue from school trust lands. It is welcome news, but small: $33 more per student, from about $68 to $101, with the first payment in July […]
text:
The author argues that school districts have become overly reliant on local property taxpayers, who are in turn increasingly rejecting local levies. (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)The recent election sent a contradictory message about Minnesota public education. About 73% of voters approved a constitutional amendment increasing payouts from the state’s Permanent School Fund, which generates revenue from school trust lands. It is welcome news, but small: $33 more per student, from about $68 to $101, with the first payment in July 2027. 
Yet voters rejected 55 of the 83 school funding questions on local ballots, according to unofficial results.
How do we reconcile those results? The amendment was promoted as a way to raise school funding without raising taxes. Do Minnesotans support public education when it won’t cost them anything, but pull back when their property taxes are at stake?
If so, students unlucky enough to live in a community that is unable or unwilling to pay more in property taxes will get fewer opportunities than their classmates in other communities. 
Does that seem fair? 
Education is a statewide responsibility 
Voters should have a say in major local spending decisions, and school boards should be accountable for their budgets. The basic opportunities available to students should not be determined primarily by a community’s willingness to repeatedly approve property tax increases. 
If Minnesota truly believes public education is a statewide priority, shouldn’t the responsibility for funding it also be shared statewide?
Rejection of school levies is not new, but the Minnesota School Boards Association reports that just 30% of operating referendums, 36% of bond requests and 42% of capital project requests passed this year. In 2024, 35 of 64 school questions failed. 
The gap shows up in rural Minnesota too. In the Lake Park-Audubon district, the schools’ own leaflet estimated that its two school funding questions together would cost about $60 a year, or $5 a month, on a $300,000 home, with lake cabins paying nothing. Even so, both failed with just over 40% of the vote. In Frazee-Vergas, about 46% supported its request. 
When a levy fails, the financial pressure does not disappear. Last November, Marshall voters rejected a $2 million, 10-year operating referendum. The school board then approved cuts of at least $1.8 million for 2026-27, including districtwide staffing reductions and the elimination of programs. 
In Deer River, after multiple referendums failed, the district must now cut $2 million, or 12% of its budget. Nearly 70% of that budget goes toward staff costs, so most of the cuts will fall on staffing. 
In a June 2026 survey by the Minnesota Rural Education Association, 61% of 105 responding rural districts reported reducing instructional staff, and the survey’s write-up mentions larger class sizes and fewer secondary course offerings. The whole community feels it. If we believe rural communities must remain viable, we must consider what happens when their schools cannot adequately serve their students.
Is it time to rethink how Minnesota pays for schools?
Perhaps the bigger problem is not that voters reject referendums. Rather, Minnesota has become too dependent on local property taxpayers to finance an essential statewide responsibility. 
That creates inequities. Communities with different property tax capacity, enrollment and economic circumstances face very different odds of raising the same amount. A student’s opportunities should not depend so heavily on their ZIP code. 
It is time to examine a different balance between statewide and local funding. Options include a more progressive income tax; a carefully designed tax on accumulated wealth; and redirecting existing alcohol, tobacco and cannabis tax revenue to schools.
Each option shifts who pays, and the state’s own numbers show how differently. The Department of Revenue’s 2026 tax incidence study found that the individual income tax is the only major progressive tax. Redirecting money the state already collects is another option. Alcohol and tobacco taxes together raised about $655 million in fiscal year 2024, compared with $14.9 billion from the income tax, and the cannabis tax is now 15%. Dedicating that revenue to schools would not raise anyone’s taxes, but the general fund would lose it unless lawmakers replaced it. 
A wealth tax is a different kind of idea. This year’s HF 4616, which proposed a 1% tax on wealth above $10 million, would have reached about 5,600 taxpayers and raised an estimated $288 million in its first year, but it never reached a floor vote, and opponents warned of avoidance and departures. Just 4 of the 38 nations in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development countries had net wealth taxes in 2017, down from 12 in 1990, and the OECD found their revenues generally low.  
Another starts with the local tax base itself. Seasonal recreational property, such as lake cabins, is excluded from the base for operating referendums, so other property owners carry that cost. The exclusion dates to 2001. Cabin owners still pay other taxes, including the state levy and local building levies, but whether they should share operating costs deserves a hearing. 
None of these options is a complete solution. Each deserves an honest look at who pays, who benefits and how reliably the revenue can support schools.

name: California
title: Don’t blame the Texas blue wave on ex-Californians
description: We wanted to answer if Californians moving to Texas played an outsized role in the blue tsunami of the Lonestar State. At least for flipping the U.S. Senate seat, the answer is a clear no. More than 364,000 Californians moved to Texas from 2018 to 2023 according to Internal Revenue Service migration data, and we […]
text:
Attendees watch election results at an event for Democratic Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa in Austin, Texas on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Ashley Landis, AP Photo




We wanted to answer if Californians moving to Texas played an outsized role in the blue tsunami of the Lonestar State. At least for flipping the U.S. Senate seat, the answer is a clear no.More than 364,000 Californians moved to Texas from 2018 to 2023 according to Internal Revenue Service migration data, and we estimate that less than one third of the voting-age population were Democrats before they headed to the Lonestar State based on the latest review of interstate voter roll data. Democrat James Talarico of Texas won the Senate seat by nearly 1.2 million votes against his main opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican with close ties to President Donald Trump.
Even if we assume that every former Californian was a registered voter in Texas, then about 103,000 of the over 364,000 who moved from California to Texas were likely registered Democrats. And if every single Democrat in this model turned out and voted for Talarico, it would amount to just about 10% of his margin of victory.Other analyses back this up: About half of the Californians who moved to Arizona or Texas in the past few years said they were conservative, according to a 2023 Stanford University study. And the Public Policy Institute of California found that conservatives in California tended to head to right-leaning states.
In our analysis, every county in Texas shifted between 7 to 70 percentage points in support of Talarico compared to the 2024 presidential election, when Trump, a Republican, handedly carried the state. The five counties with the largest swing toward Democrats had fewer than one California transplant household per 1,000 households. That means that even if every California transplant hadn’t voted, Talarico still would have won.Overall, the counties with the highest rates of migration from California swung toward Talarico at levels similar to the whole state’s blue tilt toward Talarico compared to 2024. Again, that’s evidence that California transplants aren’t a major reason for Texas voters backing Talarico.

David Crockett, a political science professor at Trinity University in San Antonio, on residents who moved to Texas: “There is not an unusual or disproportionately Democratic skew.”




CalMatters Ideas Festival: 2027 Ideas Festival will expand to Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Francisco. One full day of candid conversations in each, with the leaders, innovators and changemakers shaping California’s future. Learn more.

Other Stories You Should Know


Mixed messages on tax measures


Members of the California Teachers Association and supporters of public education march to the state Capitol in Sacramento on May 22, 2019. Photo by Rich Pedroncelli, AP Photo




The Associated Press officially said that California voters on Friday approved Proposition 42, which bans new wealth taxes by barring taxes on personal property, business interests and financial investments. In combination with the defeat of the proposed billionaire tax, Prop. 40, voters reaffirmed that wealth for the ultrarich is protected.
So does that mean voters are wholly against taxation? Not exactly, write our CalMatters reporters.
The passage of Prop. 42 is somewhat tempered by both the defeat of Prop. 43, which would have made increasing taxes for local public services more difficult, and the success of Prop. 3, which makes permanent a tax on high-income earners to help fund schools.
The mixed outcome, experts say, shows that California voters embrace tax hikes — but only when they can ensure the money is funding tangible services they support.

Brandon Castillo, a ballot measure strategist in California: “Voters are willing to open up their wallet if they believe it’s for a good cause … and that it’s actually going to that place.”

Read more.



What’s next for CA’s death penalty?


An incarcerated person is escorted to their cell on death row at San Quentin State Prison on Aug. 16, 2016. Photo by Eric Risberg, AP Photo




Local prosecutors in California intend to continue to seek the death penalty, in the wake of Gov. Gavin Newsom commutation of more than 500 death row prisoners last week, reports CalMatters’ Jeanne Kuang.
Nearly 400 of those granted clemency still need approval from the California Supreme Court. But even if the high court approves all of Newsom’s commutations, the state is likely to slowly continue sending defendants to death row.
Jason Anderson, San Bernardino County’s district attorney, is one of several district attorneys who have said they’ll continue to push for death sentences when appropriate. Anderson argued that while he respects differences of opinion on capital punishment, the governor should have considered each case individually.

Anderson: “You have a law on the books that’s essentially been overridden by one person.”

Anderson has also filed a motion to unseal the criminal records of some of the condemned prisoners from San Bernardino County, so the details of their crimes and what he described as their “recidivist nature” are public. name: Kansas Reflector
title: Health, legal organizations push for changes to medical debt regulations
description: TOPEKA — A statewide health organization is coordinating efforts to change the way Kansans burdened with medical debt are treated by providers and the legal system. “We see people avoiding even getting care if they know that they’re going to incur medical debt,” said April Holman, executive director of Alliance for a Healthy Kansas, at […]
text:
Casey Johnson, director of advocacy and innovation at Kansas Legal Services, spoke Tuesday about the burden medical debt places on Kansans and systemic changes that might help. Alliance for a Healthy Kansas held a convening to discuss what could be done in the state. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
TOPEKA — A statewide health organization is coordinating efforts to change the way Kansans burdened with medical debt are treated by providers and the legal system.
“We see people avoiding even getting care if they know that they’re going to incur medical debt,” said April Holman, executive director of Alliance for a Healthy Kansas, at a Tuesday meeting in Topeka. “We know that when there is medical debt putting strain on those family budgets, that means that there is less ability to afford housing and food and transportation.”
One in five Kansans lives in a household burdened by medical debt, she said. The alliance, which represents 130 organizations concerned about affordable healthcare, is known for working to expand Medicaid in Kansas.
Now it is pulling together groups that are interested in changing how medical debt affects families and want to look at data and best practices that could be put into Kansas legislation.
The alliance began with five community listening sessions in October and a survey to hear concerns about medical costs and debt, said Marissa Alcantar, policy and advocacy manager at the alliance. 
Worries about rising healthcare costs were the overarching theme, she said. Participants talked about decreased employer health insurance contributions, rising deductibles and out-of-pocket costs, and how overwhelming it is to receive multiple bills after care, Alcantar said. 
“Another big thing that we talked about was just the lack of transparency around the cost of healthcare,” she said. “People felt they didn’t have enough understanding or information on costs for services and how those services are billed to patients, how their insurance plays into that.”
Linda Sheppard, a principal strategist in state and federal health policy at the Kansas Health Institute, spoke Tuesday says data about medical debt is difficult to gather because court cases have to be examined individually. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
The data
Kansas Legal Services would like to see the government and hospitals make changes to medical debt practices. The nonprofit’s attorneys see the result of medical debt play out in the cases it represents, said Casey Johnson, director of advocacy and innovation at Kansas Legal Services.
They helped gather data about court cases, he said.
It isn’t an easy process, said Linda Sheppard, a principal strategist in state and federal health policy at the Kansas Health Institute. Each case has to be examined individually because there is no way to search the court computer systems to determine which collection cases were related to medical debt, she said.
They ended up choosing six counties and specific dates to pull a sampling, she said.
They found people in court for medical debt as low as $39 and a significant number of cases that resulted in default judgments, meaning the debtors did not show for court, Sheppard said. 
For example, on a single day in Shawnee County, there were 69 medical debt cases, 90% had no attorneys, and 81% of those resulted in default judgments, Johnson said. Twenty percent had orders for wage garnishment.
Legal representation
Johnson said there are real concerns about debt collection cases that don’t have representation. 
“KLS has been challenging wrongful debt collection cases by nonprofit hospitals, and so far we won every one,” he said. “We’ve settled on all of them because the rules are clear: You have to have a charity care policy, you have to widely distribute that, and you have to try to determine whether people qualify before you sue them, and that’s not happening.”
The legal service has represented 38 defendants who were sued by 16 nonprofit hospitals, Johnson said. They’ve had $400,000 forgiven or returned, if it had already been garnished. 
When people don’t show up for court dates or don’t have representation, they don’t know the regulations that are put on nonprofit hospitals, such as widely advertising their charity care policies. 
“These are, for the most part, people that are very low-income,” Johnson said. “One of the things that we see, too, when you’re filing a case in limited actions, which includes most debt collection cases, there’s no requirement if there’s any supporting documents. We see these bare bones petitions.”
Johnson shared examples of one- to two-page documents that were the only court submissions, with no detail of services received.
“They say sunshine is the best disinfectant, so we’re shining a light today on this epidemic of no attorneys in collection dockets,” said Matthew Keenan, Kansas Legal Services executive director. “Debt buyers are infiltrating this very receptive system that we have here, and they’re doing what Casey describes: no documentation.”
 
Serving debtors
The debtor must be notified about a court hearing, but there is no requirement in Kansas that debt collectors find a current address, Johnson said.
“What’ll happen is a lot of times debt collectors will have a four- or five-year-old address,” he said.
When they try to serve papers and no one is home, they post a copy on the front door and then mail a slip notifying them at that same address that they posted the paperwork on the front door.
“A lot of times, what we find is that our clients are very transient,” he said. “Years down the road, the debt collector finds out where they work or where they bank, and they start getting garnished, and that is the first time that somebody finds out that they were sued.”
Half of the people who end up with a default judgment, which occurs when one party in a lawsuit doesn’t show up and the judge makes a ruling against them, may not know they have been sued, Johnson said.
Their paychecks are garnished, which federal regulations set at a maximum of 25%, he said. Some states lowered that amount, but Kansas hasn’t. 
Karen Braman, senior vice president with the Kansas Hospital Association, said hospitals are concerned about medical debt.
“Costs have just absolutely surged in recent years, and that really started during the pandemic, and we saw issues with labor costs tripling, and some of that has not slowed down,” she said. “Many Kansans remain uninsured and underinsured due to Kansas not being a Medicaid expansion state. It’s only getting worse.”
Braman said hospital expenses are growing at about twice the rate of reimbursements.
“Our workforce accounts for more than half of hospital costs, about 60%,” she said. 
Many rural hospitals are at risk in Kansas, Braman said. 
“In the most recent Kansas data that we have, 81% of Kansas hospitals had an operating loss in 2024,” she said. “The average operating margin across every Kansas hospital in 2024 was minus 7%. So we’ve got a situation here where the pressures and the needs of high labor costs and the drug costs and supply chain costs are going up, yet our hospitals’ margins are shrinking, shrinking, shrinking, and their ability to even stay open in some of our rural communities is at risk.”
 
Best practices
Maanasa Kona, an associate research professor with the Center on Health Insurance at Georgetown University, spoke to the group about legislation and changes other states have taken to address medical debt problems.
She said states can consider protections at multiple levels in the healthcare process, such as requiring hospitals to share their charity care programs and assess patients for financial assistance, limiting the amount of interest that can be charged, and setting conditions or guardrails around when medical debt can be assigned to collection agencies.
The state also could limit wage garnishment, which is federally set at 25% of an individual’s salary. Some states have set up sliding scales, with smaller percentages for those who make less income, Kona said.
“Colorado requires screening of uninsured patients both for public coverage, that’s Medicaid, as well as for financial assistance, unless the patient declines,” she said. “At an earlier point, so that before a bill can be sent off to collections, insured patients in Colorado can also request screening.”
It is important to take as much of the burden as possible off of patients, Kona said.
“They’re already clearly in a tough time of their lives, and then putting the onus on them to become aware of these processes, to fill out the paperwork, and to advocate for themselves might be a bridge too far,” she said.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Commentary: Response to national ground stop highlights errors in public reassurance, says USC expert
description: Thousands of travelers were stranded on Nov. 13, 2026, when the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all domestic flights in the U.S. because of what they said were failures in decades-old air traffic communications systems. Crisis communications expert Shannon A. Bowen, a scholar at the University of South Carolina’s College of Information and Communica[...]
text:
A plane prepares to land at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Thousands of travelers were stranded on Nov. 13, 2026, when the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all domestic flights in the U.S. because of what they said were failures in decades-old air traffic communications systems. Crisis communications expert Shannon A. Bowen, a scholar at the University of South Carolina’s College of Information and Communications, spoke with The Conversation’s Politics and Legal Affairs Editor, Naomi Schalit, about how the Trump administration handled the first day of the crisis.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Is there a first principle in crisis communications?
The first principle would be to react quickly and react with accuracy, react with everything you know at the moment, truthfully, but always react quickly.
Because if you delay until you gather information, a vacuum will ensue. Information fills that vacuum that may not be accurate.
And so that’s the enemy of accurate crisis communication, but you want to always speak quickly and be the most authoritative and definitive source, even if very little information is known.
What did we see on the day of the ground stop?
A crisis unfolded and to the administration’s credit, they did react very quickly, in a way that offered the information that was known at the time, even though not a lot was known about why the ground stop was issued until later.
You’re speaking about the short press conference that afternoon with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin?
He did keep saying that nothing nefarious was at hand. And for a crisis communication scholar, you would not want to introduce the idea that something nefarious was at hand, unless, indeed, something nefarious was at hand.
So, by the very act of introducing this concept and this idea, I think the talking point, “Nothing nefarious,” then went across multiple networks, and it became the center of a controversy rather than quelling a controversy.
By saying nothing nefarious is at hand, that indeed confirmed something nefarious was at hand, even if the nefariousness was only the mismanagement of the air traffic control systems routers that they claimed caused the problem. By introducing this idea, I believe it did bring to mind that there may be other state actors behind whatever happened, that it could be a cyber attack.
It would have been better to say, “We have evidence that this was not a cyber attack but a hardware failure.”
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin tells reporters that there was no indication of ‘nefarious’ activity causing the nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, 2026.
How did the later press conference with Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy go from your perspective as an expert on crisis communications?
They handled the questions that they received correctly. They told us as much information as they knew.
However, they did seem to downplay the extent of this crisis, because we have to remember the traveling public is not just people trying to get to business meetings.
We had football teams stranded.
Now football Saturday, all over the SEC, has been disrupted. And there’s probably disruption in other areas of the country, but to us in the South, SEC football is almost a religious experience on Saturday.
Luckily, the University of South Carolina football team had already flown out.
But our marching band was stuck in this crisis, and so we have a lot of ripple effects from something like this happening, and it definitely says to me that this was an emergency situation. It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale.
If it were simply routers being overloaded, as we’ve been told, why wouldn’t they already know this situation and restart those routers the night before or over Friday night after most of the traveling public is out of the air?
What was Mullin’s and Duffy’s job when they got out there? What did they need to do?
To inform the public about the danger, why this happened, the extent of the problem, and what they’re doing to remediate the problem.
We keep hearing that they’re asking for $30 billion and more to repair the whole infrastructure for the air traffic control system, which is great, but what are they doing right now?
How do we know that flights in the air, right this minute, are any safer than the ones yesterday, a minute before the ground stop? Do we have that information? I don’t feel confident that they addressed that question appropriately.
I don’t think that the traveling public entirely feels safe at this point or adequately informed that they will arrive at their destination.
Press conference with Markwayne Mullin and Sean Duffy on Nov. 13, 2026.
They introduced politics into the press conference as well, didn’t they?
It’s something that they have the prerogative to do. They are both political appointees and members of the Cabinet. So I understand that aspect, but I really wish they had addressed the traveling public’s concerns more overtly before making it political, that they need more money to fix this.
We know they need more money to fix it, and I’m sure the American taxpayers are aware of the problem and willing to fund those corrections. But the more expedient issues would be, what about all these people who were stuck in airports?
Were there warning signs for this crisis?
I believe there were.
We had another ground stop about three years ago, due to air traffic control problems, and that is what we call in crisis communications a “prodrome,” a warning sign of larger impending problems. When you see these types of warning signs, it really gives us a reason to think it’s going to get worse.
Duffy did say on Nov. 13 that, because of the condition of the air traffic infrastructure, “you will have more” ground stoppages. If you had a piece of advice for the administration regarding their future communications, what would you tell them?
I would say to communicate in advance as much as possible, so if you’re even considering a ground stop, it may be a good idea to put out a public notice so that people don’t go to the airport on a vacation flight, maybe they delay that for a week or two.
It might also be a good idea to speak with the airline industry representatives and say, “Here’s what we’re thinking. Can you work with us? How can we make this better for the traveling public?”
Also, if 17 of 22 routers were malfunctioning, could we have had a partial ground stop at only the affected airports, rather than a nationwide stop?
My silly last question: Do crisis communications experts have any theories about Friday the 13th?
We consider it more of a superstition, but I have noticed that there does tend to be a lot of activity on Friday the 13th. It might be placebo effect, it might be because we expect something bad to happen and we’re looking for it. But that day does seem to always have some type of activity.
This is also when organizations release bad news, oftentimes, they say, “Let’s hold it until Friday the 13th, because bad news is expected.” People will assume, on Friday the 13th, that negative things are going to come out, so the shock value won’t be as much.
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: Michigan’s new lawmakers must deliver on affordability
description: Last week, at least 4.8 million Michiganders cast their ballots, and preliminary reports certainly indicate a record-breaking turnout. In January, a new governor will take office and a new Legislature will be sworn in, including many lawmakers who will step into their roles for the first time. But whatever your opinion of the results, things […]
text:
Michigan Capitol building. (Photo by Susan J. DemasLast week, at least 4.8 million Michiganders cast their ballots, and preliminary reports certainly indicate a record-breaking turnout. In January, a new governor will take office and a new Legislature will be sworn in, including many lawmakers who will step into their roles for the first time. But whatever your opinion of the results, things did not magically change on election day.
It’s no secret that “affordability” was a key theme during campaign season, but for Michiganders, the affordability crisis has been brewing for some time. All around the state, from Detroit to Ironwood, people continue to face stagnant wages and higher costs for basics like food, housing, and childcare.
Our new administration and lawmakers must take note that affordability is more than a line on campaign mailers. Michiganders need them to make economic security a top priority.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The median wage in Michigan has increased by just 3.87% since 1978 when adjusted for inflation. According to the 2026 United for ALICE report, 1.63 million Michigan households — 40% of the state — are either in poverty or struggling to make ends meet. Most of them are working, but not able to get ahead. A recent report from the Michigan League for Public Policy explored the affordability crisis and identified important solutions. We hope our new leaders will take note.
Let’s address work. A full-time job should cover rent, food, and utilities, but for many workers in Michigan, it doesn’t. A living wage is vital if we want to keep families and communities strong. Beyond wages, Michiganders need to know that their job is safe if they need time to recover from a serious illness, to welcome a new child, or to take care of a loved one. A statewide paid family and medical leave program will strengthen economic security, support the workforce, and improve health for parents, children and caregivers.
Costs are clearly a significant barrier for many, and not just due to recent spikes caused by tariffs and inflation. Childcare, for example, has been out of reach for many families for decades. Right now, for a full-time worker earning minimum wage, infant care in a center eats up over 49% of their household budget. That’s $14,000 per year to care for just one child. And at the same time, childcare workers are woefully underpaid and receive few benefits. The state can dedicate revenue for childcare and invest directly in the early childhood workforce.
Crowd gathered in Lansing for the Michigan United Coalition’s annual Capitol Day and Mothering Justice Action Fund’s annual Mamas March. April 29, 2026 | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance
Childcare isn’t the only cost creating roadblocks for families. Housing costs are skyrocketing, with the median Michigan rent increasing 31.5% since 2019. It’s time to slow the pace of housing costs, improve the supply of housing and make sure tenants have the protections they need to stay in their homes. But housing expenses don’t end at the monthly payment. Utility bills also continue to rise, driven by aging infrastructure and increased equipment prices. The state can make sure providers are able to maintain services without passing the burden on to households.
Along with enacting new solutions, lawmakers also have a responsibility to protect the programs that already work. Medicaid and SNAP keep millions of Michiganders healthy and fed, but our new leaders need to push back on the federal cuts and red tape that are putting both programs at risk and work to mitigate the harm from these changes.
Rx Kids, which gives cash to new moms and babies, has shown excellent results in health and economic security and should be expanded statewide. And we know that the federal Child Tax Credit (CTC)  has a history of reversing poverty — it’s time to create a state-level CTC to help families make ends meet.
We know this work is hard, and we know Michigan will have to pay for it. That starts with looking at our tax system, which needs to be modernized to generate more revenue. In the short term, that can mean raising taxes on unhealthy habits and industries like tobacco and vape products, as well as gambling. Longer term, it could mean a true overhaul of the current flat tax, which benefits wealthy corporations and individuals while leaving workers with low incomes to pay an unfair share.
The election on November 3 answered the question of who will have a seat in the Capitol, but we hope that January will allow us to see true leadership. Lawmakers will not agree on every detail, nor should they. But they must agree that solving Michigan’s affordability crisis should be their number one job.
