name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Flying blind: How the EPA let a key chemical detection program unravel
description: The program was designed to respond around the clock to emergencies involving toxic chemicals, oil spills and radiation.
text:
Black smoke rises from the Smitty's Supply Inc. facility in Roseland after an Aug. 22, 2025, explosion. (Photo by John Gardner of the Tangipahoa Parish Sheriff's Office)This story is from Floodlight, a non-profit newsroom that investigates the powers stalling climate action. Sign up for Floodlight’s newsletter here.
When an ammonia leak outside a hotel in Weatherford, Oklahoma, injured 74 people last November, the federal government’s chemical-detection plane stayed on the ground.
When a fire tore through a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, in March, the plane sat idle.
And when massive blasts killed two workers at an industrial recycling plant in Toledo, Ohio in August, it stayed put, despite a fire surrounding tanks of flammable solvents.
“Ten years ago, it would have gone to all of them,” said Mark Thomas, a former U.S. Environmental Protection Agency official who for years managed the airborne detection effort.
The program, known as ASPECT, was designed to respond around the clock to emergencies involving toxic chemicals, oil spills and radiation. The plane’s sensors could identify chemicals in the air within minutes, giving emergency responders crucial information about the dangers nearby communities face.
The EPA’s ASPECT plane, shown in 2010, was designed to fly over chemical emergencies and quickly identify pollutants in the air. Three former program insiders told Floodlight the program has deteriorated to the point where it is now of little use. (Photo by Eric Vance/EPA)
For more than two decades, the plane has flown over many of the country’s worst disasters, from New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina to the deadly West Fertilizer explosion in Texas to the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico.
But since early 2021, the single-engine Cessna has responded to just seven emergencies. And former ASPECT scientists said two of those missions — the 2023 train derailment that sent toxic clouds over East Palestine, Ohio, and the 2025 fire at Smitty’s Supply in Louisiana — were badly mismanaged.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At Smitty’s, the EPA declared the air safe, but a former ASPECT scientist later found toxic chemicals the agency had missed. And the agency’s inspector general is now auditing the response to the East Palestine derailment, including the data behind its public assurances about air quality.
Now — at a time when chemical emergencies are increasing — the plane can no longer do its job. In June, the EPA Inspector General found the plane’s systems can’t identify chemicals within minutes, as designed. Instead the process takes about a week, far too long to help anyone on the ground who’s deciding whether to evacuate.
The EPA said the plane’s chemical sensors are wearing out and expects replacements to be working by mid-2027.
But five people who helped build and run the program told Floodlight that the EPA is fixing the wrong problem. The old sensors still work, they said. What the agency lost, in their view, is the initiative and expertise that made the program a powerful tool when disaster struck. Replacing the old sensors, they warn, could leave the EPA even less capable of detecting hazardous chemicals in an emergency.
“I fear that the public is at risk,” said Robert Kroutil, a longtime ASPECT scientist who helped develop the program and later became a whistleblower. “It’s such an important program, and they’ve allowed it to waste away to nothing.”
The EPA did not respond to Floodlight’s requests for an interview or questions about ASPECT’s decline, its handling of emergencies, the replacement of its sensors and allegations of mismanagement by former program scientists and managers.
Robert Kroutil, a former EPA contractor, helped develop the software for the agency’s chemical-sensing aircraft. Kroutil later became a whistleblower, raising concerns about the deterioration of the government program. (Photo courtesy of Robert Kroutil)
A promising start
The country’s need for a chemical-sensing plane grew from the smoldering, toxic debris in Manhattan on Sept. 11, 2001, when the EPA’s monitoring trucks were stranded on the wrong side of the Hudson River, unable to cross after bridges and tunnels into the city closed.
Kroutil was a program manager for the Department of Defense at the time, leading a research team that had developed the technology that would become ASPECT, short for Airborne Spectral Photometric Environmental Collection Technology.
The military transferred the program to the EPA for use in detecting hazardous chemicals during civilian emergencies.
It became a critical tool for emergency responders over the next 20 years.
For 72 hours after Hurricane Katrina struck, it was the only emergency response aircraft flying over New Orleans, where it helped locate a missing 55-gallon drum of potentially lethal chloroacetic acid.
During the Deepwater Horizon disaster, it became a key tool for tracking oil slicks in the Gulf of Mexico.
And when a fire engulfed 15 massive tanks at a chemical storage terminal east of Houston in 2019, the ASPECT plane helped emergency responders track the plume, which contained the carcinogen benzene.
Richard Lawhorn, an assistant chief with Harris County’s hazardous materials response team in Texas, said the plane could detect chemicals at elevations beyond the reach of ground crews and survey a much wider area in a short time.
“They’re monitoring the products we can’t reach,” he said.
Firefighters in Harris County, Texas, work to cool equipment during a 2019 chemical storage terminal fire east of Houston. The EPA’s ASPECT plane flew over the site to detect hazardous chemicals released into the air by the massive blaze. (Photo courtesy of Harris County Fire Marshal’s Office)
The program’s success lay in its intellectual rigor: Kroutil and the program’s radiological lead held Ph.Ds., as did Mark Thomas, the former EPA official. The team wrote the code, designed the mounts that held gear, and analyzed the raw data themselves.
“We were very, very hands-on and intimately familiar with every part of that aircraft,” said Thomas, who later went to work for a company that develops chemical-sensing technology.
“I think that’s changed now.”
How the program lost its way
The decline began with the departures of key ASPECT personnel during President Donald Trump’s first administration.
As part of an agency reorganization, the EPA told the program’s staff in 2019 that they had to relocate to Texas, where the plane was based, or face termination, documents show.
The mandate was unnecessary, according to Thomas, because the program had been designed for remote operation. Rather than leave his elderly parents in Kansas, he retired. Then, ASPECT’s radiological lead left the division, and the engineer who helped build and manage the plane’s sensors accepted a demotion to stay in Kansas.
According to Kroutil and two of his former colleagues, the EPA then failed to fill those vacancies with scientists who had any experience with airborne chemical detection.
“They lost the institutional knowledge of the program, and quite frankly, lost the momentum of the program,” Thomas said.
During its first two decades, the plane flew almost 80 emergency missions — an average of roughly four a year. In the past five years, however, it has flown an average of just one a year.

In October, hundreds were evacuated — and more than 50 were treated at hospitals — when a 5,500-gallon industrial tank in Toledo leaked glycidyl methacrylate, a chemical used in making plastics that is a probable carcinogen suspected of causing genetic defects. It was one of at least 80 chemical emergencies this year that the plane did not respond to.
The decline comes as accidental chemical releases are becoming more common. The U.S. Chemical Safety Board tracked 133 last year, up from 83 in 2021.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, is proposing to roll back federal safeguards designed to prevent chemical disasters, including requirements for some plants to undergo independent safety audits and provide hazard information to nearby communities.
Former ASPECT program managers said they used to actively track chemical emergencies and urge EPA on-scene coordinators — who manage environmental emergencies — to deploy the plane. After they left, that proactive approach vanished: The plane stayed in a Texas hangar until coordinators requested it, they said.
Scott Smith, an independent environmental tester who’s often called on by local communities to investigate chemical contamination after industrial accidents, said ASPECT could help him target his soil and water testing by mapping the path of chemical plumes. Deployed regularly, he said, the plane could save lives.
Instead, “It’s being shut down and not used.”
Missed opportunity in East Palestine
On Feb. 3, 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight train carrying the carcinogen vinyl chloride and other hazardous chemicals derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, near the Pennsylvania border.
As fires from the derailment smoldered, emergency responders feared an explosion — and made the controversial decision to vent and burn five railcars containing vinyl chloride, sending a towering plume over the town.
ASPECT missed the vent-and-burn operation, and its services weren’t requested until more than two days after the initial disaster. Even then, it was used sparingly. Despite the derailment being one of the nation’s worst chemical disasters in years, Kroutil said, the plane collected just eight minutes of chemical data when it finally flew over East Palestine on February 7 — a fraction of what it typically gathered during an emergency.
A February 2023 aerial view of the train derailment wreckage in East Palestine, Ohio. (Screenshot from NTSB B-roll recorded Feb. 5, 2023)
Had the plane been deployed earlier — or flown over the site en route to Pittsburgh, the nearest major airport — its thermal detection equipment might have helped determine that the tank cars were not in danger of exploding, Kroutil later said in an affidavit.
The National Transportation Safety Board later concluded the vent-and-burn operation had been unnecessary. It found no evidence of the dangerous chemical reaction that Norfolk Southern and its contractors said threatened an explosion. Temperature readings showed the railcars were cooling.
An EPA inspector general investigation later found a series of errors in the East Palestine response: The agency had poorly documented its procedures and failed to adequately inform emergency responders of the plane’s capabilities. The on-scene coordinator, who didn’t request the plane until two days after the derailment, wrongly believed ground-level monitoring would provide better data.
Frustrated by how EPA officials were running the program, Kroutil retired. Two of his colleagues also left, further draining the program’s pool of experience and expertise.
Then came Smitty’s.
‘It was raining oil’
On Aug. 22, 2025, a massive explosion ripped through Smitty’s Supply, a facility that blended and packaged oil and other engine lubricants in Roseland.
Less than four miles away, Ronnie Polezcek and his family heard something hitting their roof that afternoon. At first, they thought it was raindrops.
But when they walked outside, Polezcek said, “It was just like it was raining oil.”
The dark residue covered the family’s 23-acre farm. Polezcek said he had to burn his hay, move his cows temporarily to Mississippi and replace a metal roof that could not be scrubbed clean. Two of his cows miscarried soon afterward, he said, and a veterinarian found arsenic in one of them. Polezcek sued Smitty’s in September 2025. The lawsuit has been consolidated with an ongoing class-action case.
The Smitty’s fire burned for nearly two weeks, sending a huge plume of smoke into the air. Local authorities ordered a one-mile evacuation around the plant, and the EPA dispatched ASPECT — the plane’s first emergency deployment in 19 months.
The agency didn’t publicly post findings from the ASPECT flights until August 31, nine days after the fire began. Those reports show the air around Smitty’s contained ozone and three other pollutants but at levels considered safe.
A later analysis of the raw flight data, though, told a very different story.
The destroyed Smitty’s Supply facility in Roseland nearly six weeks after it caught fire and exploded. (Photo by Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)
Working with the Government Accountability Project, a nonprofit that advocates for whistleblowers, Kroutil obtained data from ASPECT’s third flight over the disaster area. He said it took him weeks to analyze it, doing by hand what the plane’s software was designed to do in minutes.
Kroutil identified high concentrations of the neurotoxicant toluene and the carcinogens trichloroethylene and naphthalene, among other toxic chemicals. He concluded that the levels of toluene were so high they could have put nearby communities at risk.
Many of the findings also matched what Smith, the independent environmental tester, detected in soil and water after the fire.
The EPA later acknowledged a similar problem, according to records that the Government Accountability Project obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request.
In a May 2026 email, an EPA manager said some target chemicals might have been present in data from the third flight but weren’t flagged at the time the data was collected. The manager suggested that deterioration of the aging sensors might have contributed to the failure.
More than a year later, Polezcek said, the residue still coats much of his property. When his grandchildren play outside, he said, they come back inside with “little black feet.”
“That’s my biggest concern,” he told Floodlight. “What is it doing to them?”
Polezcek believes officials should have evacuated a larger area.
“I really think it was a pitiful job,” he said. “They just kept saying, ‘There’s nothing to worry about, you’re good to go.’”
EPA’s ASPECT aircraft team members process the day’s data from flights over the 2010 BP Oil Spill in the Gulf of Mexico. Left to right, Paul Kudarauskas, John Cardarelli, Bob Kroutil, Tim Curry and Mark Thomas. (Photo by Eric Vance/EPA)
The wrong fix?
In June, the EPA Inspector General confirmed that Kroutil’s warnings were justified: The plane could no longer provide chemical-monitoring data within five minutes. 
Instead, scientists had to conduct manual analysis that would take about a week. The EPA also failed to tell on-scene coordinators that the program isn’t working as designed. 
EPA officials blamed the delays on old sensors. The agency bypassed competitive bidding to award a Canadian company, Telops, a $1.7 million contract for replacement sensors designed for several applications, including gas detection and mineral mapping. Integrating the new sensors won’t be complete until “early to mid-2027,” according to the EPA. 
In contract documents, the EPA cited peer-reviewed studies showing the Telops sensors had been field-tested and proven. But much of the research on the new equipment has focused on tracking methane leaks, not the wide range of toxic chemicals released during complex industrial emergencies.
Five people formerly involved with ASPECT have raised concerns that the new sensors will be less capable than the old ones at detecting hazardous chemicals during industrial emergencies. 
Exosens, the parent company of Telops, told Floodlight that its system and the old one use “different measurement architectures.”
The new sensors, it says, can identify hundreds of chemicals and distinguish chemical plumes from surrounding objects. 
Chris Manning, an infrared spectrometer expert with no ties to Telops, the EPA or the firm where Thomas now works, said the new Telops sensors could complement ASPECT’s older sensors but would be a poor replacement. They are slower, less sensitive, and less suited to moving targets, he said. 
“To say, ‘We’re just going to replace these other two instruments’ … I mean, that’s ludicrous,” he said.
The old sensors had problems, too. Their artificial intelligence software had not been retrained after an electrical malfunction several years ago, Kroutil and Thomas said. In early 2023, contract scientists with the program presented the EPA with a plan to retrain the software, emails show. But the EPA never took the required steps, Kroutil said.
He and his former colleagues said they have no confidence that the new sensors will fix the problem. They expect the program to deteriorate further. 
In the affidavit submitted to the Government Accountability Project, Kroutil offered a dim prognosis: “Unless major changes are made at EPA and with the ASPECT program, it is not going to get any better and EPA will be flying blind.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: New Arkansas museum chronicles worst maritime disaster in US history
description: The 1865 explosion of the steamship Sultana in the Mississippi River killed nearly 1,200 people and remains the deadliest maritime disaster in U.S. history. But the ship isn’t as widely known as other doomed boats, such as the Lusitania or the Titanic. A new museum in east Arkansas aims to change that, with an array […]
text:
Exhibits on display at the Sultana Disaster Museum in Marion, Arkansas on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026 (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)The 1865 explosion of the steamship Sultana in the Mississippi River killed nearly 1,200 people and remains the deadliest maritime disaster in U.S. history. But the ship isn’t as widely known as other doomed boats, such as the Lusitania or the Titanic.
A new museum in east Arkansas aims to change that, with an array of artifacts, records and high-tech displays chronicling one of the deadliest but little known chapters of American history.
The Sultana Disaster Museum, which opened Saturday in Marion, is housed in a renovated 1939 school gymnasium and auditorium. The 21,000-square-foot, $11 million facility walks visitors through the events leading up to the steamship disaster, the explosion itself and the aftermath. 
A model of the steamship Sultana on display at the Sultana Disaster Museum in Marion, Arkansas on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026 (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)
“It’s an instructive lesson in humanity in so many ways — the worst of humanity and the best of humanity,” Jeff Kollath, executive director of the museum, said during a preview of its exhibits last week.
The Sultana’s sinking, which occurred early in the morning on April 27, 1865, is often overlooked because it occurred during one of the most momentous months in the nation’s history. It occurred within weeks of the Civil War’s end and Abraham Lincoln’s assassination. 
The Sultana had a capacity of 376, but was overloaded with more than 2,000 people — mostly Union soldiers who had been prisoners of war and were headed home after being held in captivity. Exhibits detail how a boat captain and a Union army officer conspired to put thousands of people in danger for their own personal gain.
But the museum also details how communities on both sides of the Mississippi River responded to the disaster, going out into the darkness to rescue survivors.
“It’s a story of reclamation, human reclamation, in some ways,” Kollath said. “History like this, Civil War history especially, is much more interesting when you talk about the individuals. You’ve got 2,130 stories you can tell.”
Those stories are accessible to visitors through touchscreen displays that include  photos and stories about each of the ship’s passengers. Museum guests can also look up detailed drawings and layouts of the steamship on touchscreens.
Artifacts recovered from the disaster, including a brass letter opener, an engineer’s wrench and bricks, are displayed. A large model of the steamship and a 1835 steam engine salvaged from another steamboat are also featured. 



Images of alligators figure prominently in the museum and its gift shop, a nod to a large pet alligator that was kept in a wooden box on the deck of the ship by the crew. A soldier who survived the Sultana disaster, William Lugenbeal, said he was saved by using the box as a float in the river. Souvenirs that Lugenbeal collected in the years following, including a cigar box with a pewter alligator, are among the items museum visitors can see.
The museum features interactive exhibits including videos depicting the ship’s chief engineer, and a simulation of steamships racing in the river.
The museum was the result of the work of descendants of Sultana’s victims and survivors who had pushed for a way to chronicle the disaster and educate others about it. It started with a small display in Marion in 2012 and three years later a small museum opened in the town.
“The story is so important and the lessons it teaches, lessons of unintended consequences of corruption, of greed, the unintended consequences of political favoritism,” said John Fogleman, a retired judge who heads the Sultana Historical Preservation Society. “All of this is impacted by our museum.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: After star-studded Denver summit, Colorado Democrats hope party leaders will return in 2028
description: The splashy What’s Next conference that wrapped up in Denver over the weekend might have served largely as an audition for Democratic rising stars eyeing the 2028 presidential primary — but it doubled as another for the Mile High City, where Colorado Democrats hope the primary’s eventual winner will be formally nominated two years from […]
text:
Denver Mayor Mike Johnston speaks on stage at the What's Next conference hosted by Majority Democrats in Denver on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)The splashy What’s Next conference that wrapped up in Denver over the weekend might have served largely as an audition for Democratic rising stars eyeing the 2028 presidential primary — but it doubled as another for the Mile High City, where Colorado Democrats hope the primary’s eventual winner will be formally nominated two years from now.
Denver is among three finalists, along with Boston and Philadelphia, being considered by national Democrats to host the next Democratic National Convention, scheduled to be held Aug. 7 to 10, 2028.
Denver Mayor Mike Johnston, a Democrat who has led the city’s DNC bid, opened and closed two days of main-stage programming at Mission Ballroom, welcoming party leaders, consultants, influencers and media to the festival-like event put on by the political action committee Majority Democrats.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Denver I call the home of the open frontier,” Johnston said. “It’s a place where it’s open to anyone, but there’s opportunity for everyone.”
It was a Denver-centric spin on the message that Majority Democrats, an influential and deep-pocketed group launched in 2025, believes will resonate with voters across the country. Among its founding members are Johnston and U.S. Rep. Joe Neguse of Lafayette, who opened a busy day of speeches and panels Friday with a florid address calling on Democrats to do what it takes to “save the country.”
“I remain enthralled by the simplest of prescriptions for what ails our civic society today,” said Neguse. “It is a paradoxical truth that perhaps the most glaring absence in our society is of a fundamental concept, a value, an idea that once defined our country: opportunity.”
‘What’s Next’ for Democrats? A 2028 supermajority, party leaders say in Denver.

Among the many rumored Democratic presidential hopefuls speaking at the What’s Next summit were former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, Rep. Ro Khanna of California and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro.
Colorado Sen. Michael Bennet, a Majority Democrats member and a former presidential candidate himself, also appeared on stage at the conference, as did Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, the two-term attorney general who defeated Bennet in the 2026 primary for Colorado governor.
The convening of so many party leaders in Denver, a little over a week after a nationwide Democratic landslide in the 2026 midterms, was no accident. Johnston told 9News he’d “pitched (Majority Democrats) to host it here almost a year ago.” Colorado, the What’s Next conference’s website said, is “proof of what’s possible.”
“In 20 years it went from reliably red to purple to blue — not by accident, but by investing in people and institutions, building a coalition and then delivering,” said Majority Democrats.
The 2028 DNC will mark 20 years since the last time the event was held in the Mile High City, when former President Barack Obama accepted a historic nomination in front of a crowd of more than 80,000 people at what was then known as Invesco Field at Mile High.
Johnston invoked Colorado’s last two decades of political transformation at Democrats’ election night watch party, also held at Mission Ballroom, on Nov. 3. Obama’s 2008 victory in Colorado marked just the second time since 1964 that the Centennial State had awarded its electoral votes to a Democrat. Although it had nearly as reliable a record of electing Democratic governors during the same period, Republican Gov. Bill Owens had recently won two terms in office, and the state Legislature had also been in GOP hands for decades.
“Folks in this state said, ‘You know what? We can do better. We can organize. We can mobilize. We can make a difference,’” said Johnston, a former school principal who served in the Colorado Senate from 2009 to 2017. “In 2004, we won back both the (state) House and Senate chambers. In 2006, we won back the governor’s race. And then in 2008, we invited the country to Denver to nominate a Black guy with a funny name named Barack Obama, who took back the White House.”
“We might just prepare again to invite the whole country back to Denver in 2028 and elect a new Democratic president,” Johnston said to cheers. “Are you ready?”

title: Fossil dig pit could add another learning experience on North Dakota Capitol grounds
description: A fossil dig pit on the Capitol grounds in Bismarck may soon stimulate young minds about the science of paleontology. During an October meeting of the Capitol Grounds Planning Commission, State Geologist Clint Boyd said the fossil dig sand box could accommodate about a dozen children at a time and would expand the offerings of […]
text:
Graphic rendering composed by Zerr Berg Architects of a proposed fossil dig pit next to the French Gratitude Train on the North Dakota Capitol grounds. (Illustration by Zerr Berg Architects/for OMB)A fossil dig pit on the Capitol grounds in Bismarck may soon stimulate young minds about the science of paleontology.
During an October meeting of the Capitol Grounds Planning Commission, State Geologist Clint Boyd said the fossil dig sand box could accommodate about a dozen children at a time and would expand the offerings of the North Dakota Geological Survey’s summer education programs.
“It’s envisioned as a supplement to our public fossil dig program in the summer that we run right now,” Boyd said.
The state Geological Survey invites North Dakotans to sign up for its public fossil digs across the state, but the minimum age for those events is age 10, he said.
“We’ve had a lot of requests for activities for kids under 10, especially if they are part of families that are going on the fossil dig and part of the family has to stay back,” Boyd said. 
Interior graphic rendering composed by Zerr Berg Architects of a proposed fossil dig pit next to the French Gratitude Train on the North Dakota Capitol grounds. (Illustration by Zerr Berg Architects/for OMB)
The dig pit could also benefit summer school programs, he said, where half the class is getting a tour of the Heritage Center and its paleontology collection while the other half is learning how to excavate fossils.
The sand box pit will be about 144 square feet and be enclosed with a roof and screened walls to keep animals from nesting inside. The commission will discuss the final design and cost during its November meeting, but preliminary estimates expect the project cost to be $120,000 to $250,000.
Boyd said the project cost will be split between donations already received and the leftover biennial budget of the state Geological Survey, which spent less than anticipated on excavation projects in 2026.
The fossil dig pit will be constructed next to the French Gratitude Train on the Capitol grounds, near the Military Gallery expansion at the Heritage Center.
The $78 million Military Gallery expansion will include new walking paths on the Capitol grounds that will connect to the area near the train car and the proposed fossil dig site.
Bill Peterson, director of the State Historical Society of North Dakota, said the idea for the fossil dig pit came up because the architects and planners were already “in the room” and constructing the Military Gallery.
“Clint (Boyd) came up with this way to engage different audiences in a way outside that we don’t currently have and it builds on the fact that the paleo collection is housed in the building downstairs,” Peterson said. “It’s kind of a continuation of paleo’s education outreach that I’m sure would be utilized by the Heritage Center and everybody else.”
If final approval is given by the commission in November, construction of the new fossil dig pit would begin in spring 2027.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Commentary: Tommy Tuberville, back on the attack
description: I’d like to give our incoming governor the benefit of the doubt. Really, I would. In most cases, officials deserve at least a limited grace period to show what they’re about. But Tommy Tuberville never allows doubt to linger. Give him a minute and his priorities and his contempt for many Alabamians become clear. That […]
text:
Alabama Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville speaks to supporters after declaring victory during an election night watch party at The Hotel at Auburn University on Nov. 3, 2026. (Larry Robinson for Alabama Reflector)I’d like to give our incoming governor the benefit of the doubt.
Really, I would. In most cases, officials deserve at least a limited grace period to show what they’re about.
But Tommy Tuberville never allows doubt to linger. Give him a minute and his priorities and his contempt for many Alabamians become clear.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That was evident in what appears to have been his first major speech since the election.
You could be forgiven if by the end of the fall campaign, you thought a Gov. Tuberville would spend his time and limited powers on affordability and local control. He endorsed repeal of the state grocery tax. Tuberville pivoted from praising data centers to saying he would protect local communities from them.
He released a policy agenda — a “playbook,” because the politician really wants you to think he’s still a coach — that emphasized affordability, business development and education. It also ignored his campaign’s previous calls for worshipping President Donald Trump, protecting guns and attacking transgender Alabamians.
A voter could think Tuberville got the message from voters and wanted to address their concerns. 
And then Tuberville spoke at a far-right event hosted by a far-right news outlet.
Did he talk about the cost of living? Based on the reporting, not really. Data centers? Nope. 
What did our governor-elect say? That Alabama would “stand with Israel.” (The Alabama governor does not conduct foreign policy, in case you were wondering.) That Trump, who Tuberville ghosted during the campaign, was a success. Tuberville also went off on a tirade about “gender studies,” demeaned the value of a four-year college education, and babbled about building a “shield” around Alabama against “socialist, Islamist propaganda.”
The play was affordability, but Tuberville called an audible into the culture war.
To take “the playbook” seriously, one had to assume that Tuberville enjoys policy and administration. He provided little evidence of that in his six years in the U.S. Senate. Instead, Tuberville has worked like a conservative influencer, often attacking many of the people he represents.
Back in 2022, Tuberville said descendants of enslaved people “do the crime.” That’s 1.3 million Alabamians right there.
Tuberville has called immigrants “garbage.” That’s 200,000 to 230,000 people in this state.
People who live in big cities? Rats, according to Tuberville. If you go by Alabama’s four biggest urban areas, that’s 800,000 people.
Muslims? He joined in attacks on a Hoover Islamic school and claims that Muslim Alabamians — who may number about 25,000 — would “try and overwhelm” a state of over 5.1 million people.
Transgender people? He wants them put in mental institutions and doctors who provide gender-affirming care to be arrested. Another 25,000 people.
Oh, and metro Huntsville is rife with socialists and communists. Now, I don’t know that socialist is necessarily an insult — Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. was one — but in Tuberville’s mind, it is. Another 500,000 people, per the U.S. Census.
And teachers. He attacked inner-city teachers in 2023, suggesting they couldn’t read or write. Take all teachers together, and you’ve got another 48,000 or so.
“A lot of you didn’t vote for me,” Tuberville said on election night. “I don’t understand why.”
I hope that list helps.
Tuberville defines himself by who he’s against, not what he’s for. That makes optimism about the incoming administration difficult. If you think the governor-elect can make a face turn and suddenly become a constructive and serious leader, let me ask: why?
How do you expect this man to find his way from racist statements and clout chasing to public service and thoughtful policy?
What makes you think he can be an effective governor? His campaign? That turned out to be a mess. He struggled to deliver a coherent message on data centers. He made a bizarre, distracting claim about furries on planes in a week when he rolled out a new education ad. Tuberville proposed sending the National Guard into Montgomery, an expensive idea that would do nothing for crime, threaten local residents and keep the city’s Democratic margins high into 2028.
Like all governors, Tuberville will be constitutionally weak compared to the Legislature. But Tuberville appears to think he’s a coach who can call the plays. That’s not how Alabama government works. Tuberville wants to expand the divisive CHOOSE Act, the state’s school voucher program. The powerful education budget chairs have signaled they don’t want to increase spending on the program. Tuberville has made promises to start cutting state income taxes — which pay teachers’ salaries — in a year when both state budgets are facing major challenges with health insurance.
Could the office magically transform Tuberville? Make him realize the governor is not a coach but one of many people in a collaborative process? Or focus his mind on something other than conservative media obsessions?
Sure. There’s always a chance.
But after seeing this man demean Alabamians for six years, I have my doubts.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: Question everything: To do otherwise sets the stage for disaster
description: Politicians desperately want to tighten their hold on power and control. They can’t be so blind as to not clearly see what’s so crystal clear to so many of us. And they can’t be so deaf as to not hear the cries of the oppressed they claim to represent.
text:
The West Virginia State Capitol. (Photo by Perry Bennett | West Virginia Legislative Photography)Realizing that the title of this commentary might be better utilized in the text of the commentary itself, I still chose to use the words in the title. The unsettling trend right now is to get along at all costs, choosing not to ruffle any feathers, upset the apple cart, and turn a blind eye to all that is unraveling around us, whether in our state or our country. And that’s exactly what West Virginia leadership and the country’s leadership hope we will do, if for no other reason than from sheer exhaustion.
Politicians desperately want to tighten their hold on power and control. They can’t be so blind as to not clearly see what’s so crystal clear to so many of us. And they can’t be so deaf as to not hear the cries of the oppressed they claim to represent.
I think about the troubling declining enrollment in West Virginia schools. I think of the rising cost of living for the basic needs alone. I think of the exodus of young West Virginians who yearn to stay but choose not to stay, knowing full well of the opportunities that wait for them outside our boundaries. I especially think of creatives whose passion for a good story, a moving score, and a reflective painting are all too often given so little of the limelight as to be barely discernible.
Recently, I questioned a publisher of a vast amount of my work who made the decision to no longer publish me because I disagreed with her and voiced my disagreement. I introduce this unsettling incident to tie in with what introduced this commentary. It’s a prime example of what happens when you question those with whom you disagree. 
This is an example of why the movement to no longer question those in power, knowing that so much of it will be received as a personal attack is in full force right now. It’s not personal. It’s business. And when we are of the ilk (as so many are right now) that we refuse to listen to someone’s concerns, refuse to invite someone’s unease, then we are crossing a line to inhabit space where only those in power, in control can reside. Indeed, very, very dangerous territory.
In the end, when the band stops playing, the occupants will all look the same, sound the same, and lead in the same way. It’s quite possible that our state, the world as we know it, is being cordoned off. Pay attention. Pay very close attention, because the days of a true democracy are  fading fast. Will you be silenced or will you use your voice?

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: KY universities caved to anti-DEI threats. Now they must answer for the damage.
description: The Chao Auditorium at the University of Louisville’s Ekstrom Library was packed. Students sat on the floor to make room and there was still standing room only. Many had to watch the livestream from overflow rooms. It was Oct. 28, and community members had gathered to listen to Ricky Jones, Ph.D. as he talked about […]
text:
Dr. Ricky Jones of the University of Louisville and Simmons College. (Photo by Bonnie Jean Feldkamp for Kentucky Lantern.)The Chao Auditorium at the University of Louisville’s Ekstrom Library was packed. Students sat on the floor to make room and there was still standing room only. Many had to watch the livestream from overflow rooms. It was Oct. 28, and community members had gathered to listen to Ricky Jones, Ph.D. as he talked about what has been happening to Black students and Black faculty at the University of Louisville.
Jones is the Dr. Charles Parrish, Jr. Distinguished University Scholar at Simmons College of Kentucky and Professor of Pan-African Studies at the University of Louisville. This was a Black community mass meeting.
The meeting location was purposeful. Jones said, “We very intentionally wanted to meet on this campus tonight, and dare this university to say we couldn’t.”
This may sound hyperbolic but when Jones laid out what Black students and faculty have lost in recent years alone, attendees understood that it was a real possibility.
In 2025, following Trump’s anti-DEI executive order, the U.S. Department of Education sent a letter to educational institutions, beginning “Dear Colleagues,” and threatened to withhold federal funds from institutions that did not gut their diversity, equity and inclusion objectives, claiming they were illegal. Jones quipped,  “The man ain’t got no love. Sent the thing out on Valentine’s Day.”
Then in Feb. of 2026, the letter was invalidated in court. However, damage was already done. The University of Louisville (along with hundreds of others across the country) scrambled to comply when they should have stood firm.
This debate is nothing new. Critical Race Theory was the big fear of 2021. The U.S. Supreme Court effectively repealed affirmative action in college admissions with its 2023 ruling, which spurred the denouncement of all things diversity, equity and inclusion. Piece by piece, equitable initiatives in American education have been chipped away, dialed back or dismantled.
That’s how change happens— good and bad— with a chip, a chip, a chip, then a fall.
Trump’s Department of Education hoped to dismantle DEI with its “Dear Colleagues” letter and in some ways it succeeded thanks to states passing anti-DEI legislation. In Kentucky, House Bill 4 passed in late March after the legislature overrode Gov. Beshear’s veto.
HB4 banned DEI offices, training and initiatives. It required institutions to eliminate existing DEI programs by June 30, 2025, and mandated annual reports on compliance. The bill also required public universities to develop policies promoting viewpoint neutrality.
However, the Trump administration pushed its anti-DEI agenda beyond the legal limits. The American Civil Liberties Union immediately challenged the “Dear Colleagues” letter in court and got a preliminary injunction in April of 2025 to block the threats from being enforced while the case proceeded. Universities should have followed the ACLU’s lead and challenged HB4 legally but they rolled over instead.
Then, In October 2025, a U.S. District Court ruled the “Dear Colleagues” letter violated the Administrative Procedure Act and violated the First Amendment.
The Chronicle of Higher Education, which has been tracking the dismantling of diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts since 2023, stated that “The pace of change ramped up in 2025,” following political pressure.
A litany of loss
Here is some of what Kentucky students have lost as reported by The Chronicle of Higher Education:
The University of Louisville canceled a graduation ceremony for LGBTQ graduates; eliminated four identity-based employee groups; renamed its Department of Inclusive Excellence to the Office of Access and Opportunity; and dissolved its Commission on the Status of Women and the Commission on Diversity and Racial Equity. Also, the Porter Scholarship which was originally set up exclusively for African American students, awarded only 18% of those scholarships to Black students for this year’s incoming class.
The University of Kentucky closed its Office of Institutional Diversity and replaced it with the Office for Community Relations only to then close the office completely one year later. UK canceled graduation ceremonies for first-generation college students, Black and LGBTQ+ students and it no longer requires employees to write diversity statements.
Northern Kentucky University closed its Office of Inclusive Excellence following the resignation of its chief diversity officer; renamed its Center for Student Inclusiveness to the Center of Community and Connections; eliminated the center’s African American, Latino and LGBTQA+ Student Initiatives; renamed its Educational Diversity and Access Scholarship to the Educational Access and Success Scholarship; stopped offering scholarships that consider race, color, national origin, sex, or religion; stopped coordinating orientations, mentoring programs, and graduation celebrations exclusively for certain groups of students; renamed its Inclusive Excellence Council to the Campus Community Council; cut off university funding for employee affinity groups; dissolved alumni affinity groups; and will not sponsor DEI training “that promotes differential treatment based on race, color, national origin, religion, or sex.”
Western Kentucky University established a committee to review around 50 course syllabi “to confirm that alternative viewpoints are presented alongside dominant perspectives, that learning objectives remain free of normative claims, and that course materials reflect a broad range of ideological perspectives;” prohibited faculty and staff from attending diversity, equity and inclusion specific conferences or trainings; adopted a viewpoint neutrality policy; and directed its Society of Black Alumni to remove “Black” from its name, prompting the organization to cut ties with the university.
Murray State University canceled an LGBTQ student-graduation ceremony; renamed its Pride Center to the Oakley Student Lounge; renamed its Women’s Center to the Oakley Resource Center; renamed its Office of Multicultural Initiatives to the Office of Student Enrichment, Academic Excellence, and Leadership; and adopted a viewpoint-neutrality policy.
Now, the “Dear Colleagues” letter is dead. In January, the government quietly withdrew its appeal. and a US District Court determined that the letter was legally void, and it cannot be enforced. The Department of Education’s threats were deemed illegal and unconstitutional.
Did the Kentucky universities reinstate the faculty, scholarships, programming and funding they undermined and removed?  No.
Did they lead the charge with legal action against racist state laws and challenge the fact that these laws now stand in direct conflict with federal law? No.
Did they at least recognize what they did was pre-emptive and unnecessary? Of course not.
Neither did hundreds of other universities across these United States. They shrugged their shoulders and continued on without rectifying anything.
Children deserve better from our institutions of higher education. State lawmakers and university administrators must be held accountable. Families, students and communities need to question every course of action. Universities have to acknowledge the harm done, the time and money wasted, and must restore what they have dismantled.
The “Dear Colleagues” letter served as an important test. One that Kenucky universities have failed miserably.
Throughout the conversation in that packed auditorium in October, Jones urged everyone present to not get distracted. This is not about anti-DEI. Just like it was not about CRT. Those are all distractions. Jones said, “What this is about, folks, is the reaffirmation and maintenance of white supremacy. Period.”
And, this iteration of white supremacy “is to roll back the gains of The Civil Rights Movement,” Jones said. Not just in the politically red state of Kentucky, but across the country.
We must all work to confront it and do our part to hold the predominantly white institutions that unnecessarily complied to the “Dear Colleagues” directive accountable.
Step one was Jones’ informational and educational session on how racism has played out over the decades at the University of Louisville. Education is the first step. Now, it’s time to organize.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Amazon pledges millions to cover in-demand career training at Virginia community colleges
description: Eligible community college students at select Virginia institutions could soon save money as they pursue credentials in high-demand fields like healthcare, information technology, advanced manufacturing and skill trades, after Amazon Web Services committed to investing “tens of millions” over the next several years in Virginia’s Community Colleges System. Th[...]
text:
A view from outside Rappahannock Community College in Warsaw, Va.. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Eligible community college students at select Virginia institutions could soon save money as they pursue credentials in high-demand fields like healthcare, information technology, advanced manufacturing and skill trades, after Amazon Web Services committed to investing “tens of millions” over the next several years in Virginia’s Community Colleges System.
The e-commerce and cloud computing company announced the deal on Thursday, capping off the 60th Anniversary Governor’s Luncheon, attended by local and state leaders, including Gov. Abigail Spanberger and five of her predecessors. Amazon did not provide a specific investment total or per-student amount during the event.
Officials said the Amazon Built Together Virginia Fund, the largest private sector investment in VCCS’s history, will be distributed to the colleges by the Virginia Foundation for Community College Education.
Brightpoint, Germanna, Laurel Ridge, Northern Virginia, Piedmont Virginia, Rappahannock, Reynolds, and Southside Virginia Community Colleges will be the first to offer the program covering costs including tuition, fees, books and certifications.

David Doré, VCCS chancellor, said in a statement that the 23-school system is grateful for Amazon’s investment, which helps strengthen Virginia’s future workforce’s connection to opportunity and employers.
“By helping cover costs that financial aid does not, this partnership removes a barrier for students ready to gain valuable skills and move into in-demand careers,” said Doré. “We’re grateful for Amazon’s investment in our students, our employers and the commonwealth.”
Amazon has also partnered with VCCS on workforce training, launching the world’s first cloud computing associate degrees at 13 VCCS colleges and offering hands-on training programs in fields like data center operations. 
Roger Wehner, vice president of economic development for Amazon Web Services, said the company has been part of Virginia’s communities for two decades after opening the first of 90 data centers in 2006 and investing more than $190 million in data centers, HQ2 and Virginia’s communities. 
He said investing in the commonwealth means investing in the future of the people who live here.
“Through Built Together, our community investment framework for the places where we operate data centers, we’re doubling down on that commitment and supporting Virginia’s Community Colleges so tens of thousands of Virginians can earn a degree or credential close to home and build on the skills that lead to long-term careers,” Wehner said. 
Spanberger and Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi, a former community college professor, attended the celebration, highlighting VCCS’s lasting impact in providing open access and economic mobility to Virginians. 
Five former state governors —George Allen, Tim Kaine, Bob McDonnell, Terry McAuliffe and Ralph Northam — shared how their administrations contributed to the system’s strength in a panel session during the event. 
Former Gov. Glenn Youngkin congratulated VCCS on its milestone via a video message.
Pictured from left to right: Maurice Jones, senior vice chancellor for strategic partnerships for the Virginia Community College System, alongside former Virginia Governors George Allen, Tim Kaine, Bob McDonnell, Terry McAuliffe, and Ralph Northam. (Photo courtesy of the Virginia Community College System)
Before the program closed, each governor gave a different response on one area they would invest in to transform community college education over the next decade.
Northam said he would help expand dual enrollment, so high school students can gain technical skills and graduate with a clearer path to work or further education.
McAuliffe said he would invest in preparing students for artificial intelligence, urging VCCS to lead in teaching and developing skills for the rapidly changing field.
“We ought to be the best in AI development and teaching,” McAuliffe said. “We ought to be the best in America.”
McDonnell focused on investing in training for in-demand technical careers less vulnerable to automation, including maritime and construction trades, energy, and technology; he emphasized close employer partnerships.
Kaine, who is now a U.S. Senator, said he would invest in using new Pell Grant eligibility for high-quality career and technical programs. 
Allen’s investment would go to education and workforce development, aligning training with employers’ needs, learning from other states, and removing stigma around skilled trades such as electrical work and HVAC, he said.
“Don’t fear change,” the former governor advised. “Embrace it as an opportunity to improve opportunities for our fellow citizens.”
VCCS officials said current and future students considering the program should contact the eligible schools for more information.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: The election is over. For Virginia’s congressional delegation, now the real work begins.
description: Virginians first elected Don Beyer to the U.S. House of Representatives in 2014 and with the recent midterms, he won a seventh term. The 8th Congressional District representative discovered an inspiring tradition when he arrived at the nation’s Capitol. Once a month, every member of  Virginia’s U.S. House delegation met, along with the state’s two […]
text:
(Photo illustration by States Newsroom)Virginians first elected Don Beyer to the U.S. House of Representatives in 2014 and with the recent midterms, he won a seventh term. The 8th Congressional District representative discovered an inspiring tradition when he arrived at the nation’s Capitol.
U.S. Rep. Don Beyer, D-Alexandria, was elected to represent Virginia’s 8th Congressional District for a seventh term on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Kerley/Virginia Mercury)
Once a month, every member of  Virginia’s U.S. House delegation met, along with the state’s two U.S. senators, to discuss ways they could help each other. One member would bring the others lunch. 
That tradition carried on pretty much undisturbed until the Jan. 6, 2021 insurrection, when supporters of Donald Trump invaded the Capitol to try to stop the peaceful transfer of power to newly-elected President Joe Biden. 
After the attack, GOP U.S. House members from Virginia still refused to certify 2020 election results from two states. That caused a split in the delegation’s bipartisan spirit, Beyer said.
That division eventually healed, and the monthly bipartisan caucus returned to normal until 2025, when Virginia’s Democratic-run General Assembly decided to redraw House districts to favor Democrats. 
It was a reaction to Trump’s order to Republican-controlled legislatures in several states to redraw maps to favor Republicans. 
After that, Beyer told me, Virginia’s Republican U.S. House members “have not come to a single lunch.” They stayed away, even after the  Supreme Court of Virginia overturned the referendum that would have favored Democrats in 10 of 11 districts,a decision the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed. 
Now that the ugly 2026 election season is over, it is time for them to return to the monthly bread-breaking. And time for Democrats to welcome them back.
“This might be an opportune moment for members to find common ground on issues the public was pleading for in the election,” George Mason University professor and political analyst Mark Rozell told me.
But, he added, “the pressure is on the new majority party to do the outreach.” 
On Nov. 3, the failure of Trump’s policies spawned a national voter revolt that caused Republicans to lose control of the House and Senate by huge margins. 
In Virginia, supporting Trump’s unpopular policies cost two Republican incumbents their seats in congressional districts drawn to favor Republicans.
In this year’s midterms, the rest of the country learned what Virginia has known for a while

That fight is over. The Virginia delegation needs to resume helping one another. 
Though they may continue to disagree based on political philosophies, their responsibility is to constituents who look to them for help, not the culture wars, name-calling and attack ads of the 2026 elections. 
There is no fairy tale ending here. Real differences exist between Democrats and Republicans on critical issues, including solutions for affordable healthcare and taxes. What everyone should agree on is who they serve.  
I reached out to every member of Virginia’s new U.S. House delegation to ask about meeting together in the same room to find issues they could all support in  Virginians’ interest, rather than the president’s.
Beyer told me he hopes the remaining three Republicans representatives in the delegation – Morgan Griffith, Ben Cline and John McGuire  — will return to the monthly lunch meetings.  
“All three are good men,” he said. 
Griffith, who represents the most Republican district in the state, sent me a one-sentence statement: “I am always willing to work with my colleagues for the betterment of Virginians.”
I hope he will prove it by rejoining the monthly caucus and bringing Cline and McGuire with him.
Democrat Shannon Taylor, who narrowly defeated 19-year incumbent Rob Wittman in Virginia’s 1st District, was a little more expansive: 
“Virginians are struggling with spiraling costs and making ends meet, fueled by corruption,” she said in a statement. “I am willing, and eager, to sit down with anyone regardless of party who wants to work together cooperatively to address these issues … and I’ll support bipartisan work that moves us toward those critical goals.” 
I hope she and others in the Virginia delegation will prove it by doing what longtime Virginia Republican Congressman Bill Whitehurst, who died recently at 101, called “recognizing that the other person has a piece of truth themselves.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: After an Election Day trouncing, Pennsylvania Republicans look to the future
description: “This election was a referendum on the president of the United States,” Dent said, adding that the backlash this year was notably severe because of what he called “the six Cs”: cost, conflict, corruption, chaos, cruelty, “and sometimes crazy.”
text:
Poll workers wait for voters at a polling place in a garage on Willett Road in Brentwood, Pennsylvania, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)On Election Day, Pennsylvania Republicans suffered their most stunning defeat at the ballot box in at least 50 years, amid turmoil in Washington, another Middle East war and crippling price hikes at home. 
Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro sailed to a second term, while state Democrats expanded their one-seat majority in the state House to 13 and flipped the Senate, which has been under GOP control almost continuously since 1978.
And four Republican incumbents lost their U.S. House seats, contributing to a nationwide blowout in Congress where Democrats picked up at least 40 seats in the lower chamber and eight in the Senate.
The Capital-Star spoke to Pennsylvania Republicans about what the party can learn from its Election Day rout to prepare for upcoming elections. They include two seats on the state Supreme Court next year, and the U.S. Senate seat held by Democratic Sen. John Fetterman, who is widely expected to face primary challengers in 2028. U.S. Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-4th District) told Politico she is “considering” a run for Senate against Fetterman. 
“Every couple years, the voters have a chance to basically tell you how they’re feeling, and they spoke loud and clear that they’re unhappy with Republicans,” House Minority Leader Jesse Topper (R-Bedford) said. “And I think there are Republicans who are unhappy because they feel we didn’t do what we said we were going to do, particularly at a national level.”
House Republican Leader Jesse Topper (R-Bedford) speaks during swearing-in day on the chamber floor on Tuesday, Jan. 7, 2025. (Capital-Star/Peter Hall)
In that respect, said former Congressman Charlie Dent, the Nov. 3 election was like most midterm elections.
“This election was a referendum on the president of the United States,” Dent said, adding that the backlash this year was notably severe because of what he called “the six Cs”: cost, conflict, corruption, chaos, cruelty, “and sometimes crazy.”
“When I talk about cruelty, I’m not just talking about treatment of immigrants,” he said. “I’m talking about the treatment of Canada, of [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelensky in the White House and … the name calling, the never ending discourteous behavior,” added Dent, who represented the Lehigh Valley for seven terms.
As inflation and the war against Iran drove up the cost of petroleum this year, Trump dismissed the affordability crisis as a “Democrat hoax” and told rallygoers in Nebraska last month that the higher gas prices were a small price to pay for a non-nuclear Iran.
Former House Majority Leader Kerry Benninghoff, a Centre County Republican who won reelection, said it was clear to those campaigning that rising prices were the primary cause of voters’ frustration. 
“I hear from my daughters who do the primary amount of grocery shopping. So a lot of us knew that those were going to be some of the driving force issues, which we don’t necessarily have a lot of control over.”
Republicans across the country need to have a deep debate over the future of the party, Dent said, adding that it will be a battle between legacy Republicans and MAGA Republicans. 
“I do think the MAGA movement is badly damaged by this,” Dent said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Messaging and money
Charlie Gerow, a conservative commentator and a candidate for governor in the 2022 GOP primary, said at least some of the blame falls on state Republican leaders, who he said need to get back to traditional campaigning.
“R​​ather than having paid door knockers and a bunch of digital gobbledygook, they need real campaigns run by real people, the old-fashioned way,” Gerow said.
The party also failed to adequately back the top of its ticket, said Dennis Roddy, a former journalist and media strategist. He said state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, the GOP nominee for governor, was a strong candidate but wasn’t able to tell her story.
Pennsylvania Treasurer Stacy Garrity, who is seeking the GOP nomination for governor in 2026, speaks during a rally with Vice President J.D. Vance at the Uline shipping materials warehouse in Lower Macungie Township on Tuesday, Dec. 16, 2025. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
“If Josh Shapiro outshone Stacy Garrity, it was because he had the money to pay the electricity bill, you know, to illuminate,” Roddy, who said he’s no longer a member of the party, noted. “She was without funds.”
Garrity, a businesswoman and U.S. Army veteran, raised $9.2 million through mid-October compared with the $66.3 million that Shapiro’s campaign spent.
Pennsylvania Republican Party Chair Greg Rothman, a state Senator from Cumberland County, declined an interview. Spokesman James Markley said in a statement that Garrity “worked as hard, if not harder, than any candidate across the country.” 
“As the party in power during a midterm election, Republicans around Pennsylvania and the nation put forth a full and organized effort to defy history and hold the line, but sadly that did not materialize,” he said, adding that the party will analyze the results, talk with voters and prepare to come back stronger to face the challenges ahead.
“The Republican Party of Pennsylvania remains focused on growing our movement across the Commonwealth, supporting conservative leadership, and fighting for policies that return power, freedom, and hard-earned money back to the people of Pennsylvania,” Markley said.
A clear message
Topper, who was reelected House minority leader last week, said the first order of business is for the party “to pick a direction.”
“One of the issues that we run into now is that President Trump put together a coalition largely based on the idea of America First,” he said. “I think those America First folks are confused as to what that means now with a war in the Middle East, with gas prices that they’re seeing as a cause of that.”

Likewise, the administration’s trade policies, Topper said, are unclear.
“Are we a party of free trade? Are we a party of tariffs? Are we a party of building things in America? Are we a party of making sure that we are able to build things abroad and make things cheaper?” he asked. “Right now, we’re trying to do a little bit of both, and I just don’t believe that works, and I don’t believe that’s a clear message.”
Winning back the independent and young voters who swing elections will depend on advocating for policies that create opportunities for people of all walks of life.
“We have to outline what the American dream is right now,” Topper said, adding that homeownership, higher wages and upward mobility seem out of reach for many voters who turned to Democratic social-welfare policies for help. “That’s not the American dream.”
Former U.S. Rep. Charlie Dent
Dent, who served for 14 years in the General Assembly, agreed Pennsylvania Republicans need to have an agenda based on ideals and principles. The party for too long has focused on  fealty to the president, whose goals are unclear, he said. 
“The party really became less of one based on ideals and principles, and more focused on following a man who has unfixed policy positions, and they shift constantly,” Dent said.
What the GOP stands for is a key question, said Gerow, suggesting that the party needs to align itself more closely with blue-collar and working-class people.
“We have to define ourselves in those ways on the issues that matter to that constituency,” he said. 
During the campaign, in which Trump implored Republicans to vote like he was on the ballot, the president appeared indifferent to the effects of his policies on regular people.
Roddy, who worked as an aide to Republican ex-Gov. Tom Corbett, said the party needs to return to its past as the centrist party he joined after growing up in Cambria County in the 1960s. There, he said, Democrats were known for having a socially conservative wing.
“The Democrats were not a progressive party. They were not a forward-thinking party. They were not a party known for tolerance and acceptance,” Roddy said. 
That branch of the Democratic party was eradicated as the parties took sides on issues like abortion, guns, God and gay rights, he said. 
“But right now, the Republican Party is the one that is in most need of remediation,” Roddy added, “because racism, religious bigotry, and just plain bloody mindedness have found their way into too much of the dialog.”
Looking ahead
Dent noted that the party also suffered from a degree of complacency, noting that more than two dozen of the Republicans defeated in the U.S. House were in districts that Trump won in 2024 by 10 to 20 points. Incumbents in those districts, he said, tend to focus only on the 20% to 30% of the electorate that votes in primaries.
“Well, I got news for folks: the other 70, 80% showed up, and you know you have to speak to a much broader audience,” Dent said. Politics is a game played between the 40-yard lines, and for a lot of folks in both parties, this game is playing closer to the end zones, staying hard in the base.”
And while the Republican party has a deep hole to get out of in Congress and the Pennsylvania Legislature, he said it remains to be seen whether Democrats will be able to consolidate their gains.
“Democrats need to be somewhat humble and recognize that this remarkable victory for them might be a temporary phenomenon, and that they should govern accordingly, carefully, and you know not go too far left,” Dent said.
He noted that while a wave election can take out strong incumbents, suboptimal candidates who ride the tide may prove to be vulnerable in subsequent elections.
“It throws up a lot of driftwood on the beach, and you know there are going to be several loose logs close to the shoreline,” Dent said “They’re going to be pulled back in the rip tide, which will come in a cycle or two.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland blasts Air Force for unpermitted golf course work at Joint Base Andrews
description: Maryland Department of the Environment officials, already feuding with the Air Force over a fuel leak at Joint Base Andrews, say base officials are also reconstructing a golf course there without required permits.
text:
Maryland Department of the Environment officials, already feuding with the Air Force over a fuel leak at Joint Base Andrews, say base officials are proceeding with the reconstruction of a golf course there without permits and with “incomplete” documents. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Local environmental officials are sparring with the federal government over the redesign of a Washington-area golf course being touted by President Donald Trump (R). Construction has begun without state permits, and in August, an environmental inspector was denied access to the site.
It’s probably not the course you’re thinking of.
The National Park Service’s plans to rebuild Washington D.C.’s public East Potomac Golf Links have drawn headlines and judicial rebukes, while work by the Air Force to reconstruct the Courses at Andrews in Prince George’s County— open only to members of the military, civilian Pentagon employees and their guests — has flown under the radar.
But not for Maryland Department of the Environment officials, who say the Air Force has shared only “incomplete” documents related to controlling erosion on the construction site at Joint Base Andrews, even though parts of the golf complex sit directly over former unpermitted landfills.
In June, Trump issued a sweeping presidential determination exempting “each and every effluent source” associated with the redesign of the Andrews courses from a variety of federal, state and local environmental requirements.
That followed a missive from the president on Truth Social, during which he accused Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) of delaying the course renovations. Moore said at the time his agency wasn’t delaying the project. In fact, it hadn’t received a single permit request.
Maryland Secretary of the Environment Serena McIlwain in a file photo from Oct. 2, 2025, at the Conowingo Dam. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
The president’s proclamation could violate federal law, said Jon Mueller, an attorney who leads the Environmental Law Clinic at the University of Maryland, Baltimore. The applicable statute allows the president to suspend environmental laws exclusively for projects that are in the “paramount interest” of the nation, Mueller said.
“I can’t see anybody arguing with a straight face that reconstruction of a golf course — or revitalization and rehabilitation, as the presidential determination puts it — meets that standard,” said Mueller, who was a senior attorney in the Justice Department’s Environment and Natural Resources Division from 1987 to 2004.
In an October letter to Col. Karl Seekamp, installation commander at Joint Base Andrews, outgoing Maryland Environment Secretary Serena McIlwain urged him to provide a new date for an environmental inspection, and to submit the additional documentation.
“While the June 26 presidential exemption sought to waive water pollution regulations, the federal government should be a good neighbor and adhere to the same environmental standards as everyone else,” read a statement from the Maryland Department of the Environment.
An Air Force spokesperson said in a statement that the base is building a “first-of-its-kind course designed with accessibility in mind for wounded warriors and disabled veterans.”
“To achieve this, we are working closely with the State of Maryland and all necessary federal entities while complying with environmental regulations and safety requirements throughout the process,” the spokesperson said.
The dispute is unfolding at the same time as an ongoing jet fuel leak beneath a tarmac on the Air Force base, which has also attracted concern from Maryland’s environmental agency.
Located on the southern portion of the base, the Courses at Andrews began as one course, constructed between 1948 and 1949. Nicknamed the “president’s golf course,” it’s the largest golf complex operated by the Department of Defense, and includes two 18-hole courses and a third decommissioned course.
Plans provided by the Air Force show an overhaul of the north course, along with “future proposed renovations” that include a new 18-hole south course, a driving range and a nine-hole accessible course for individuals with disabilities.
“However, those concepts are under development and are not being assessed as part of this proposed action,” reads an environmental assessment provided by the Air Force.
The plans, some of which bear the insignia of Nicklaus Design, former pro Jack Nicklaus’ course design company, also show the addition of two new retention ponds on the courses, meant to capture rainwater.
According to the plans, the Air Force will use some of the water collected in the ponds to irrigate the course, reducing demand on aquifers that supply the base.
The environmental documents say the redesign will avoid wetlands where possible, and add new habitats at the retention ponds, making up for the wetland areas impacted by construction, including a wetland where a new bridge will be built for golf carts.
“Although the proposed renovations would be conducted within 100-year floodplains, the project is expected to reduce overall flooding,” reads the environmental assessment, provided by the Air Force.
Tree removal would be “limited to the areas marked for removal,” which “includes forested land where tree removal would be beneficial for purposes of forest management.” Trees will be replanted at other locations on the base, the environmental assessment says.
But Maryland officials said  the glowing environmental review seems to ignore pressing environmental realities.
One planning document, provided by the Air Force, shows a plan to redesign the north golf course at Joint Base Andrews, and add two new stormwater retention ponds. (Plan courtesy U.S. Air Force)
The courses are on the Environmental Protection Agency’s National Priorities List and sit over unpermitted former landfills with documented contamination, including PFAS and PCBs.
In the first phase of its construction, the Air Force has informed the state that it is focusing on the north course, and it will not disturb soil over the landfill caps.
“Although base leadership has shared draft documents and indicated the initial phase will not dig into the landfill caps, they have not submitted complete applications, have indicated they do not intend to seek wetlands authorizations, and have stated plans to proceed before receiving state approvals,” read a statement from MDE spokesperson Jay Apperson.
On Aug. 28, a Maryland environmental inspector arrived at Andrews to inspect the golf course construction, after a complaint that sediment-laden stormwater could be escaping the site, Air Force officials denied him access to the courses for an inspection.
Instead, from a road on the perimeter of the course, the inspector could see an active construction site, with crews clearing the land and grading the soil. He noticed gaps in silt fencing meant to contain runoff, so that golf carts could come and go, and recommended that additional fencing be installed in some places.
To Mueller, the episode was a startling display of defiance from the Air Force, closer to what one might expect from a recalcitrant private company, rather than a government entity.
“He had to walk around the perimeter. I mean, was he out there with binoculars trying to figure this out?” Mueller said. “I’ve never heard anything like that.”
A spokesman for Joint Base Andrews said in a statement that the inspector “was granted access to the base” and “he was able to perform an inspection of the area he requested.”
For now, MDE is waiting for an answer from the base about its permit applications, and it “remains committed to conducting physical inspections to monitor compliance.”
“If plans change and soil over the landfills is disturbed, MDE will enforce proper management and disposal of contaminated soil under applicable environmental laws,” read a statement from the agency.
