name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland still fighting Joint Base Andrews over unresolved fuel leak, 8 months later
description: Nearly eight months after Maryland officials first learned jet fuel was leaking from a pipe buried under the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, the exact cause of the leak is not known — nor is the amount of fuel that might still be under the concrete.
text:
A great blue heron devours a fish on lower Piscataway Creek near Fort Washington. State officials say a jet fuel leak about 15 miles upstream at Joint Base Andrews is continuing to contaminate the creek, months after it was first reported. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Nearly eight months after Maryland officials first learned jet fuel was leaking from a pipe buried under the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, the exact cause of the leak is not known — nor is the amount of fuel that might still be under the concrete.
Water testing, meanwhile, continues to show evidence of fuel in the environment, flushing out into local waterways when it rains.
In a late October letter to base leadership, Maryland Environment Secretary Serena McIlwain said the pace of the base’s response to the spill “has not matched the urgency of the situation.”
“After seven months of coordination between our teams, I am troubled that fundamental questions about the source of the releases and the actions necessary to prevent further contamination remain unanswered,” McIlwain wrote. “The presence of an unknown amount of fuel under the ground continues to leak into Piscataway Creek.”
Air Force officials see things differently.
They argue that after the leak was discovered, the offending pipe was quickly isolated from the fueling system and drained. They say the complex effort to detect the precise point of failure in the fuel system is continuing at a reasonable clip — particularly given that it’s occurring on one of the nation’s most important airfields, home to Air Force One.
An underflow dam and oil absorbent booms were installed along a section of Piscataway Creek at Joint Base Andrews in response to a fuel leak at the base earlier this year. (Photo by Airman 1st Class Tylan Alicea/Air Force)
When it rains, fuel that previously leaked into the surrounding soil spills into the Piscataway Creek, which empties into the Potomac River about 15 miles to the southwest. But base engineers say that a multipronged fuel collection system captures much of the fuel before it flows downstream.
Any fuel remaining below ground is likely “localized,” they say, based on the results of initial borings. Tests involving more extensive underground boring that began last week, after a lengthy debate with Maryland about methodology, should answer many of the unanswered questions, they say.
“We recognize and agree with the Secretary that urgency and timeliness of the response is of utmost importance. We also want to ensure we are lockstep with our regulators with a full-coordinated plan to address all concerns prior to moving forward,” base officials wrote in response to McIlwain.
The base’s fuel inventory indicates that some 22,000 gallons of fuel are unaccounted for, but it has yet to determine how much of that fuel actually entered the environment. A fuel recovery operation has collected an estimated 1,000 gallons of pure petroleum hydrocarbon product from 801,404 gallons of impacted water so far, said a base spokesperson.
In her letter, McIlwain pointed to “broader concerns” with the fuel inventory system, noting that records showed evidence of fuel losses that were not investigated.
“These issues raise broader concerns about the integrity of the fueling infrastructure and the adequacy of the systems intended to detect and prevent future releases,” McIlwain wrote.
Jet fuel can be toxic to aquatic flora and fauna, but the substance is known to evaporate quickly from open water, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. In this instance, no fish kills were reported in connection to the fuel spill. Officials also do not believe that the spill contaminated drinking water.
The episode on the tarmacs is unfolding at the same time as Andrews has embarked on a redesign of the base’s golf courses, which sit atop unpermitted landfills. Construction has begun without any of the typically required state permits.
Residents who live along Piscataway Creek, and environmentalists who advocate for the creek and the Potomac, aren’t sure what to think.
Though the Air Force claims the end is near, it’s been a frustrating saga to watch, said Betsy Nicholas, president of the Potomac Riverkeeper Network, an environmental nonprofit that unites several riverkeepers in the region.
“I simply don’t understand why they aren’t able to resolve this more quickly,” Nicholas said. “They have the skill and capability there. I mean, this is the United States military. That’s a lot of capacity, and they are not prioritizing this.”
To that, McIlwain has a response. Her letter sets a series of deadlines over the next few months for the Air Force to meet on testing underground fuel pipes, and correcting the inaccuracies discovered in the base’s fuel inventory records.
“If these deadlines are not met, I will consult with our Office of the Attorney General to determine appropriate next steps,” she wrote.
‘A very important airfield’
To Maryland environmental officials, the story begins in December, when the fuel system at Andrews, which snakes below tarmacs on the base for an estimated ten miles, first began to show signs of trouble.
On Dec. 11, the system failed an assessment known as a precision tightness test, which is meant to catch potential fuel losses. But the Air Force didn’t report the failed test to the state.
Base officials believe the failed test was caused by a faulty valve, and no fuel was lost. They acknowledge the issue wasn’t reported until later. But Maryland officials say the base was required to flag it right away.
In January and February, the base’s fuel inventory shows that jet fuel was escaping the system, which also went unreported, according to MDE.
The Piscataway Creek has been on the receiving end of thousands of gallons worth of jet fuel that flowed from Joint Base Andrews after the failure of an underground pipe. Maryland environmental officials say a residual amount of contamination is continuing, months later. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Visitors to Piscataway Park fish from the pier at National Colonial Farm on the Potomac River, near where it meets the Piscataway Creek, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)A fisherman casts his line into the Piscataway Creek near its confluence with the Potomac River, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Chuck Bean, a Fort Washington resident who lives along the Piscataway Creek, said he was distressed to learn that thousands of gallons of jet fuel entered the creek due to a leak at Joint Base Andrews. Maryland officials say there is still ongoing residual leakage of fuel into the environment. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)
On March 23, the Air Force notified the National Response Center and MDE, after an oil sheen and petroleum odors were observed in Piscataway Creek.
Letters between base officials and Maryland show a monthslong disagreement about the method the Air Force wanted to use to test the fuel system and pinpoint the leak. Maryland officials repeatedly pushed back against the use of fuel in the testing, warning that could lead to more contamination.
Twice in July, Maryland denied testing plans submitted by the base. In mid-September, the state agency reluctantly agreed to a test involving the circulation of fuel, but only if certain contingencies were met. It also warned that the base “may be subject to further enforcement action for any additional release of a regulated substance into the environment.”
While the debate persisted, key questions remained.
“Until those questions are resolved and the problem is fixed, we cannot verify that the releases have ceased or that additional fuel is not entering the environment,” read a statement from MDE spokesman Jay Apperson. “Downstream communities, including minority and working-class neighborhoods and members of the Piscataway people, deserve accountability.”

These days, Air Force officials believe they can narrow their focus to a specific servicing lateral that branches off of the main underground fuel line. But that lateral is nearly half a mile long, said Air Force Lt. Col. Brendan Dorsey-Spitz, commander of the 316th Civil Engineering Squadron. And it runs under 18 inches of concrete that aircraft park on or taxi over.
“Air Force One taxis over it. President Xi, when he was here for the state visit, taxied over it,” Dorsey-Spitz said of the September visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Contractors conduct concrete coring and soil borings along the flightline at Joint Base Andrews on Friday. (Photo by Airman 1st Class Tylan Alicea/Air Force)
For recent testing on the 2,500-foot lateral, crews installed probes every 3 to 6 feet, in search of the exact place that the pipe failed. With some of the probe locations on active taxiways, tests had to be carefully scheduled, said Dorsey-Spitz.
“Hopefully, fingers crossed, we’re able to identify the location so that we can identify what repairs need to be made, communicate that to our mission partners and get after the final fix,” he said.
“We’re being very methodical about our approach, taking the vast majority of the system out of contention for the source of the leak, and really narrowing all of our resources — both manpower and money — after that segment that we believe it’s in,” said Dorsey-Spitz.
Once the testing reveals the extent of the damage and the location, the Air Force will have to arrange for construction on the nation’s preeminent airfield.
“[It’s] a very important airfield that supports the United States of America,” Dorsey-Spitz said. “We want to make sure that when we know the exact location, we know exactly how long it’s going to be down for,” Dorsey-Spitz said.
‘How much more can the river take?’
The spill has drawn concern from environmental watchdog groups in Maryland, along with residents who live downstream of the Air Force base.
It’s not their first frustration with the base, which is a known source of PFAS, or “forever chemical,” contamination. In October 2021, Piscataway Creek became the first place in Maryland for which state officials issued fish consumption advisories because of PFAS, after tissue sampling revealed elevated levels of the cancer-causing chemicals in three different species.
To Potomac Riverkeeper Dean Naujoks, it feels as though the Potomac’s watershed is weathering one pollution blow after another in 2026. Earlier this year, the Potomac was inundated with millions of gallons of sewage when a large underground pipe known as the Potomac Interceptor collapsed in Montgomery County.
Construction crews work on a historic water tower at Joint Base Andrews on Oct. 13. The base faces scrutiny from Maryland officials about an ongoing underground jet fuel leak. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
“How much more can the river take?” Naujoks said.
Nicholas, of the Potomac Riverkeeper Network, compares the base’s response to the cleanup effort from DC Water after the Potomac Interceptor collapse.
“That entire gigantic pipeline was all underground when it collapsed, and in a matter of weeks, they had the location identified, they had a bypass in place and they were developing a plan to fix the pipeline,” Nicholas said. “Here, it doesn’t seem like we’ve even gotten off the starting block.”
Anjela Barnes sees it all from Piscataway Park, near the creek’s confluence with the Potomac River, and visible from George Washington’s historic home at Mount Vernon. Barnes leads the Acokeek Foundation, which stewards 200 acres in the park, part of the ancestral homelands of the Piscataway people.
“The word interconnectedness always comes to my mind,” said Barnes, who is a member of the Piscataway tribe.”They’re not one-offs. This is just the latest in centuries of environmental impacts.”
‘It unnerves everybody’
When Arlington, Virginia, residents Chuck Bean and his wife were looking for their perfect retirement home, the sun-soaked home on a Fort Washington hillside checked all of their boxes. There was that pier stretching all the way down to the water, the community park just down the road and the secluded trails nearby.
Three years after moving in, the couple delights in watching the wild residents of the shallow creek, and spending time aboard their pontoon boat the Proud Mary, whenever the tide allows, or their kayak whenever it doesn’t. Bean can motor alongside Mount Vernon or historic Fort Washington and a host of surrounding National Park lands.
“We see an eagle every day. We see herons all the time,” Bean said. “We’ve got these really cute tree frogs that attach to the window, an owl that puts on a hooting show every other night.”
“It’s awesome,” he said.
Chuck Bean, who lives along Piscataway Creek in Prince George’s County, is among residents concerned by recent jet fuel pollution of the creek from Joint Base Andrews. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
So Bean, who serves as treasurer of the Piscataway Hills Citizens Association, was alarmed to hear that a fuel leak at Andrews had dumped thousands of gallons of jet fuel into the Piscataway.
“We want this to be a pristine watershed,” Bean said. “The idea of jet fuel coming into it unnerves everybody.”
The citizens association wrote to the Maryland Department of the Environment in mid-April, expressing concerns about a lack of information on the spill. The agency later held a meeting in the community, Bean said.
“In the neighborhood, we were all surprised — shocked — to learn that this had happened,” he said.
After the initial dust settled, Bean said he assumed the spill had at least been contained. But recently he realized that Maryland officials were still sparring with the Air Force over the possible solutions.
“We all deeply respect our Air Force, but we hope that they can do a better job of protecting us,” Bean said.
Nearby at Piscataway Park, which boasts a sizable fishing pier, a sign warns anglers about PFAS contamination in fish tissue. But in many secluded fishing spots along the creek, there aren’t any posted notices, Barnes said. And there weren’t any notices on the creek about the jet fuel leak.
“There’s just not enough education,” Barnes said.
But as residents learn about high-profile spills, their confidence in boating and fishing on the waterway and its banks could also diminish, she said.
“There’s just going to be a loss of public confidence, because of these incidents that seem to happen one after another,” Barnes said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Commentary: Rhode Island pays the highest prices for public safety. Where is the receipt?
description: Every investigator learns the same lesson early: A number by itself proves nothing. You need to know what it measures and what it leaves out. The Rhode Island Public Expenditure Council (RIPEC) recently handed taxpayers numbers worth investigating. In August, the business-backed research group reported the state’s cities and towns spent $931 million on polic[...]
text:
Local and state law enforcement officers are shown on the Elm Street Pier in Newport where a stolen yacht with the body of a suspect aboard was towed on the morning of Aug. 26, 2026. Police were on scene in the Point neighborhood until well into the evening conducting an investigation. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)Every investigator learns the same lesson early: A number by itself proves nothing. You need to know what it measures and what it leaves out. The Rhode Island Public Expenditure Council (RIPEC) recently handed taxpayers numbers worth investigating.
In August, the business-backed research group reported the state’s cities and towns spent $931 million on police and fire protection in fiscal 2024. Fire spending ranked first in the nation per capita, at 1.8 times the national average. Police spending ranked ninth. Together, the two departments consume about a quarter of municipal budgets, and RIPEC names them a key driver of property tax growth.
Now the other side of the ledger. Rhode Island posted the fourth-lowest violent crime rate and the third-lowest property crime rate among the states in 2024. Fires accounted for roughly 2% of fire department calls in 2023. Medical calls made up more than 70%.
First in spending. Near the bottom in crime. Fires are a rounding error in the call log. The people paying for this picture deserve to see the evidence behind it.
I spent 20 years with the East Providence Police Department. Nothing here argues that those jobs do not matter or that the people doing them earn too much. Median firefighter pay in Rhode Island ranks 12th nationally; median police pay ranks 20th. Salaries do not explain a first-place ranking.
Staffing models do. Rhode Island ranks first in professional firefighters per capita, at nearly twice the national rate, because most of the country leans on volunteers. We built a system sized to fight fires, then sent it, overwhelmingly, to medical emergencies. Maybe that is the right design. Nobody can say, because we rarely measure what each dollar buys.
Consider overtime. A 2019 state law mandates time-and-a-half for firefighters averaging more than 42 hours a week, and it counts paid leave as hours worked. Take a sick day, then pick up an extra shift at premium rates. The Hummel Report estimated the practice cost Warwick about $500,000 in a single year. When the bill passed, a union lobbyist argued it was a fairness issue.
Then put that language, and its price tag, in public view.
Pensions add their own weight, eating more than a fifth of police spending and more than a quarter of fire spending, with at least eight local plans under 60% funded.
Then there is Newport, which spent $1,586 per resident on police and fire, the most in the state, and fields 3.4 officers per 1,000 residents against a New England benchmark of 1.8.
On paper, the worst offender.
But an investigator checks the denominator before trusting the ratio. Per capita figures count roughly 25,000 year-round residents. The city puts annual visitors near 5 million. RIPEC itself concedes Newport’s staffing may partly reflect seasonal residents and visitors its population count misses.
On Aug. 26, the Newport harbormaster’s office spotted a 40-foot sailboat reported stolen from New Jersey at anchor in Newport Harbor. Police say when officers went out to it, the man aboard retreated into the cabin, armed himself, and opened fire. A sergeant took a round in the leg. Officers returned fire and killed the suspect. The city has released body camera footage. State police and the attorney general’s office continue to investigate, and nothing here prejudges their findings.
The staffing lesson stands on its own. The call demanded officers on the water while the rest of the city still needed patrol coverage. Anyone who has run a shift knows the math. A department sized for 25,000 residents lacks the bench to do both. 



Quotation







First in spending. Near the bottom in crime. Fires are a rounding error in the call log. The people paying for this picture deserve to see the evidence behind it.


So here is the real question for Newport and every seasonal community from Narragansett to Westerly. Staff year-round for the peak, or staff for the baseline and buy the surge through seasonal hires, overtime, and mutual aid with neighboring departments? Each answer carries a cost and a risk.
Defenders of current spending raise fair points. Dense cities and old wood-frame housing carry real fire risk. Low crime may reflect, in part, the policing we pay for; you cannot prove a negative by pointing at the outcome you bought. The core question remains: What do we get for the money, and how would we know?
Here is where to start.
First, require every city and town to publish an annual public safety report in one standard format: calls by type and by month, response times, staffing, overtime hours and dollars, injured-on-duty cases, and pension cost per active member.
Second, match the response to the call. If 7 in 10 calls involve medicine, communities should test dedicated medical units instead of rolling a full engine company to every chest pain.
Regional dispatch centers and shared services belong in the same discussion.
Third, the General Assembly should stop passing labor mandates without a price. Every bill touching municipal public safety staffing or overtime needs a fiscal note before the vote, starting with a fresh look at the paid-leave provision in the 42-hour law. RIPEC’s own recommendations include limiting costly state mandates.
None of this cuts a single firefighter or police officer. It demands what every investigator, every auditor, and every taxpayer has the right to ask: Show me the evidence.
We pay first-place prices. We deserve a receipt.
The recent report by the Rhode Island Public Expenditure Council shows Newport had the highest municipal spending on police and fire services among Rhode Island’s 39 cities and towns in fiscal year 2024 as a share of total non-education spending. (From “Police and Fire Protection in Rhode Island,” Rhode Island Public Expenditure Council, Aug. 31, 2026.)

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: With their new legislative majorities, NH Democrats eye education changes
description: When the New Hampshire Supreme Court found New Hampshire’s school funding unconstitutionally low in 2025, its directive to lawmakers was clear. “We urge the legislative and executive branches to act expeditiously to ensure that all the children in public schools in New Hampshire receive a State funded, constitutionally adequate education,” wrote Justice Jame[...]
text:
Rep. Dave Luneau, a Hopkinton Democrat, is among the Democrats who will be proposing several changes to education in New Hampshire. Here, Luneau addresses the House on Jan. 7, 2026. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)When the New Hampshire Supreme Court found New Hampshire’s school funding unconstitutionally low in 2025, its directive to lawmakers was clear. “We urge the legislative and executive branches to act expeditiously to ensure that all the children in public schools in New Hampshire receive a State funded, constitutionally adequate education,” wrote Justice James Bassett.
Over the following two years, legislators made few changes to the state’s school funding formula. 
But in January, 292 House and 15 Senate Democrats will be seated in the state’s 400-member House — pending any changes from recounts. And some Democrats are proposing major changes to education.
Many of the most ambitious ideas could get vetoed by Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who maintained the corner office. And any changes that would increase taxes are sure to attract the criticism of Republicans eager to win the Legislature back in two years.
But as concerns about property taxes have increased, Democrats say they are hoping to capitalize. 
“New Hampshire is dead last in the country when it comes to the state share of funding public schools,” said Hopkinton Rep. Dave Luneau, the ranking Democrat on the House Education Funding Committee. 
Here’s what to watch in the 2027 legislative session affecting education. 
Repealing education freedom accounts
Some Democrats will seek to repeal the education freedom accounts program, which was created in 2021 and allows families to take the per-pupil amount given to public schools and use it toward private or home school education costs. In 2025, Ayotte and Republicans removed remaining income limits on the program; the program currently has a 12,500-student cap and is projected to cost about $68 million for the coming school year. 
But other Democrats are proposing a number of less dramatic changes that would tweak the EFA program. Rep. Jonah Wheeler, of Peterborough, is seeking to require private schools accepting EFAs to maintain the same admissions standards as public schools. 
Luneau raised other potential approaches from Democrats, like restoring an income eligibility limit; instituting audits against the nonprofit organization that administers the program, Children’s Scholarship Fund; introducing anti-fraud protections against people misusing EFAs; and gradually winding down the program with a sunset clause that would allow current families to keep using their EFAs. 
Increasing state funding to public schools
Many Democrats are interested in increasing the amount of state funding to public schools, arguing the measure is necessary to help reduce property taxes. But lawmakers have a wide array of ways to do it.
Luneau plans to reintroduce his proposal for “opportunity grants,” in which New Hampshire’s per-pupil school funding would no longer be uniform, but would instead be based on specific factors: a district’s poverty levels, special education needs, teacher-salary costs, and other factors, such as enrollment size and population density. 
He also supported exploring homestead property tax exemptions, which would allow New Hampshire property owners to receive exemptions up to a certain threshold, such as the first $300,000 of their home’s assessed value.
Rep. Mark Vallone, an Epping Democrat, wants to reverse cuts to the state’s business taxes instituted by Republicans in 2015. Vallone is planning to reintroduce House Bill 1708, which the House killed this year without debate. That bill would restore the business profits tax rate from 7.5% to 8.5% — its level before the 2015 tax cuts began — and would use some of those tax increases to lower the total amount of statewide property taxes the state requires municipalities to collect, by about $90 million per year. 
In an interview, Vallone called the proposal a “small-ball bill” in the grander scheme of school funding. But he argued by pairing business tax increases with property tax reductions, Democrats could win over constituents who might ordinarily oppose such increases. “This one actually gives tangible reductions in a bill that people need,” he said.
Republican lawmakers passed a law that also temporarily reduced the total amount collected by the statewide education property tax, or SWEPT, in 2021, bringing down the total number from $363 million per year to $263 million per year for one year. At the time, critics argued the approach was poorly targeted because it benefitted property-wealthy towns more than property-poor towns. 
Some of the most sweeping proposals come from a Republican lawmaker. Rep. Walter Spilsbury, of Charlestown, says he plans to reintroduce a trio of bills he has attempted in recent years that could radically change the state’s relationship to property taxes.
Spilsbury’s first bill would require towns that collect more statewide education property taxes than they need to fund their own schools to send that extra revenue to the state, which could then redistribute it to property-poor towns. That concept, which is echoed in other bills by Democrats for next year, would restore an earlier “donor town” version of the SWEPT repealed in 2011.
The second of Spilsbury’s bills would recreate last session’s House Bill 1800. That bill required all cities and towns to collect $5 per $1,000 in property taxes  — up from the current average of $1 — and send the excess to the state, with up to 40% reductions available to people who are over 65, have no children in the public school system and who are living in their primary residence. 
Spilsbury’s third bill would create a study committee to explore alternative revenue sources.
Spilsbury said he opposes an income tax, but could be open to a limited form of sales tax — provided it had guardrails and was designed to collect only enough revenue to replace the current amount sent to schools.
But he said he is open to any creative solution.
“If we could completely eliminate any funding of schools from property tax, I think that’d be best,” he said. 
To the New Hampshire School Funding Fairness Project, which has assisted in one of the recent lawsuits brought against the state’s education funding formula, the new Democratic majorities create an opportunity for creative proposals to change the state’s school funding model.
“There’s still a significant shortage, in our opinion, in the amount of funding provided by the state,” said Zack Sheehan, the organization’s executive director. The solutions, Sheehan argued, lie in taking a look at reversing Republican cuts to business taxes and the elimination of the interest and dividends tax.
“We’ve invested billions in this tax strategy, in theory for a benefit to us as citizens, and there’s no evidence of it,” Sheehan said. 
New Hampshire Republicans have pointed to large majorities of voters opting for tax caps over their school districts on Election Day as evidence that New Hampshire residents support limits on school funding, even as they voted in Democrats to power.
“I see no evidence that voters issued a mandate for higher taxes, nor do I believe Republicans should abandon the principles of fiscal restraint and educational freedom that we’ve consistently advocated,” said Rep. Ross Berry, a Weare Republican who lost his reelection on Nov. 3, in comments to InDepthNH. 
In a press release, Rep. Jason Osborne, an Auburn Republican recently chosen to be House Republican leader in the 2027-2028 session, castigated Democratic Rep. Eileen Kelly for filing a bill that would repeal the tax cap ballot question law. “Just four days ago, Granite Staters overwhelmingly said they wanted a property tax cap,” Osborne wrote on Nov. 6. “Now, the first order of business for the new majority seems to be ripping away the property tax cap their voters themselves enacted.” 
But Sheehan argued the majority support for ballot question 2 proves only that most Granite Staters are tired of paying more for property taxes. Democrats should use that message, he argued.
“I do think that there’s a lot more of an appetite nationally and locally to talk about how government invests in things that people care about,” he said. 
Smaller changes in past two years
Any Democratic proposals may crash against a longstanding political reality: New Hampshire’s school funding is often very slow to change. 
In the last legislative biennium, lawmakers did not make major changes to the formula, despite the Supreme Court directive. The “base” per-student adequacy payments sent to public schools rose by the statutorily required 2% per year.
The Legislature appropriated $32 million more toward special education costs in the two-year budget passed in 2025. It reintroduced a targeted funding approach to give more state funding to towns with less property wealth, known as “fiscal capacity disparity aid.” 
Republican lawmakers also removed income limits from the education freedom accounts program, and passed House Bill 1815, which sought to nullify the Claremont and Contoocook Valley School District Supreme Court school funding decisions by declaring “adequate” education funding to be a joint responsibility of the state and municipalities. 
Other education changes
The volume of school-related bills has expanded so rapidly that in 2025, the New Hampshire House and Senate split their education committee into two committees, to separate education funding from education policy matters.
And lawmakers have plenty of education bills that are not related to school funding.
Sen. Donovan Fenton, a Keene Democrat, has filed legislation to provide free lunches in schools. Rep. John Cloutier, of Claremont, has filed a bill to repeal HB 1815, and restore the state’s statutory accountability to the Supreme Court decisions. And Rep. Wayne Burton, a Durham Democrat, is seeking to repeal “all prohibitions of diversity, equity and inclusion within state agencies and in public schools.”
Some Republicans are looking for smaller measures that might get bipartisan support. 
Sen. Daryl Abbas, a Salem Republican, is introducing legislation that might earn the support of public schools. In June, Ayotte signed House Bill 1817, which allows education freedom account students to attend classes and programs offered by their local public schools without needing to pay extra — as long as the EFA recipients do not exceed 50% of the public school’s instructional class time.
Public school advocates argued the bill would short them by requiring them to take EFA students but providing no compensation. Abbas will introduce a bill that would require the state to send school districts 15% of per pupil adequacy aid for each course that an EFA student takes, which amounts to about $653 per full-credit course. That reimbursement formula has long been used for non-EFA home-schooled students who use public school resources. 
Abbas said he supports the intent of HB 1817: “A home-school student is a home-school student; whether they’re EFA or not EFA should not matter,” she said. 
But, he added, his bill is aimed at making the process fairer for districts.
“Since we made the law say that the schools cannot exclude the home-schooled EFAs, then they at the very least should get the (15%) adequacy funding,” he said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: Indiana’s behavioral health future depends on the decisions we make today
description: It’s time for Gov. Mike Braun and state lawmakers to expand Indiana’s Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic (CCBHC) demonstration statewide. Indiana has already invested heavily in changing how behavioral health care is delivered. The state has secured federal participation, enacted legislation, invested millions of dollars, and begun demonstrating wh[...]
text:
A Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic is a specially designated clinic that provides a comprehensive range of mental health and addiction services and be in compliance with the state’s criteria, developed by the Division of Mental Health and Addiction. (Courtesy State of Indiana)It’s time for Gov. Mike Braun and state lawmakers to expand Indiana’s Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic (CCBHC) demonstration statewide.
Indiana has already invested heavily in changing how behavioral health care is delivered. The state has secured federal participation, enacted legislation, invested millions of dollars, and begun demonstrating what a more accessible and coordinated system can accomplish.
The state now faces a consequential choice: Build on that progress and extend the model to all 92 counties, or leave much of Indiana’s behavioral health system operating without the full benefits of this evidence based model. Senate Enrolled Act 1 from 2023 advanced Indiana’s efforts to implement CCBHCs, a model designed to improve access to comprehensive mental health and addiction services.
Indiana subsequently secured a place in the federal Medicaid CCBHC demonstration and selected eight community mental health centers to lead the transformation. Services began in January 2025, yet access remains limited to only 35 of Indiana’s 92 counties.
The state’s long-term objective is statewide access, but that goal remains unfinished. Indiana’s CCBHC program needs to expand.
For far too long, getting behavioral health services in Indiana meant waiting weeks or months for an appointment. Under the CCBHC model, patients are connected with care as soon as they need it. The model also requires a broader continuum of services, bringing outpatient treatment, addiction care, crisis response, stabilization, and primary care into a more integrated system. The result is a system designed to respond to people’s needs before those needs become more difficult and more expensive to address.
Since 2023, investments of more than $216 million have increased capacity for community based crisis response and stabilization. Early results are encouraging. Participating centers have seen improvement in access and quality of care, along with reductions in hospitalizations and incarcerations. In one year, mobile crisis teams responded to nearly 15,000 crisis calls. Crisis receiving and stabilization centers logged nearly 24,000 visits during the same period.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Behind these numbers are Hoosiers experiencing psychiatric distress, families facing behavioral health emergencies, and individuals struggling with addiction. Community-based services give them more opportunities to receive treatment rather than enduring the revolving door of emergency departments, hospitals, and jails. Not every crisis response prevents a hospitalization or arrest, but there is no question a CCBHC based system provides opportunities to intervene before situations escalate. Every Hoosier deserves access to that care, regardless of their ability to pay.
There are also compelling financial reasons to expand. Through participation in the federal demonstration, Indiana receives the benefit of enhanced Medicaid reimbursement. Every month we wait to cover all 92 counties, Indiana leaves $4 million on the table. Delaying expansion postpones that opportunity while untreated behavioral health conditions continue to contribute to costly emergency department visits, inpatient hospitalizations, law enforcement involvement, and incarceration. Under a statewide CCBHC model, these crises could have been addressed earlier.
Statewide expansion is especially important for rural Indiana. Rural communities face persistent challenges recruiting clinicians, maintaining services, and ensuring access to treatment. A person’s ZIP code should not determine whether timely behavioral health care is available. Hoosiers should not have to travel long distances or wait until a condition becomes a crisis to receive appropriate care. Extending the CCBHC model across all 92 counties would strengthen the network for delivering comprehensive behavioral health services in rural communities while improving coordination among community providers, hospitals, primary care practices, schools, and the justice system.
Indiana has already made great strides. The state secured federal demonstration status, enacted enabling legislation, selected eight participating centers, addressed payment and implementation challenges, and established a framework for delivering and measuring a broader range of services. Participating centers have been building the workforce, partnerships, and crisis-response infrastructure needed to make this model work. Indiana should extend that infrastructure to the rest of the state.
Expansion will require continued attention to financing, workforce capacity, implementation, and accountability. Those are certainly reasons to plan carefully, but not reasons to leave the work unfinished. Indiana can establish clear milestones and guardrails, monitor outcomes, evaluate costs, and hold participating providers accountable for delivering the services and results the model requires.
Indiana has done the hard work of getting the CCBHC demonstration started. Eight community mental health centers are delivering services, the state has invested in crisis response, and early results are encouraging. But 35 counties are not 92 counties.
Indiana has an opportunity to lead. Seize this opportunity. Strengthen behavioral health services by expanding CCBHC to all Hoosiers.

name: National
title: States, cities move to ban cryptocurrency kiosks as scams mount
description: States and cities across the country are cracking down on cryptocurrency kiosks as financial scams involving the ATM-like machines continue to mount, costing Americans nearly $389 million last year alone. Four states — Indiana, Minnesota, Tennessee and Vermont — enacted statewide bans this year, while dozens of communities have moved to prohibit the machines[...]
text:
A cryptocurrency kiosk, right, at a Royal Farms gas station in Wallops Island, Va., stands ready to accept cash for a variety of crypto products including Bitcoin, Dogecoin and Ethereum. The FBI received 13,460 complaints involving cryptocurrency kiosks in 2025, with reported losses totaling nearly $389 million. (Photo by Barb Barrett/Stateline)States and cities across the country are cracking down on cryptocurrency kiosks as financial scams involving the ATM-like machines continue to mount, costing Americans nearly $389 million last year alone.
Four states — Indiana, Minnesota, Tennessee and Vermont — enacted statewide bans this year, while dozens of communities have moved to prohibit the machines or impose new restrictions on their use. A new law in Hawaii, which went into effect in October, bans consumers from depositing cash into kiosks to buy cryptocurrency.
The crackdown comes as scammers increasingly direct victims to cryptocurrency kiosks, often located in gas stations, convenience stores and grocery stores, to deposit cash that is converted into digital currency and transferred to accounts controlled by criminals.
Texas becomes the first state to buy bitcoin as more states eye cryptocurrencies

The FBI received 13,460 complaints involving cryptocurrency kiosks in 2025, with reported losses totaling nearly $389 million. Complaints increased 23% from the previous year, while financial losses jumped 58%, according to the agency’s cybercrime report, which was released in April. 
Older Americans have been particularly hard hit. More than half of the complaints involved people older than 50, who reported more than $302 million in losses last year.
The mounting losses have prompted policymakers across the country to pursue tighter restrictions and outright bans on cryptocurrency kiosks — efforts that consumer advocates say are urgently needed to prevent further financial harm.
“Every day that these laws aren’t passed are days where victims are having money stolen from them, and that money, because it’s through cryptocurrency and the nature of the kiosk, it’s just almost impossible to get any of that money back,” said Françoise Cleveland, AARP’s government affairs director, in an interview with Stateline. 
Indiana became the first state to ban cryptocurrency kiosks in March, followed by Tennessee and Vermont in July and Minnesota in August. The measures mark a shift from earlier efforts to regulate the machines through transaction limits, fraud warnings and licensing requirements.
At least 35 states have enacted legislation addressing cryptocurrency kiosks since 2023, including 18 that passed laws this year, according to AARP, which has advocated for stronger consumer protections. 
Local governments are stepping up, too. In Massachusetts, at least 20 communities have banned cryptocurrency kiosks as of August. In late October, a crypto kiosk ban took effect in Jackson, Michigan — the first of its kind in the state. Operators must remove machines by the end of January. The fast-growing city of Star, Idaho, passed a ban in September requiring kiosks to be removed by this month.
Other municipalities have opted to allow the machines but add stricter restrictions, including requiring fraud warnings, identification checks or transaction limits.
Attorneys general in several places, including the District of Columbia, Iowa and Massachusetts, have sued cryptocurrency kiosk operators, alleging they exploited residents and failed to implement adequate safeguards against fraud. 
A three-year investigation by the Iowa attorney general’s office found that 98% of transactions at Bitcoin Depot kiosks in the state were linked to scams, compared with 94% at CoinFlip kiosks. The findings, released in February, prompted the state to sue both companies. 
Bitcoin Depot has since filed for bankruptcy, citing increasingly restrictive state regulations and bans. The company took its kiosks offline in May.
In recent years, some kiosk operators have pushed back against outright bans and some proposed restrictions, arguing that the machines serve legitimate customers and that stronger fraud safeguards, rather than prohibitions, would better protect consumers.
Earlier this year, Larry Lipka, the general counsel for CoinFlip, which operates more than 5,000 kiosks in the U.S. and other countries, testified against the statewide ban in Minnesota, arguing that regulators should strengthen enforcement instead. 
“It is inappropriate to ban a legal product because fraud is happening. Not our fault,” Lipka said. 
Some operators, including CoinFlip, have also implemented holding periods during which transactions can be reversed, offer refunds to scam victims and provide 24/7 customer support.
How the scams work
Unlike traditional ATMs, which allow customers to withdraw or deposit money from bank accounts, cryptocurrency kiosks allow users to purchase digital currencies such as Bitcoin with cash. Some machines also allow customers to sell cryptocurrency in exchange for cash.
Scammers exploit the machines by calling victims and persuading them to withdraw money from their bank accounts and deposit it into a kiosk, often providing a QR code linked to a digital wallet controlled by the criminal.



Quotation







It’s just almost impossible to get any of that money back.


– Françoise Cleveland, AARP’s government affairs director


Once the cash is deposited, the machine converts it into cryptocurrency and transfers the funds to the designated digital account, called a “wallet.” Those transactions generally cannot be reversed, making it difficult for victims to recover their money. Kiosk operators also charge transaction fees, regardless of whether the transaction was fraudulent, typically ranging from 20% to 30%, depending on the company.
The scams take several forms. Criminals may impersonate law enforcement officers, government officials, bank employees or technical support representatives, falsely claiming that victims owe money, face arrest or need to move their savings to protect them from fraud.
Other scammers establish romantic relationships online or promote fraudulent investment opportunities before directing victims to deposit money into the machines.
In many cases, scammers remain on the phone with victims throughout the transaction, providing step-by-step instructions on where to find a kiosk and how to send the money.
Beyond financial scams
Although older Americans account for a disproportionate share of reported losses involving cryptocurrency kiosks, some investigators say the machines can also play a role in crimes affecting younger people.
Matt Hogan, a detective with the Connecticut State Police who investigates financial crimes, said kiosks have been used in connection with financially motivated sextortion, in which perpetrators threaten to distribute intimate images or videos unless victims pay them money.
The schemes can target teenagers and young adults, who may be coerced into sending money to prevent explicit images from being shared with family members, friends or classmates.
The FBI has warned that financially motivated sextortion increasingly targets teenage boys, particularly those between 14 and 17. Criminals may demand payment through mobile payment applications, gift cards or cryptocurrency.
“That’s definitely an up and coming problem,” Hogan said.
Hogan also pointed to the use of cryptocurrency kiosks in other criminal activity, including money laundering, narcotics-related offenses and payments involving child sexual abuse material.
Federal authorities have raised similar concerns. In an August 2025 notice, the federal Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network warned that cryptocurrency kiosks were being used to facilitate scams and launder suspected drug proceeds.
A 2022 report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office also found that drug and human traffickers have used cryptocurrency kiosks to convert cash into digital currency and obscure the source of illicit payments.
“Everybody is a potential target for fraud,” said Cleveland, of AARP.
Regulation or outright bans?
Despite those concerns, Hogan expressed reservations about banning cryptocurrency kiosks altogether.
He said he supports many of the consumer protections being adopted across the country, but worries that outright bans could push criminals toward alternative methods of transferring money that may be more difficult for investigators to trace.
Citing potential for fraud, blue and red states pass new crypto ATM laws

Transactions involving Bitcoin and many other cryptocurrencies are recorded on public digital ledgers known as blockchains, allowing investigators to follow the movement of funds between digital wallets. Advances in investigative techniques have also given law enforcement more tools to trace cryptocurrency transactions, although identifying the people behind those transactions and recovering stolen funds is still sometimes difficult.
“If these machines do get shut off, bad guys are ingenuitive,” Hogan said of potential kiosk bans. “They are able to pivot. They have no care for authority or morals, so they will pivot to a place that we likely will have less visibility.” 
Industry representatives have also pushed back against the growing wave of bans, warning of the economic consequences for businesses and the customers who rely on their services.
That debate played out in Indiana earlier this year, where lawmakers initially considered legislation requiring kiosk operators to obtain licenses, verify customers’ identities and comply with transaction and fee limits.
But after hearing testimony from law enforcement, scam victims and industry representatives, lawmakers abandoned the proposed regulations in favor of an outright ban.
“I can think of no legitimate reasons, no substantial legitimate reasons,” to warrant the kiosks, Republican state Sen. Scott Baldwin said during a February committee hearing.
CoinFlip, which had operated in Indiana for eight years, criticized the decision, saying it had worked with lawmakers in 17 other states to adopt consumer protections without prohibiting the machines.
“We are shocked to learn that the state of Indiana would eliminate an entire industry based on a lack of understanding of digital assets and the services we already provide to 17,000 Hoosiers around the state,” a company spokesperson told the Indiana Capital Chronicle.
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.

title: Rokita presses governor over Charlie Kirk posts after no Indiana educator licenses revoked
description: More than a year after warning that Indiana teachers could lose their licenses over social media posts about Charlie Kirk’s assassination, Gov. Mike Braun says the complaints did not warrant disciplinary action, despite Attorney General Todd Rokita’s renewed demands for punishment. Rokita said his office referred 25 licensed educators to the Indiana Departme[...]
text:
A dispute over educator discipline has put Gov. Mike Braun and Attorney General Todd Rokita at odds over First Amendment protections and Indiana's professional licensing standards. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)More than a year after warning that Indiana teachers could lose their licenses over social media posts about Charlie Kirk’s assassination, Gov. Mike Braun says the complaints did not warrant disciplinary action, despite Attorney General Todd Rokita’s renewed demands for punishment.
Rokita said his office referred 25 licensed educators to the Indiana Department of Education for possible discipline and now accuses Braun and Education Secretary Katie Jenner of failing to follow through on the governor’s original warnings.
Gov. Mike Braun speaks at a news conference on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, in Indianapolis. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Braun, however, defended his administration’s handling of the complaints, saying last week that the cases went through the state’s established review process and did not meet the legal standard for licensing action, in part because of First Amendment concerns.
“It involved First Amendment issues,” Braun said. “And it simply didn’t meet the threshold level to do it.”
The Republican governor acknowledged Rokita’s concerns but characterized the attorney general’s public criticism on social media as part of the normal workings of state government.
“I think that all was in the normal back and forth of what he ought to be doing to make sure we’re staying on point,” Braun said. “And in this case, we did to the extent we could.”
Rokita disputes that explanation, though, and continues to insist that the state should at least hold disciplinary proceedings to determine whether educators who posted about Kirk’s death violated Indiana’s professional standards.
“I’m not saying that every license has to be revoked or anything else,” Rokita said Friday during an appearance on WIBC’s Hammer and Nigel Show. “But there should be a process and a hearing and a decision made as to what’s happening to these teachers.”
Indiana law permits disciplinary action against an educator’s license for immorality, misconduct in office, incompetency or willful neglect of duty.
Rokita’s office did not answer multiple inquiries from Capital Chronicle.
Tensions after the election
The public disagreement comes days after Indiana Republicans suffered significant losses in the Nov. 3 election, raising questions about the party’s direction and relationships among its leading officials.
Gregory Shufeldt, a political science professor at the University of Indianapolis, said Rokita’s approach fits his longstanding emphasis on politically divisive issues.
Greg Shufeldt, a political science professor at the Univeristy of Indianapolis. (Photo from the University of Indianapolis website)
“He does it for the headlines,” Shufeldt said. “He does it to draw attention. He does it to highlight politically cultural clashes.”
Shufeldt said the attorney general’s decision to publicly pressure members of his own party could also be viewed through the lens of future Republican leadership contests.
He noted that Braun and Rokita have developed different political approaches, with the governor appearing more willing to adjust his message in response to changing circumstances.
Marjorie Hershey, a professor emerita of political science at Indiana University Bloomington, said disagreements between officials in the same party are not necessarily surprising, particularly when each may be responding to different constituencies.
“The fact that they’re both in the same party doesn’t mean an awful lot with respect to their level of agreement on issues,” Hershey said.
She suggested Braun may be more attentive to the broader electorate after the midterm results, while Rokita has consistently appealed to socially conservative Republican voters.
Both political scientists raised the possibility that Rokita’s criticism could serve longer-term political ambitions, including that he could challenge Braun for governor in 2028.
Rokita was asked about that possibility during the Friday radio interview but did not announce any plans to run.
“Not saying I’m running for anything,” Rokita said. “Not saying anything like that.”
He added he wanted Braun to run for reelection and succeed.
Shufeldt suggested that the dispute may ultimately be less about what happened in Indiana classrooms than about the contrasting political approaches of two Republican officials.
“My read on the situation is that this is politics,” Shufeldt said. “It’s not policy.”
No Kirk-related licenses revoked
The state’s public educator offenses database shows 21 license revocations between Sept. 10, 2025, the day Kirk was killed, and Nov. 13, 2026.
None was related to the Kirk controversy, according to confirmation from the Office of Administrative Law Proceedings and the attorney general’s office.
The revocations involved offenses including child seduction, possession of child pornography, immorality, misconduct in office and other violations.
The database, maintained by IDOE, contains information about former educators reported to the department under state law, including certain school employees convicted of specified felony offenses. It does not necessarily reflect every complaint received or investigated by the agency.
Braun said the education department evaluated the allegations and determined they did not justify license revocations.



Quotation







I want a process. There has to be some accountability ... there has to be some discipline.


– Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita


IDOE did not respond to questions from the Indiana Capital Chronicle about the status of the 25 referrals, including whether investigations were completed, the legal standards applied or whether officials considered an arrangement allowing the attorney general’s office to handle the cases.
“I want a process,” Rokita said during Friday’s radio interview. “There has to be some accountability … there has to be some discipline.”
Although no professional licenses have been revoked over the Kirk controversy, some educators faced immediate employment consequences last year.
A March investigation by the Capital Chronicle found that at least six K-12 educators faced consequences at the local level after their social media posts circulated publicly.
At least four resigned, while others were placed on leave or agreed to retire.
The March review also found that all 22 K-12 educators then identified on the Eyes on Education portal retained active teaching licenses.
The employment actions taken by individual school corporations are separate from state licensing proceedings. Losing a local teaching job does not automatically result in the loss of an educator’s professional license.
Rokita points to educators’ posts
Rokita maintains that the administration has failed to provide the formal process and accountability he believes are required.
The Republican attorney general revived the controversy in a Nov. 9 social media post, accusing the Braun administration of failing to act on educator complaints submitted after Kirk was fatally shot during an appearance at Utah Valley University.
The attorney general said his office had identified 25 licensed educators whose social media comments appeared to celebrate, excuse or justify the conservative activist’s killing.
The referrals followed a broader effort by Rokita’s office to collect complaints about educators through its Eyes on Education portal, which invites members of the public to submit information about alleged inappropriate conduct and political bias in Indiana schools.
After Kirk’s death, the attorney general’s office encouraged people to report educators’ social media posts, bringing additional scrutiny to comments made outside the classroom.
Indiana educators faced firings, resignations after Charlie Kirk posts — but no licenses revoked

“Despite repeated requests, no action was taken,” Rokita wrote, directly addressing Braun. “More than a year has passed. When will your administration act?”
He called on the governor to direct IDOE to address the referrals and pursue appropriate licensing action.
Rokita also shared screenshots of several educators’ social media comments, naming individuals he said still held active teaching licenses.
One post criticized Kirk’s positions on gun rights and suggested the activist’s death was a consequence of those views.
“With all due disrespect, Charlie Kirk can suck it,” the post read. “He became exactly what he said was ok and acceptable in order to have gun rights. I call that manifestation.”
The educator said he was not saying the killing was right, but described it as “only fitting,” while contrasting public reactions to Kirk’s death with those to the Sandy Hook school shooting and other victims of gun violence.
Another social media post criticized what the writer described as racial double standards in public responses to violence.
The post questioned why people of color are often characterized as violent or aggressive and criticized expressions of “thoughts and prayers” following shootings. It ended by questioning whether Kirk’s death was “still worth it to him.”
Other screenshots shared by Rokita included a comment describing Kirk’s killing as ironic in light of his views on the Second Amendment.
“I don’t think it’s funny, but it’s ironic,” the comment read. “And I’m also never sad personally when racist, misogynistic homophobes die.”
A separate comment described the killing as karma and accused Kirk of supporting violence against immigrants and transgender people.
Rokita argued that the comments raised questions about whether students with political or religious beliefs similar to Kirk’s could feel safe and respected in those educators’ classrooms.
“Such conduct raises serious questions about an educator’s fitness to teach,” Rokita wrote. “Many Hoosier students share those beliefs, so how can they feel safe and respected in a classroom led by someone who publicly states that the world would be better off without people like them?”
A day later, Rokita said in an additional post that his team had contacted the governor’s office again in September, ahead of the anniversary of Kirk’s death, and offered additional assistance.
“Despite our efforts to help prompt action over the past two months,” Rokita wrote, “the Braun Administration still has done nothing.”
During Friday’s radio interview, Rokita said he was not necessarily seeking revocation of every educator’s license. Instead, he argued that the state should consider a range of potential disciplinary consequences, including verbal or written reprimands and suspensions.
He also accused the administration of stalling private discussions about having his office undertake the disciplinary work.
“I even offered, and we got very close to me doing the work,” Rokita said. “We were going to do the work and bring these cases.”
A dispute over free speech, professional standards
The latest disagreement marks a difference in emphasis from Braun’s initial response to the controversy.
In September 2025, Braun warned that teachers who celebrated or encouraged political violence online could face suspension or revocation of their professional licenses.
“While we must protect the First Amendment,” Braun said at the time, “calls for political violence are not freedom of speech and should not be tolerated.”
He said Jenner’s department would review statements made by K-12 teachers and administrators that appeared to celebrate or incite political violence.
IDOE confirmed shortly afterward that it was aware of comments made by a small number of educators and was reviewing the matters.
Indiana law permits disciplinary action against an educator’s license for immorality, misconduct in office, incompetency or willful neglect of duty. But the law does not expressly define immorality, leaving questions about how that standard applies to off-duty political speech.
Story continues below.

Rokita has argued that the provision gives the state grounds to pursue discipline in at least some of the Kirk-related cases.
During Friday’s interview, he acknowledged that public school employees have constitutional protections against government retaliation for speech, but argued those protections are not unlimited.
“There’s an immorality clause in our state statute,” Rokita said. “So, the free speech is just it’s not it’s not endless.”
The attorney general previously issued guidance to school officials arguing that schools have substantial authority, consistent with the First Amendment, to discipline employees whose speech disrupts school operations. The guidance addressed schools’ authority as employers.
Still, First Amendment advocates have warned that constitutional protections for public employees cannot be set aside merely because their views are unpopular or offensive. They emphasized that the government faces significant constitutional restrictions when punishing employees for speaking as private citizens on matters of public concern.
Those free speech concerns were central to a federal lawsuit involving a Ball State University employee who lost her job over comments about Kirk.
In May, the university agreed to pay former employee Suzanne Swierc $225,000 to settle a federal First Amendment lawsuit stemming from her dismissal over social media comments about Kirk.
The settlement did not constitute an admission of wrongdoing by the university.
Rokita criticized that outcome Friday, saying he would not have agreed to settle the case if his office had represented the university.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana legislative leaders plan latest start for session in many years
description: Indiana’s 2027 legislative session will get off to its latest start in more than a decade following significant membership turnover and new top leadership in both the House and Senate.
text:
Indiana Senate members debate a bill in February 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana’s 2027 legislative session will get off to its latest start in more than a decade following significant membership turnover and new top leadership in both the House and Senate.
Both chambers are set to convene Tuesday for their annual Organization Day that will see newly elected lawmakers sworn into office and rules voted upon for the upcoming session.
The House is then scheduled to reconvene on Jan. 11, with the Senate returning on Jan. 19, the Republican majority offices for those chambers said Friday.
A review of General Assembly online records shows Jan. 9 in 2023 as the latest date that a legislative session began since at least 2011. Other sessions began as early as Jan. 3.
The later Senate start was set “with preparation in mind,” said Molly Swigart, the spokeswoman for new Senate Republican leader Chris Garten.
“It will also allow more time to ensure new senators are properly oriented and committee chairs are prepared for the tasks that lie ahead,” Swigart said in an email to the Capital Chronicle. “That extra preparation means fewer hiccups and a faster start when we’re gaveled in. It’s a practical choice, not a political one, and it helps us serve Hoosiers efficiently from day one.”
The 50-member Senate will have 13 new senators — seven Democrats and six Republicans — along with 14 new committee chairs following Democratic gains in this month’s elections. Democrats added five senators to their ranks, but Republicans will continue to hold a 35-15 majority.
The House will have 24 newcomers among its 100 members — 17 Democrats and seven Republicans. Democrats gained 16 House seats, narrowing the GOP majority to 54-46. Republican Rep. Ben Smaltz is set to be elected as the new House speaker next week.
State law requires the General Assembly to “reconvene in session no later than the fourth Monday in January” — which will be Jan. 25 in 2027.  
The later start means that legislators will have essentially two fewer weeks to complete action for the 2027 session as state law sets adjournment for no later than April 29. 
Next year is the General Assembly’s long session as it is responsible for adopting a new two-year state budget.
