name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: US Has Lost Measles Elimination Status, Global Health Authorities Say
description: The U.S. has officially lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago. Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country’s status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission [...]
text:
A doctor and mother in Utah worries about her 4-month-old, sleeping here at home, who is too young to be vaccinated while measles spreads in the community. (Amy Maxmen/KFF Health News)The U.S. has officially lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago.
Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country’s status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country. PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17. In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country’s sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That’s no longer happening in the United States.
“It’s a very sad moment,” said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO’s decision. “Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death.”
Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can’t spread.
In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized with measles in the U.S. More than 8,000 people have been sickened in outbreaks that have cost roughly $125 million in medical care, public health response, and productivity losses, Johns Hopkins University researchers estimate. States have reported 13 measles-associated deaths, including a 7-month-old in New York and infants in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin in recent months. Babies typically aren’t vaccinated before they’re a year old.
PAHO, an international group that oversees health in the Americas and works with the World Health Organization, based its assessment on two analyses: one by the CDC and another by an independent group of measles experts. Researchers anticipated this conclusion after an outbreak in Utah surpassed the one-year mark in June.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, Emily Hilliard, attributed the resurgence of measles to vaccination gaps that opened years before this administration. Indeed, rates of childhood vaccination have steadily declined since the covid pandemic started.
But many scientists also blame the Trump administration for spreading vaccine misinformation and stifling a swift, strong response to outbreaks. For example, the administration cut millions of dollars from children’s immunization programs run by state health departments and terminated funds for research on vaccine hesitancy.
After health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sacked CDC director Susan Monarez in August 2025, she told Congress she was fired because she would not preapprove changes to vaccine recommendations “without reviewing the evidence.” She added that “we already have seen the largest measles outbreak in more than 30 years” and that, “if vaccine protections are weakened, preventable diseases will return.”
Spokespeople for HHS and the White House defended the administration, including Kennedy, who led a prominent anti-vaccine organization before he took the helm at HHS. “The President and the Secretary have repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, coordinated with states, and facilitated the deployment of vaccine doses across the country,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster wrote in an email.

Past Administrations Sounded Alarms
For more than three decades, the federal government treated measles as a preventable tragedy, with sizable outbreaks triggering national efforts to boost vaccination and stop the virus from spreading. That’s no longer the case, said Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a new initiative that educates the public about vaccines and assists health workers responding to outbreaks.
Stinchfield was a pediatric nurse at a children’s hospital in Minnesota during the nation’s last surge of measles before elimination, from 1989 to 1991. She recalled an entire ward devoted to children with measles and the enormous effort required to prevent the virus from spreading to kids with cancer and weakened immune systems. Two children at the hospital died of measles. “That changed my career forever,” she said.
Back then, she said, the federal government “saw the urgency.” Officials held press conferences, spoke on the news about vaccines, issued clinical guidelines, and published reports in the CDC’s flagship journal — the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, or MMWR — that drove policies.
When data suggested that some children weren’t mounting a strong response to a single dose of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, a CDC advisory committee recommended two doses of the shot. When CDC analyses found that many children with measles hadn’t been vaccinated due to cost, the government launched the Vaccines for Children program to make immunizations available free of charge to underinsured families.
Cases plummeted. By 2000, the CDC and PAHO determined that measles was no longer a national threat — measles transmission had been eliminated. “Elimination” allows for occasional outbreaks, because measles is not eradicated worldwide and a small fraction of people, such as young infants, can’t be protected by vaccines.
People infected abroad sparked occasional outbreaks after U.S. elimination, but — until now — those fizzled out because of herd immunity. With at least 95% of people within communities immunized, outbreaks petered out and vulnerable people were protected.
Anna Fajardo, a public health nurse, offers vaccines at a school registration event in southwestern Utah. (Amy Maxmen/KFF Health News)
It would be 14 years before a significant outbreak in the U.S. Then in 2015, the virus took off among unvaccinated children at Disney parks in California, giving rise to outbreaks elsewhere. Congress saw some 125 cases as an emergency and summoned the CDC’s Schuchat to testify on the situation. “Vaccination wasn’t a partisan issue,” she recalled. “This was about problem-solving: What can we do about this?”
National television aired a video of then-U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy talking with Sesame Street’s Elmo about vaccination. HHS officials worked with vaccine experts on strategies to boost public confidence in vaccines. California and Vermont tightened vaccine requirements.
In 2019, House and Senate committees met again about measles, as a large outbreak concentrated in Orthodox Jewish communities in New York and New Jersey took hold. Congress asked HHS leaders how the administration planned to curb the rise of vaccine misinformation online.
“Internet fraudsters who claim that vaccines are not safe are preying on the unfounded fears and daily struggles of parents, and they are creating a public health hazard that is entirely preventable,” Lamar Alexander, then a Republican senator from Tennessee, said at the time.
Alex Azar, health secretary during the first Trump administration, and then-CDC Director Robert Redfield held a press conference stressing the “importance of on-time vaccination.”
And during the 2014, 2015, and 2019 outbreaks, the CDC’s MMWR published detailed articles within weeks of data collection. Timing matters since the reports guide emergency response. “The MMWR is the voice of the CDC,” Schuchat said, “alerting the nation, the media, clinicians, and public health experts to events that require action.”
‘The Dog Didn’t Bark’
Just after President Donald Trump took office in 2025, a measles outbreak exploded in West Texas. Within seven months, it surpassed the size of any in the U.S. since 1992, spread to Mexico and at least three other states, sickened more than 4,500 people in the two countries, and killed at least 16. Instead of broadcasting clear, repeated messages on the importance of measles vaccines, Kennedy falsely claimed on Fox News that they lead to “deaths every year.”
Congress didn’t call a hearing, and HHS didn’t send funds until after the emergency in West Texas had subsided. Besides an annual measles update, the MMWR didn’t publish a single report on the outbreaks that year.
“A lot of this is the dog didn’t bark,” said Dorit Reiss, a vaccine policy researcher at the University of California Law-San Francisco. “Something that normally happens isn’t happening.”
Political appointees have delayed or blocked several MMWR articles, according to multiple CDC officials whom KFF Health News agreed not to identify because they feared retaliation for speaking with the press. “There’s a deliberate effort to downplay vaccine-preventable diseases by the administration,” one official said.
“Measles reports from West Texas and New Mexico were intentionally shelved,” another scientist at the agency said. In April, The Washington Post reported that Jay Bhattacharya, who temporarily led the CDC this year and remains head of the National Institutes of Health, had blocked the publication of a study in the MMWR finding that covid vaccines halved the likelihood of emergency department visits.
“The suggestion that HHS is deliberately suppressing information about measles or other vaccine-preventable diseases is false,” Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, said in an email to KFF Health News. She said Kennedy and the CDC have provided approximately $100 million in additional funding to respond to outbreaks. The timing of MMWR reports, she added, varies due to factors such as data analysis and scientific review.
More than a year after data was collected from Texas, a few reports came out in the CDC’s journal. One study on 60 people hospitalized for measles in West Texas revealed that two required intubation and mechanical ventilation and that a baby born to a mother with measles experienced potentially lethal brain swelling due to the virus.
A sign outside a clinic along the Arizona-Utah border warns people who haven’t been vaccinated against measles to wait outside if they have a fever, cough, or other symptoms. (Amy Maxmen/KFF Health News)
The MMWR still hasn’t published detailed reports on massive outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah, and Pennsylvania. The CDC’s national measles update hasn’t appeared in the MMWR this year either. Instead, the journal has featured less urgent articles on scientific techniques that may help characterize future outbreaks.
CDC scientists told KFF Health News that they continue to analyze data but no longer expect to publish their findings in the MMWR because the process has become slow, opaque, and unpredictable. An urgent CDC report on the risks of measles to pregnant women was withheld, The Washington Post reported recently.
“We have two CDCs now,” an official at the agency said. “One is staffed by CDC scientists and civil servants who are committed to public health, and the other is political appointees who go in and change the website.”
The CDC’s measles dashboard counts four fewer measles deaths than state health departments have reported this year. Kennedy has disputed some deaths and made unsubstantiated claims that Pennsylvania health officials misrepresented data.
Kennedy personally instructed the CDC to alter language on a webpage that said vaccines do not cause autism, he told The New York Times last year. It now suggests a potential link between the two and no longer lists a slew of peer-reviewed studies that rigorously searched for an association and found none. These have been replaced with speculation about a correlation and unsubstantiated accusations that the scientific establishment has buried a potential link in order “to prevent vaccine hesitancy.”
The Trump administration has muddied the message on vaccines in other ways, Reiss said. Trump incorrectly said in August that the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine could be “quite lethal,” and he repeated the debunked idea that vaccines may cause autism. Stephen Miller, now Trump’s White House chief of staff, has falsely said doctors “pump your kids full of shots days after birth with no understanding of the long-term consequences.” Recommended vaccines and the vaccine schedule have been thoroughly studied.
Kennedy has made such claims for two decades, including as health secretary. “Having top leadership disseminating rumors, disinformation and flat-out falsehoods has been unforgivable,” Schuchat said.
When pressed by journalists and Congress, Kennedy and Trump have recommended measles vaccines. But they haven’t repeated the message clearly and unprompted on social media or on the podcasts and videos that Kennedy regularly appears in.
Kennedy also replaced vaccine experts on a panel advising the CDC with fringe researchers holding anti-vaccine views. And under his leadership, the CDC has laid off or forced out many vaccine specialists, including all of those in a group that partners with community organizations and pharmacies, the Immunization Services Division partnership branch.
At the same time, Kennedy has devoted resources to searching for potential harms from vaccines, including through an attempted clinical trial considered unnecessary and unethical by medical societies and the WHO.
To regain measles elimination status, the current U.S. outbreaks must end — then, future outbreaks must stop spreading within a year, said Paul Rota, a microbiologist and former CDC official. With outbreaks expanding in several states, he said, that moment isn’t on the horizon.
“Bigger fires create more embers, and any one of those embers can seed another fire,” he said.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: There’s a contested race for Maine attorney general. The public won’t get a say.
description: State Sen. Anne Carney and lawyer Timothy Shannon are vying to be Maine’s next attorney general. But unlike the recent midterm election cycle, where candidates worked to win over Mainers’ votes, these candidates’ appeals are being made to state lawmakers.  Maine is an outlier in having the Legislature appoint constitutional officers and state auditors. Most [...]
text:
Yarmouth attorney Timothy Shannon (left) and Maine Sen. Anne Carney of Cape Elizabeth are vying to be Maine's next attorney general. (Courtesy photo of Tim Shannon; Carney photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)State Sen. Anne Carney and lawyer Timothy Shannon are vying to be Maine’s next attorney general. But unlike the recent midterm election cycle, where candidates worked to win over Mainers’ votes, these candidates’ appeals are being made to state lawmakers. 
Maine is an outlier in having the Legislature appoint constitutional officers and state auditors. Most popularly elect their treasurer, secretary of state and attorney general, while states vary more on how they select auditors. 
For decades, some lawmakers have proposed changing the selection process, such as allowing the public to decide through a direct popular election, but such attempts have failed, including several last year.  
While campaigning happens out of public view, Carney and Shannon — both Democrats — are competing to win over legislators, who will meet on Dec. 2 to get sworn in and select these positions. Democrats now have larger majorities in both chambers after the Nov. 3 election. 
The Maine Legislature selects the state’s constitutional officers every two years, the length of the legislative session. Attorney General Aaron Frey, a Democrat, terms out at the end of the year. Meanwhile, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows and State Treasurer Joe Perry have each said they will seek another term and do not currently have any known challengers. 
The current term for State Auditor Matt Dunlap does not end until 2029. Dunlap unsuccessfully ran for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District seat this year.
Who will be the next attorney general? 
Maine’s attorney general represents the state and its agencies in court and directs investigations into major crimes, among other responsibilities. The contenders competing to replace Frey would each bring vast legal experience to the position, but in different areas. 
Carney, a Cape Elizabeth resident, has represented Cumberland County in the upper chamber since 2020, and served one term in Maine’s House of Representatives before that. Prior to her legislative service, Carney practiced employment, civil rights and municipal law at Norman, Hanson & DeTroy, LLC, for 17 years representing both plaintiffs and defendants. She was then an in-house volunteer attorney for Pine Tree Legal Assistance, providing free legal representation to low-income Mainers. 
Shannon, who lives in Yarmouth and previously served on the town council, is a trial and appellate lawyer representing high-tech companies, inventors, and patentees in commercial litigation and patent disputes. He’s worked in private practice for 24 years. Shannon has run for attorney general before, during the crowded race in 2018 when Frey was first selected for the role. 
“I have been watching the office closely for eight years,” Shannon said. “I think what ultimately nudged me back into running again is I am not satisfied with the state of the law, our state or our country with respect to some fundamental problems.” 
Both Shannon and Carney said standing up to President Donald Trump would be a top priority. Frey has been part of a coalition of Democratic attorneys general who have consistently pushed back against the president, participating in lawsuits challenging federal funding freezes and attempts to exert more federal control over elections, among others.
Carney and Shannon would also both make consumer protection a priority. Carney pointed to the millions of dollars leaving the state every year because of financial scams foisted upon Mainers, often those with retirement savings. Shannon said there needs to be guardrails around Artificial Intelligence, comparing it to “lacing drugs with even worse drugs” when it comes to the impact on social media and addictive apps. 
They have slightly different perspectives on how they’d tackle these shared concerns. 
Most of the lawsuits Maine has waged in recent years have been multi-state litigation. Shannon said those are important, but he thinks the state needs to protect Maine-specific interests with Maine-specific suits. 
“That’s a more robust undertaking for the office,” Shannon said. “It’s a bigger lift, but it’s potentially a much bigger reward.”
For example, he pointed to New Mexico’s attorney general who won a historic $25 billion civil penalty against Meta in October after choosing to sue separately rather than joining the multi-state lawsuit that Maine did. Maine received $56 million from that landmark settlement over the summer.
Carney has been responsible for overseeing the budget for the Attorney General’s Office in her capacity as chair of the Legislature’s Judiciary Committee. Having for the past six years been a part of the horseshoe where even small allocations are debated, she said she knows resources are limited. 
If chosen, Carney said she would decide whether to join multi-state litigation or bring a case solely on behalf of the state based on “what is most efficient and effective.”  
She would also work to improve communications to Maine people and Legislature about the status of cases and how settlement proceeds are being used. 
Many of Maine’s constitutional officers have previously served as legislators. That was the case for Frey. 
While Shannon pointed to his active practice of law as a plus, Carney sees her legislative service as a benefit, pointing to her work on the Judiciary Committee crafting three recently passed laws to counter Trump’s mass deportation agenda. 
As part of the attorney general’s authority to investigate major crimes, Frey is currently investigating the fatal shooting of Biddeford resident Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero by an immigration agent. 
An issue on which both candidates differ from Frey is tribal sovereignty. 
Frey bucked some fellow Democrats in his alignment with Gov. Janet Mills, also a Democrat, on not fully restoring sovereignty to the Wabanaki Nations, who are treated more akin to municipalities because of a land settlement agreement decades ago. But Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree plans to do so. Both Carney and Shannon said they support tribal sovereignty, with Carney pointing to her legislative work helping craft several proposals to recognize tribal rights in recent years. 
Frey’s tenure also coincided with a constitutional crisis in Maine’s indigent defense system. Recent strides have been made, many of which Carney has spearheaded, including emergency funding in the spring. Still, another funding shortfall is expected. 
Shannon said he believes “everyone’s been operating in good faith,” but added, “we need to fund it.”
Carney also pointed to a need for adequate funding, adding that, overall, “the public defense system is a lot more cost efficient for taxpayers than the system we’re transitioning from.”
The process 
Revived efforts for Maine voters to elect constitutional officers founder

Under the Maine Constitution, the state Legislature has sole authority to select the attorney general, secretary of state and state treasurer, which were created when the original state constitution took effect in 1820. The attorney general was appointed by the governor until 1856. The Legislature also picks the state auditor, a role created later in 1907. 
Back then, the attorney general largely advised lawmakers and the governor on issues that originated and ended in Maine, Shannon said.  
“But the AG’s office today, of course, is faced with much bigger, broader, multi-state problems,” he said. “I think if the framers of the constitution had known what was coming, they would have opened up the process to a public vote. But we have the system we have, and the legislators are good people trying to do the right thing.”
While lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have attempted to change the process, they have failed to secure the two-thirds support required for a constitutional amendment, which would also then need to be approved by the majority of Maine voters. 
Pointing to that bar, Carney said, “it’s not my decision one way or another,” noting that she’d still run regardless of the selection process. But she also said she sees some strengths in the current system, which relies on one-on-one conversations to win votes and is largely free from the Big Money trying to influence elections. 
“I think that in this age of overspending on campaigns, we should evaluate the benefits of our current system before automatically jumping to a different system,” Carney said. 
While each of Maine’s 186 members of the Legislature will get to weigh in when formal votes are cast on Dec. 2, it is the majority party that gets to pull the strings. 
Democrats have even more power this upcoming 133rd Legislature than the last. Ahead of the formal votes, Democratic lawmakers meet behind closed doors to settle on their nominee.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Hispanic workers deserve respect, not threats of arrest. Kansas history shows why.
description: Research four decades ago into the role the railroad played in Mexican immigration to Kansas etched indelible impressions of the workers who trusted the cross-shaped Santa Fe logo and a name that means “sacred faith” to leave their families to work 10-hour days on the tracks for 12.5 cents per hour. As the 1900s dawned, […]
text:
in 1903, the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway began recruiting Mexican labor and sending thousands of men north to Kansas, writes our columnist. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)Research four decades ago into the role the railroad played in Mexican immigration to Kansas etched indelible impressions of the workers who trusted the cross-shaped Santa Fe logo and a name that means “sacred faith” to leave their families to work 10-hour days on the tracks for 12.5 cents per hour.
As the 1900s dawned, Mexican men were recruited to Kansas to work on the lowest rungs of railroad labor — the extra gangs and section crews. The extra gangs were housed in boxcars so they could be moved wherever needed, and the section crews slept in crude housing built of railroad ties held together with mud or concrete.
I first meant to honor Hispanic Heritage Month (Sept. 15-Oct. 15) by dusting off — literally, since the project involved handwritten notecards and a typewriter — the grant-funded project to recognize the significant contributions Mexican immigrants and their descendants have made to a place many came to call home. The column took on greater urgency after gut-wrenching reports of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in unmarked vans targeting meatpacking plants in southwest Kansas.
Since the first influx of Mexican workers to Kansas in the first decade of the 20th century — due almost entirely to the railroad’s need for cheap labor — these workers have met the call for hard-to-fill jobs. The 1900 Kansas census showed 71 “foreign-born Mexicans” living in the state. That number surged past 8,400 by 1910, the greatest increase of any state in the country.
It’s no coincidence that in 1903 the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway began recruiting Mexican labor and sending thousands of men north to Kansas. By 1910, all divisions of the Santa Fe in Kansas were dependent on Mexican labor for track maintenance. According to the 1910 census, most of the 8,429 foreign-born Mexicans living in Kansas were employed by the railroad.
The census likely undercounted foreign-born residents. As a census taker noted in 1905 when trying to enumerate Mexican residents in Herington: “I find a class of railroad men that it is impossible to get any information in regard to their names, age or birthplace; (part are) laborers in bunk cars that make headquarters here and are in and out.”
From 1910 to 1927, Mexicans comprised at least 82% of all track laborers in the four Santa Fe divisions operating in Kansas. In 1920, the Kansas census recorded 13,750 foreign-born Mexicans. A 1925 census report showed that 95% of first-generation Mexican residents were employed as laborers. Their addresses were often listed simply as “Mexican camp,” “boxcar,” or in Topeka as “Santa Fe railyards.”
At the time of my research, few books had been written about Mexican immigration, though one published in 1930 by the University of Chicago Press stated that Kansas ranked fifth in the country in 1910 and 1920 for foreign-born Mexican residents. Since those were pre-computer days, I sifted for information in the Kansas historical archives at the old Memorial Building across from the Statehouse in Topeka. I found only a few master’s theses and a dissertation. Histories of the railroad mostly failed to even mention the foreign-born laborers.
But the archives of the Santa Fe railway told a different story.
The December 1910 Santa Fe payroll book listed 50 consecutive pages of Mexican laborers’ names on one division in Kansas. By 1912, most of the extra gangs were made up exclusively of Mexicans and were housed on the outskirts of dozens of towns along the main and branch lines of the railroad. A commissary car sold them overpriced goods because they were not allowed to shop in most towns.
Then there were the official Santa Fe publications. The November 1914 issue of Santa Fe Magazine included an article by a foreman on how to handle Mexican labor. Some excerpts:
“A great many men make the mistake of thinking them stupid. In some ways they are.”
“A peon’s mind is very much like that of a nine or ten year old child, with the difference that the child’s mind matures and the Mexican’s never does.”
“When properly handled they are willing to do a great deal for a man, often working for ridiculously low wages.”
The article closes by advising foremen to learn at least some Spanish — not to better communicate with the crew but to know if they are talking about him.
Articles published in 1912 and 1913 advised that “Mexicans must be handled like a bunch of overgrown boys” and described their “crude” lifestyle: “Tortillas, chile and beans, potatoes, eggs and coffee constitute their principal articles of diet. Their household facilities are simple, consisting principally of bunk cars, stoves for heating purposes in the winter and water.”
To obtain more information, I read Kansas newspapers on reels of microfilm and conducted interviews with some who had worked on the railroad.
I discovered a letter published in a 1927 Topeka Daily Capital written by Jose Garcia, who became a U.S. citizen and later lost his son in World War II. In response to an article questioning why more Mexicans did not become citizens, Garcia attempted to explain: “In the City of Topeka there are some theatres where they can go and some where they are not welcomed. Last summer I went to the swimming pool at Ripley Park and was informed that Mexicans could not swim there. … There are some places in this City where when a Mexican buys a lunch he is given it in a sack, to go and eat it out in the streets, because they are not allowed to sit at the counter.”
Other newspaper articles matter-of-factly reported that Mexicans were allowed in swimming pools only at night in Newton, and only on the day the water was changed in Lyons and at the Wichita YMCA. Mexican Americans still could only swim on certain days in 1950 Kansas City. In some towns, the Red Cross would not give Mexican children swimming lessons but asked parents for blood donations.
Even veterans and those who paid taxes were not allowed to sit at many drug store counters or have their hair cut in some barbershops. In other places, they were relegated to the back rows of theaters and churches. An article from the late 1940s pointed out that only a few restaurants in Emporia allowed Mexicans and that one restaurant in Wichita on East Douglas in 1945 had a sign posted that plainly told them: “Mexicans Keep Out.”
One of the oral interviews was with Joe Palacioz, then assistant city manager of Hutchinson. He told me that both of his grandfathers had come to Kansas to work on the railroad and that his mother, Consuelo Cuellar, had lived with her parents in the Newton ranchitos, red-brick section houses the railroad provided for Mexican workers. He said several families lived in the half-block long apartment building and shared a common toilet.
To put himself through Wichita State University in the late 1960s, Palacioz worked on the section crew in Newton, just as his grandfathers and father had. Determined not to have to continue track work, he practiced typing the Constitution to improve to 60 words a minute, allowing him to apply for an office job at the railroad. He went on to complete a master’s degree at WSU and serve as Hutchinson city manager for nearly two decades.
Another interview was with Santiago “Jim” Martinez, who was 8 years old when his family boarded a train north in 1915 to escape the chaos of the Mexican revolution. The train made stops along the way to deposit workers where labor was needed. The Martinez family and another couple were left in Burrton.
Jim excelled at school, and when his family returned to Mexico in 1919, he worked hard so he could return to the United States to finish his education. He returned when he was 17 and was hired on a section crew at Udall for 35 cents an hour. Though he worked there for two decades, he was never promoted above section crew laborer.
A drafting correspondence course led to a job in Hutchinson in 1942 and the opening of his own business in 1957. In 1968, he was elected to the Hutchinson city commission.
Dodge City protesters gather at Wright Park on Sept. 25, 2026, to march to U.S. Rep. Tracey Mann’s office. They were protesting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions in the community. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
With the increase in ICE arrests and deportations, I’ve thought often of the immigrants who literally built the rail arteries that ensured our state’s future.
As federal officials recently insisted the raids in southwest Kansas targeted only “heinous criminals,” I found a Sept. 19 report that showed ICE arrests had surged since mid-June, particularly for those with no criminal record. The report was compiled by the Data Deportation Project at UCLA, which obtains data from government immigration agencies through Freedom of Information Act requests.
 Only 1.6% of 41,850 ICE arrests in July were of people convicted of violent crimes, according to the report. Seventy-three percent had no criminal record at all, a jump from 45.2% in January 2025.
Then I found a 2019 master’s thesis written by Zaira Ruiz for her sociology degree from Kansas State University. She surveyed 23 first- to third-generation Hispanic workers at National Beef Packing, Liberal’s largest employer.
In it, she recounts employees describing how the chain carrying cow carcasses past blood-stained, knife-wielding employees had been gradually increased so that 3,500 cows per shift could be processed. Employees described jobs such as burning off skin, pulling out esophaguses, and cutting off ears to tag and place in baggies.
And people believe that immigrants are taking sought-after jobs from white Kansans?
Not only are they filling essential froles in the Golden Triangle of Meatpacking — Dodge City, Garden City and Liberal — Mexican immigrants have fueled the only population growth Kansas has experienced in recent decades. The 2020 Kansas census reported 382,603 Hispanic or Latino residents, a 25% increase from the prior decade, while Kansas population overall grew by only 3%.
Four counties in southwest Kansas have a greater than 50% Hispanic population. In contrast, Hispanics make up only 13% of the total Kansas population. For the same period, several counties in northwest Kansas showed double-digit percentage drops in population.
Kansas ranked fourth in the country in 2020 for number of meatpacking employees, with 17,893, according to the Economic Policy Institute. It reported that 66.8% of meatpacking employees in the United States are Hispanic and that 56% of all workers are foreign-born. The report, which relied on U.S. labor data, reported 3,600 meatpacking employees in Finney County, 5,700 in Ford and 3,500 in Seward.
A quarter of the country’s beef comes Kansas meatpacking plants, and disrupting the process increases prices even more.
While Mexican nationals were originally brought here as transient laborers, thousands put down roots, bought homes, paid taxes, became citizens, raised children and started businesses. Hispanics now make up 11.7% of the Kansas workforce and own 8.3% of businesses, according to the SBA Office of Advocacy.
Even if you ignore the vast cultural contributions Mexican immigrants have made to Kansas and the core belief that helping others improve their lives benefits everyone, the bottom line is that Kansas needs them for economic stability and growth.
Employers, schools, universities and communities need them — just as Coldwater needed a dedicated mayor. How is actively targeting people who are on the path to becoming citizens — and who want to live and work here — making Kansas a better place?
 It’s no coincidence the Mexican communities in Kansas first appeared along the main railroad lines – Kansas City, Topeka, Emporia, Newton, Wichita — and it’s no coincidence that Kansas growth is occurring in the southwest quadrant of the state, where meatpacking plants are located.
For more than a century when labor could not be found in Kansas, Mexican workers answered the call. They deserve to be treated with appreciation and respect — not threats of arrest.
Cynthia Mines’ recently released historical novel, “Heaven in a Wildflower,” incorporates experiences of the immigrants who settled in Kansas. Research for this column is based on “Riding the Rails to Kansas: Mexican Immigration,” which was funded by a National Endowment for the Humanities grant. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: ICE trackers win permanent injunction in federal censorship case
description: A federal judge granted a permanent injunction last week in favor of a Brown County man whose mobile application monitoring U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity was removed by Apple last year following pressure from the Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security. The order bars DOJ and DHS from formally or informally pressuring […[...]
text:
Brown County, Indiana, resident Mark Hodges holds up a cell phone displaying the Eyes Up app. (Photo by Crescent Peak Photography provided by Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression)A federal judge granted a permanent injunction last week in favor of a Brown County man whose mobile application monitoring U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity was removed by Apple last year following pressure from the Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security.
The order bars DOJ and DHS from formally or informally pressuring Apple to suppress Eyes Up.
The mobile application, founded by Brown County resident Mark Hodges, allows users to share videos of ICE activities.
It is one of at least two platforms targeted by federal authorities who pressured technology companies to suppress sites tracking immigration raids at the start of President Donald Trump’s second term.
The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, a First Amendment law firm, filed a lawsuit on behalf of Hodges and a Chicago activist whose Facebook group was also targeted.
“I’m glad the government agreed to stop targeting my speech, but it shouldn’t take a lawsuit to get the government to respect our constitutional rights,” Hodges said in a news release Friday. “People have a right to know what their government is doing. I hope that thanks to this lawsuit, others can share what they see and hear without facing this kind of censorship.”
U.S. District Court Judge Jorge L. Alonso granted a joint motion filed by attorneys for Mark Hodges and co-plaintiff Kate Rosado, who started a Facebook group to document ICE sightings in Chicago, and attorneys for the Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Will Ohio lawmakers pass data center legislation during lame duck?
description: One of the many questions looming over lame duck is if Ohio lawmakers will pass any data center regulations.  Ohio legislative leaders recently commented on that possibility, and didn’t rule it out.  Lawmakers went home in June without passing Ohio House Bill 646, which would, among other things, limit the size of new sales tax […]
text:
Outside Columbus, a host of data centers has transformed the Ohio countryside in just a few years. Soon, Eolian’s massive battery will deliver power in the midst of the AI hub. (Eolian)One of the many questions looming over lame duck is if Ohio lawmakers will pass any data center regulations. 
Ohio legislative leaders recently commented on that possibility, and didn’t rule it out. 
Lawmakers went home in June without passing Ohio House Bill 646, which would, among other things, limit the size of new sales tax breaks from 100% down to 50%. But this would not apply to any of the companies with existing contracts, like Meta, Google and Amazon.
“I think everything we’ve discussed before is up for discussion now. So generally speaking, it’s across the board,” Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, R-Napoleon, said when asked about data centers.
Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman, R-Lima, said he thinks H.B. 646 “was a good bill.” 
“There might be some other fine tuning, and I think that gives the protection to the local groups,” he said. “It incentivizes brownfields. It makes sure the water part and the electrical use, the tariffs are paid. … I think we need to work on (H.B. 646).”
Ohio voters sharply rejected data centers in this year’s election. 18 Ohio communities voted on whether to curb or ban data center development in this month’s election and all 18 communities voted yes. In some communities, 70 to 80% of voters voted against measures related to data center development.
“People in their local communities are really pushing back and really saying either we don’t want them or we want all these guardrails around them,” said Ohio Senate Minority Leader Nickie Antonio, D-Lakewood. “I think all of us legislators need to take a look at what they say in those local communities.”
While campaigning, Gov.-elect Amy Acton said she supports a conditional moratorium on data centers “if requirements on costs, union labor, transparency, environmental standards, community benefit agreements, and development are not met.”
In a quote on Acton’s campaign website, she specifies that data center developers should cover 100% of utility costs, along with “exclusively” building with union labor, and adhering to Ohio’s environmental standards.
“I do think, as governor-elect, Dr. Acton should certainly be setting the vision for what happens next in Ohio,” said Ohio House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn, D-Cincinnati. “But data centers are among the issues that we can and should have responsible government doing something about.”
Ohio has more than 200 data centers, the sixth-highest state in the country, according to Pew Research Center. Most of the data centers are in central Ohio. Cincinnati has 27 and Cleveland has 24, according to the Data Center Map. 
Ohio had more than 100 active moratoriums on data centers as of September. 
The state provided almost $1.57 billion in sales-tax exemptions on purchases of data center equipment and construction materials last year, according to the Ohio Department of Taxation. That’s nearly 12 times what state officials initially expected, according to estimates produced by the tax department in late 2024 as part of Ohio’s budgeting process.
Conserve Ohio, the grassroots organization behind a proposed constitutional amendment to ban new, large scale data centers, is collecting signatures to make the 2027 ballot.
Lawmakers are considering banning data center development in 16 states as of September, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. 
Follow Ohio Capital Journal Reporter Megan Henry on X, Bluesky, or Instagram.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Rise in Black voter turnout helps drive historic change in Georgia, transforming state government
description: Dondell Patterson spent much of Election Day nervously awaiting the results.  Months after launching her own unsuccessful bid for chief magistrate judge in Douglas County, the 47-year-old attorney gathered alongside fellow Democratic voters at a hotel in downtown Atlanta on election night to watch the vote count trickle in. “I think today everybody was on […[...]
text:
Cynthia Anderson, a 53-year-old insurance agent, shows off her "I voted" stickers outside a Fulton County polling place on Nov. 3, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderDondell Patterson spent much of Election Day nervously awaiting the results. 
Months after launching her own unsuccessful bid for chief magistrate judge in Douglas County, the 47-year-old attorney gathered alongside fellow Democratic voters at a hotel in downtown Atlanta on election night to watch the vote count trickle in.
“I think today everybody was on eggshells, just wishing and hoping for the best,” she said.
Dondell Patterson, a 47-year-old attorney, celebrated Democratic gains across the state on election night. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
By the end of the night, eight Black women had been elected to statewide offices, helping to flip the state blue up and down the ballot.
Patterson’s own run for office, she said, was a great learning experience, even though the outcome wasn’t what she hoped for. But being able to watch so many other Black women declare victory came as a welcome — and inspiring — shift.
“It means a lot,” she said. “I have two girls at home, and I can tell them now: You can be whatever you want. You can be a governor. You can be an attorney general. You can be secretary of state.”
In Georgia and other states across the South, Black voters have become an increasingly powerful force. Over 1.1 million Black people cast a ballot in the Peach State this year, with turnout among Black voters increasing more than 11% since Georgia’s last midterm elections in 2022. White turnout, on the other hand, shrank by 8%.


Black voters are also some of the most reliably Democratic members of Georgia’s electorate, playing a key role in pushing Democratic candidates across the finish line. According to data from the Associated Press, nine in 10 Black men voted for Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms this year, up from the roughly 75% who supported former ​​Vice President Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign in 2024. According to exit polling from NBC News, Bottoms’ share of support among Black women was even higher, with 93% casting their vote for her, up from the 91% who voted for Harris.
LaTosha Brown, a co-founder of the nonpartisan voting rights group Black Voters Matter, said she was excited to see more people engaging with the democratic process.
“For us to see that kind of increase in a midterm election is pretty significant,” Brown said.
US Supreme Court limits use of race in congressional district remaps, diluting Voting Rights Act

Brown, whose organization has spent a decade on the ground in Georgia, said that the Supreme Court’s decision to weaken a key provision of the Voting Rights Act also served as a “lightning rod” for political organizers across the South, and caused many voters of color to see the election more urgently than they had before.
“We just want fair and free elections,” she said. “I think the majority of people in this country want that, right? And so I believe that [redistricting] absolutely served as a vehicle to get people to pay more attention.”
The gains this year also went beyond the traditional Democratic strongholds of metro Atlanta, she added. Voters in rural parts of the state were also signaling a need for change, pressing for greater access to healthcare in rural areas and pushing back against the influx of data center proposals.
But the outcome of this year’s election, Brown said, was not just a reflection of the changing political tide in Georgia. Voters were hoping to put a check on policies from Republican leadership that targeted immigrants and caused large swaths of the country to lose access to aid through federal safety net programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP.
“It really does matter to us how human beings are being treated,” Brown said. “I think a lot of this is not as simple as just gas prices. I think it really is around the quality of life and our desire to have government work for us, not against us.”
Georgia House Speaker nominee Rep. Carolyn Hugley, a Columbus Democrat, speaks at a press conference on Nov. 12, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
And with the sweeping Democratic takeover of statewide offices, Black women now hold some of the most powerful roles in Georgia and are making state and national history in the process. Democratic state Rep. Tanya Miller will be the first woman to serve as Georgia’s attorney general. Penny Brown Reynolds will become the first Black secretary of state elected in Georgia. Columbus Rep. Carolyn Hugley, the current House Minority Leader, is on track to be the first Black speaker of the Georgia House of Representatives. And Keisha Lance Bottoms will become the first Black woman governor of any state.
Cynthia Anderson, a 53-year-old insurance agent who cast her vote at a Fulton County precinct on Election Day, said she was excited to see Black women finally get to be in the spotlight.
“It’s about time, because we’ve been running stuff for a long time,” she said. “Truth be told, everybody knows that Black women are capable.”
She hopes this year’s election will inspire more Black candidates to run for office in the future.
“I’m excited to see so many sisters on the ballot and expect to see more, and brothers too,” she said. “This is where it starts.”
Carol Anderson, a professor of African American studies at Emory University, said the fact that turnout among Black voters increased in a year when many states were working to redraw Black-majority districts and the federal government sought to limit access to absentee voting was a sign of overwhelming dissatisfaction with the status quo. Georgia Republican leaders convened a special session in part to consider redrawing its electoral maps, but ultimately decided against doing so after widespread outcry.
“You saw all of those things happening, trying to set up these barriers, and you have people going, ‘I will vote,’” she said. “That turnout really speaks to the realization that their vote has enormous power.” 
Georgia’s Latinos shift toward Democratic candidates, for now 

But she said that this year’s turnout in Georgia is not solely a product of the overarching political environment. Decades of grassroots organizing from figures like Stacey Abrams and organizations like Black Voters Matter, the Latino Community Fund and Asian Americans Advancing Justice helped get out the vote in minority communities over the past several election cycles. Anderson said that work was instrumental to this year’s election results.
“That diversity in the electorate, and that work at the grassroots — what I call root work — that work has been absolutely essential for what we’re seeing here, because this is a seismic shift,” Anderson said.
According to Brown, the historic success of Black women on Georgia’s statewide ticket will also likely counteract some longstanding assumptions about the electability of female candidates of color. That shift, she added, could have lasting impacts on future generations of political candidates.
“Anytime you break the glass ceiling, you let more light in the room, and so I think there is a path that’s being illuminated by the women who won,” she said. “They were able to change the political paradigm around who gets to lead, who gets to run for office, who’s electable, what’s possible.”
Voters file into the Jefferson Park Recreation Center polling place in south Fulton County. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
Among some voters, there was also an effort to move the conversation beyond candidates’ identity, with several people expressing a desire to focus more on their qualifications and policies.
Charice Parks, a 50-year-old driver who cast her vote at a Fulton County precinct on Election Day, said that as a Black woman herself, she was excited to see Bottoms become governor, but that it was her platform that drew her in.
“It’s not, to me, necessarily about color,” she said. “It’ll be a big historical thing, but it’s not about color. It’s who’s going to do right while they’re in office to help the people.”
She’s hoping that Democrats work to address the rising cost of living and implement better protections for workers, particularly pregnant workers.
Steven Maben, a 37-year-old postal worker who is Black, said he was excited about the prospect of more Black political leaders in Georgia, but that alone wouldn’t be enough for him to keep showing up for Democrats at the polls. He’s hoping that Democrats will take action to limit data center development and implement more environmental protections so that he can continue his hobby of fishing and pass his knowledge down to his kids.
“Of course I’d be proud, but at the same time I’m still looking for results,” he said. “It’d be great to put it in the book, it’d be great, but I still want results at the end of the day.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: NRDC urges incoming Benson administration to prioritize clean transportation
description: As lawmakers and state officials begin the transition to new Democratic leadership in Lansing, a national environmental organization is offering four recommendations for Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s administration to address affordability and promote clean transportation. In a new policy brief, the Natural Resources Defense Council argues that clean transit b[...]
text:
Electric vehicle chargers in Mackinaw City, funded by the Michigan Department of Environment Great Lakes and Energy. | Kyle DavidsonAs lawmakers and state officials begin the transition to new Democratic leadership in Lansing, a national environmental organization is offering four recommendations for Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s administration to address affordability and promote clean transportation.
In a new policy brief, the Natural Resources Defense Council argues that clean transit belongs at the center of any governor’s affordability agenda “because it lowers household costs while improving access, air quality, and economic resilience.”
According to the NRDC, the average Michigan family spends $17,000 a year on car payments, fuel, maintenance and insurance, making up nearly a quarter of the state’s median $72,000 household income. Among Michigan residents, transportation ranked as the second-highest household expense, behind housing. 
“High gas and diesel prices have been extremely hard on Michigan families, and we need to do more to provide affordable options. Michigan is behind on this front, and it doesn’t have to be this way,” Abby Clark, the Michigan director of government affairs at NRDC, said in a statement. “Michigan’s next governor and legislature can increase reliable transit options, safe ways to walk and bike, and access to electric vehicles that cost less to run and maintain. We can be less vulnerable to volatile gas prices and put real money back in people’s pockets.”
In the brief, the NRDC offers four policy solutions to lower transportation costs in Michigan. The first is to rewrite the state law governing how transportation tax revenue is distributed to prioritize investments to expand access to reliable public transit and safe walking and biking options and ensure tax dollars are spent on projects that will deliver the greatest impact for residents.
Whitmer signs directive transitioning the state’s fleet to zero emission vehicles by 2040

Its second recommendation urges state leaders to accelerate the deployment of electric vehicle charging equipment, which the NRDC says will help families save money by making the switch to an electric vehicle an easier choice. According to the U.S. Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels Data Center, there are 5,765 public charging ports within the state.
The NRDC also advised Benson and the Legislature to mitigate the impact of high diesel prices stemming from the war in Iran by supporting existing  grant programs administered by the Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy to reduce the price of electric trucks and help transition medium and heavy-duty vehicles to electric options.
The council also encouraged the state to lead by example by electrifying the states’ own vehicle fleets, cutting down on fuel and maintenance costs for the state government and taxpayers. 
“Clean transportation is essential to Michigan’s climate future, our public health and our economy,” NRDC Michigan Policy Director for Climate and Energy Derrell Slaughter said. “We can’t build a clean future for Michigan by cleaning up power plants alone. The cars and trucks we drive every day matter just as much.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio Gov. DeWine plans to commute more death sentences before leaving office
description: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said he is reviewing death row cases that may have gone awry in the legal process. The anti-capital punishment Republican said he is using one of his last acts as governor to save lives. There are currently 104 inmates on death row, but some may get to walk back into life […]
text:
Ohio Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. (Photo by Morgan Trau/WEWS)Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said he is reviewing death row cases that may have gone awry in the legal process. The anti-capital punishment Republican said he is using one of his last acts as governor to save lives.
There are currently 104 inmates on death row, but some may get to walk back into life without parole.
“The power of a governor to commute a sentence, to do something, goes back to the beginning of this country,” DeWine said.
With DeWine in charge, Ohio has had an unofficial pause on capital punishment.
On Monday, we asked him if he is planning on any forms of clemency for death row inmates. He explained he is reviewing the state’s cases, seeing who to commute to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
“It’s power to be exercised very carefully, and that’s what I’m trying to do now as I go through these cases,” he continued.
As a former prosecutor and attorney general, the governor said that lawyers and a jury can think a case has been ruled correctly, but that may not be accurate.
“The governor has additional authority to look at that and maybe see something else that is in there with that individual or with that particular case that maybe the jury legally couldn’t have looked at or the judge legally couldn’t have looked at,” DeWine said.
In the spring, DeWine commuted the sentence of a man with intellectual disabilities from death row to life in prison with no parole.
There have been five other removals from death row since January, according to Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Corrections reports. Three were resentenced to life by courts and two others died, which goes back to another one of the governor’s points.
“The odds of the death penalty actually being carried out are very low,” he said in June.
That fact is also why some Republicans want to restart capital punishment.
“You look at some of the most heinous, reprehensible cases that we see that wind up with somebody being placed on death row, and they say in those circumstances, ‘How are you going to deny that kind of punishment?'” Senate President Rob McColley (R-Napoleon) said.
McColley, unlike more outspoken supporters of the death penalty, sits in the middle of the debate: knowing in some cases it is warranted, but worrying about making sure all the evidence is there.
House lawmakers, like state Rep. Phil Plummer, R-Dayton, have been trying to find ways to restart the lethal injection process. He proposed legislation to allow for nitrogen gas to be used to kill inmates.
But incoming governor Dr. Amy Acton is following in DeWine’s footsteps.
“I will be continuing the moratorium,” Acton said in October.
DeWine added that he doesn’t plan on doing a blanket commutation for every inmate, like California Governor Gavin Newsom did this month.
If he commutes, the governor will likely start with Ohio Parole Board recommendations.
In August, the Board recommended clemency for Tyrone Noling, citing that there was too much uncertainty in his case. The board found that other suspects weren’t investigated, and all the co-defendants who blamed Noling recanted.

title: Ohio’s laws make it more difficult to right a wrongful conviction
description: This article was first published by The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Sign up for their newsletters, and follow them on Instagram, TikTok, Reddit and Facebook. Tim Montgomery looked down and sighed as he tried to explain why he lied to police decades ago about the 1992 murder […]
text:
Stock photo from Getty Images.This article was first published by The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Sign up for their newsletters, and follow them on Instagram, TikTok, Reddit and Facebook.
Tim Montgomery looked down and sighed as he tried to explain why he lied to police decades ago about the 1992 murder of two elderly sisters in Cleveland.
“I was not there. I said that thousands and thousands of times, but nobody will believe me. So I told them what they wanted to hear,” Montgomery testified at a hearing last year.
A prosecutor continued to press him about his past statements implicating him and Terry Ferrell in the home invasion and murders of Mary Mosberger, 82, and Loretta Fallat, 77.
“You want the truth?” Montgomery shot at the prosecutor from the witness stand. “I’m trying to give it to you. Nobody wants to hear the truth.”
Ferrell, stone-faced until then, leaned back in his seat and shot an approving glance at his wife, Jessica, in the gallery of the stuffy Cuyahoga County courtroom.
The hearing was a milestone in Ferrell’s two-decade-long effort to prove his innocence, which still isn’t over. An appeals court will hear Ferrell’s case Tuesday, highlighting the long and difficult road for people in Ohio prisons who say they were wrongfully convicted.
A task force convened by the Ohio Supreme Court studied the state’s drawn-out process for addressing wrongful conviction claims. At the top of its 2022 list of recommendations were changes to state law and procedure that would have sped up new trial requests.
But no one has enacted those reforms.
Instead, judges have continued to ignore or dismiss credible claims of new evidence. Delays in processing new trial requests for defendants who were later exonerated have cost taxpayers millions of additional dollars in wrongful imprisonment settlements.
All the while, people who actually committed crimes have not been brought to justice, and families are in court for decades after losing a loved one.
Across from Ferrell’s wife sat relatives of Mosberger and Fallat, who lived next door to Ferrell and his family on Seymour Avenue in Cleveland.
In December 1992, a relative found the sisters dead in their ransacked home. Cleveland police canvassed the neighborhood. Within days, investigators had Ferrell, 21, in jail. He was fingerprinted, questioned and released without being charged.
No physical evidence tied Ferrell, or anyone, to the crime. The case went cold.
Five years later, detectives finally caught a break after a 12-year-old neighbor led them to Montgomery. They questioned Montgomery but didn’t charge him. Another five years passed until a jailhouse informant who cut a deal to avoid prison time came forward as the state’s star witness.
At the trial in 2003, prosecutors argued that Ferrell and another man, who has never been identified, led Montgomery into the sisters’ home on the night of their murders.
Ferrell’s attorneys questioned the lack of evidence linking their client to the crime, how witnesses waited a decade to speak up, and a timeline for the murders that included hours when Ferrell was at a bar or a friend’s house.
A jury found Ferrell guilty of murder, aggravated burglary and kidnapping. The judge sentenced him to life without the possibility of parole.
Montgomery, who didn’t testify at Ferrell’s trial, pleaded guilty to aggravated burglary and served three years in prison for his alleged role in the crime.
Ferrell exhausted the regular appeals process in 2006. He filed motions from his prison cell to preserve evidence, which Cuyahoga County Judge John J. Russo denied. In 2016, Russo appointed Ferrell an attorney, who successfully pushed for DNA testing. It would take eight years to complete that testing due to crime lab delays and objections from prosecutors. Finally, in 2024, Ferrell’s new legal team convinced Russo to hold evidentiary hearings in pursuit of a new trial.
In several hours-long hearings over the course of six months, Ferrell’s attorneys presented a slew of new evidence: The jailhouse informant who had been the state’s star witness recanted his testimony. Detectives had developed alternative suspects, but they were never discussed at trial. And DNA on the murder weapons didn’t belong to Ferrell or the victims.
Despite all that, Russo denied Ferrell’s request for a new trial in January.
Ferrell appealed Russo’s decision. A panel of judges in Ohio’s Eighth District Court of Appeals is set to hear the case Nov. 10. It could be Ferrell’s best chance to have his conviction overturned.
Defense attorneys and prosecutors declined to comment while the case is ongoing. A relative of Mosberger and Fallat also declined to comment.

It can be difficult to impossible for older prisoners like Ferrell to prove that evidence was withheld in their cases.
The 1963 U.S. Supreme Court case Brady vs. Maryland enshrined the requirement that prosecutors share any evidence that might help a defendant through what is called discovery. The ruling made full disclosure through open discovery the national standard in criminal law. Well into the 2000s, though, many states allowed a less transparent process called closed discovery.
In Ohio, that meant prosecutors didn’t have to share paper copies of witness statements, police reports or other documents. They only had to read the files to defense attorneys in closed-door pre-trial meetings. Prosecutors kept no record of what was — or wasn’t — shared.
After sustained critiques in the press, Cuyahoga County judges unanimously voted in 2008 to adopt open discovery. The Ohio Supreme Court required open discovery statewide in 2010.
More than 1,000 Cuyahoga County defendants, including Ferrell, are still serving time in Ohio prisons after being convicted during the era of closed discovery, according to a Marshall Project review of state corrections department data.
“It was a very dangerous time for the possibility of wrongful convictions taking place because of the opaque nature of how discovery was conducted,” said Mike Donnelly, a former Ohio Supreme Court Justice who was trained to practice closed discovery as an assistant Cuyahoga County prosecutor early in his career.
The attorneys who filed Ferrell’s motion for a new trial have gathered nearly a thousand pages of police reports that included interviews and evidence that were not introduced at the trial. Witnesses had contradicted themselves or the prosecution’s timeline. Police had other suspects, including a man who admitted his involvement after pawning an item stolen from the crime scene.
Ferrell’s original attorneys — Jack Hildebrand and William McGinty, who each had decades of experience in criminal defense — said at the hearings last year that they no longer could remember what was shared with them during closed discovery. That made it harder for Ferrell to prove that prosecutors improperly withheld evidence. But they both testified that they would have used such exculpatory evidence during the trial if they had it.

No one knows how often Ohio prisoners seek new trials. Anecdotally, attorneys say judges often ignore such requests or reject them without ever weighing any evidence.
In 2022, local judges, defense attorneys and the few prosecutors on the Ohio Supreme Court’s task force recommended that state officials address a litany of often insurmountable court procedures that stall efforts to seek new trials.
For four years, neither the legislature nor the Ohio Supreme Court has made those changes.
“There’s a definite need for reform,” said attorney Rachel Troutman with the Exoneration Project, a legal clinic at the University of Chicago Law School that fights to overturn wrongful convictions in Ohio and other states. “A lot of innocent people get turned away by the court for procedural matters.”
To get a new trial, Ohio defendants must prove that they were deprived of a fair trial due to errors beyond their control. The most common of those errors, according to attorneys, is the withholding of evidence that could have helped in their defense. Still, the burden falls on defendants to show that it was not possible for them to uncover that evidence prior to their convictions.
Unlike in other states, credible evidence of a person’s innocence is not grounds for seeking a new trial in Ohio, and only people who pursue new trials while on death row are guaranteed attorneys. Troutman said Illinois offers a better model by ensuring legal counsel in post-conviction hearings and allowing new trial requests based solely on innocence claims.
Ohio prisoners with limited resources are forced to fumble around on their own to uncover new evidence and to fight without an attorney to convince a judge to hear what they may find. Ohio state Rep. Josh Williams, a Toledo-area Republican, reintroduced a bipartisan bill last year that would require judges to act on new trial requests with credible evidence.
“We’ve seen individuals waiting in prison without judges making decisions,” said Williams, who is also an attorney. His bill has not yet moved out of committee and its future is uncertain.
Since 2013, at least 10 people who were convicted in Cuyahoga County have been collectively awarded more than $50 million in settlements for their wrongful imprisonments. Seven of them were initially denied new trial requests before their exonerations.
One of them was Michael Buehner, who was convicted of murder in 2002. Buehner, like Ferrell, fought for about a decade from behind bars before his court-appointed attorneys discovered two exonerating eyewitness statements among 30 previously withheld police reports. Still, for years Buehner was denied motions for an evidentiary hearing and a new trial.
Ultimately, the appellate court reversed those decisions. A new jury found Buehner not guilty. Last year, he was awarded nearly $2 million for his 21 years of wrongful imprisonment.
“Because of all of those years of fighting, that’s more money that they got paid,” said Troutman. “It’s the state costing itself more money by not holding a hearing on the merits.”

In 2024, Ferrell’s new attorney, public defender Cullen Sweeney, motioned the prosecutor’s office to release all the evidence in Ferrell’s case, revealing for the first time the full scope of their investigation into the killings of Mosberger and Fallat.
The records showed that, nearly five years after the murders, a child in the neighborhood pointed police to a potential suspect: Montgomery. The boy told police he saw Montgomery, whom he could not recall by name until questioned again years later, hop a fence the night of the murders. Police took Montgomery in for questioning. He insisted that he wasn’t there.
Thinking he would avoid charges, Montgomery eventually said he followed Ferrell and another man into the home. Then he tried to withdraw that statement, saying he made it up so police would let him go, according to the detective’s summary of the 1997 interrogation.
On the witness stand in the 2025 hearings, Montgomery said that Cleveland Homicide Detective Gary Garisek and an FBI agent who was with him were laser-focused on Ferrell. Montgomery said he tried to tell the truth. “They would not believe the truth when I told them. So I told them what the hell they wanted to hear.”
Garisek died in 2009.
At the hearings last year, the state’s star witness from Ferrell’s trial, jailhouse informant Stephen Lenchak, also recanted.
Lenchak grew up on Seymour Avenue. He knew Ferrell like a “scary uncle” from the neighborhood, he said. In 2002, while awaiting trial on unrelated burglary and theft charges, Lenchak said he was starving, deprived of phone calls and brutalized daily by other men in the county jail.
Detectives told him his way out would be to testify against Ferrell and find others to do the same. Lenchak said Garisek left him alone in a conference room with a phone and the case file, complete with photos of the crime scene.
“If I can call these people and have them come in to talk to this homicide detective, he would bring me out of the dorm every day, feed me, and he would eventually get me out of this hell that I was in,” Lenchak told Judge Russo last year, even after being advised that he could be charged with perjury for recanting his trial testimony.
Lenchak, who got the lightest sentence possible on his own case, was one of three jailhouse informants to cut deals and testify against Ferrell. He also gave Garisek names of people, including Ferrell’s ex-girlfriends, who testified at the trial that Ferrell threatened to kill them like he did the sisters.
But it was all a lie, Lenchak testified. And he’d felt guilty for decades about his role in convicting Ferrell.
Judge Russo took a couple of months to consider whether any of the new evidence would have swayed the jurors who convicted Ferrell. Then, in a 15-page opinion issued in January, he denied Ferrell a new trial after applying “the utmost suspicion” to Lenchak’s recantation and discounting the newly discovered DNA and previously undisclosed records.
Before issuing his decision, Russo said he knew it was likely to be appealed by one side or the other.
Donnelly, the former Supreme Court justice, said he disagreed with Russo’s decision to deny Ferrell a new trial, but credited him for at least holding the evidentiary hearings. Because Ohio law doesn’t mandate it, too many judges simply never hold hearings on new evidence that might exonerate someone, he said.
“Look at any of these anecdotes where people have been exonerated and how long it took them to fight in a system that values finality over the truth,” Donnelly said. “Most of the time, they are fighting not that they’re innocent — it’s just for the opportunity to be heard.”

 Catching Our Eye

• Ground stop. The New York Times’ Karoun Demirjian is reporting, “Ground stop highlights chronic vulnerabilities in air traffic system.”
The ground stop that brought air travel across the country to a halt Friday evening highlighted persistent weaknesses in the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure, which has had several disruptive failures in recent months.
Two months ago, a circuit failure and severed fiber optic cable caused crippling ground stops and delays at airports along the East Coast. Smaller outages unfolded in October at Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina and George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston, when contractors accidentally cut into fiber line.The Friday ground stop, which was only the third the F.A.A. has issued this century, eclipsed the fallout of previous air traffic communications equipment failures.
• The governor. The Columbus Dispatch’s Laura Bischoff is reporting, “Mike DeWine’s 50 years in Ohio politics comes to a close.”
Whether cutting a ribbon on a renovated highway rest stop or guiding Ohio through a global pandemic, no assignment was too big or too small for Republican Mike DeWine as he served eight years as governor.
Over his nearly 50-year political career, DeWine likely attended more events, held more press conferences, shook more hands and navigated more crises than any politician in Ohio history.
• Congress. Ideastream Public Media is reporting, “Democrats hire independent firm to investigate harassment allegation against Brian Poindexter.”
U.S. House Democrats are investigating a sexual harassment complaint lodged by a campaign staffer against U.S. Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter.
Poindexter defeated incumbent Republican Max Miller to claim the seat for Ohio’s 7th Congressional District.
According to reports from media outlets including CNN and Politico, a campaign aide filed a complaint alleging Poindexter made comments that made her uncomfortable.
