title: Maui Police Commission’s Secret Agenda To Deal With Its Outspoken Chief
description:
Here we go again. Another public board planning to debate and take action on the performance of a top public official behind closed doors. Something that state law and the Hawaiʻi Supreme Court says needs to be done openly and in full public view. This time it’s the Maui Police Commission. The commission plans to […]
The post Maui Police Commission’s Secret [...]
text:
Here we go again. Another public board planning to debate and take action on the performance of a top public official behind closed doors. Something that state law and the Hawaiʻi Supreme Court says needs to be done openly and in full public view.
This time it’s the Maui Police Commission. The commission plans to meet on Wednesday and has outlined an extensive agenda for an executive session that appears intended to lay the groundwork for firing Maui Police Chief John Pelletier. 
He was put on paid leave by the commission in October while it conducted an administrative investigation into his oversight of MPD’s Criminal Intelligence Unit. The unit’s top officer, Lt. Michael Vaituulala, was arrested in August and has been charged in federal court with taking bribes to protect chicken fighting and drug operations. 
A few days after he was put on leave Pelletier held a press conference where he blasted the commission, demanded his job back and revealed that Maui Mayor Richard Bissen has been the subject of two criminal investigations, including a felony case being conducted by MPD. Bissen says that’s not true.
A secret session where commissioners talk about their unhappiness with the police chief and consider whether to get rid of him permanently is just wrong for a number of reasons. First and foremost, what’s happening on Maui with its police department, its chief and its mayor is of significant interest to the public and our fundamental right to know how the government is operating. 
There is nothing more important for citizens to scrutinize than the actions of police who wield extraordinary power over ordinary citizens. The Maui Police Department’s reputation for corruption and misconduct goes back decades. The previous chief lost his job after he backed his truck into a motorcycle in a parking garage and tried to cover it up. Vaituulala was already in place as head of the special investigations unit when Pelletier took over.
Pelletier, a former captain with the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, was hired over local candidates at the urging of residents concerned that nothing would change if internal promotions continued. Those Police Commission members who hired Pelletier have largely been replaced by commissioners who have taken over since Bissen has been in office. Only two of the nine commissioners were appointed by the previous mayor. Bissen has appointed some of the current members, the County Council put others in place and a couple have been brought forward by Maui’s Independent Nomination Board, a panel that some Maui residents say is also stacked with Bissen’s allies.
Maui residents concerned over what is happening with Pelletier are already mobilizing, for and against the chief. Soon after he was put on leave, dozens of people including current and former officers, business leaders and residents staged a solidarity rally to show their support for him.



A Special Commentary Project
Civil Beat is focusing on transparency, accountability and ethics in government and other institutions. Help us by sending ideas and anecdotes to sunshine@civilbeat.org.





Read More

Pelletier has the backing of members of the Maui Police Department’s Multicultural Advisory Counsel (purposely spelled that way), a group of people who had generally been anti-police activists that he called together soon after taking over as chief five years ago. 
Counsel vice chair Keisa Liu put together a 30-page analysis of the Police Commission’s decision to place Pelletier on leave and concluded the action was unwarranted and damaging to the department. She has been circulating that along with documentation of questionable political connections between Bissen and the commission to the Maui County Council, the Maui Ethics Commission, the Commission on Judicial Conduct (Bissen is a former judge) and the Campaign Spending Commission.
“I read the documents, studies, laws, and rules. I examined the decision within the larger systems of Maui County government,” she wrote to the Police Commission earlier this month, urging that the chief be reinstated. “I couldn’t understand why, with everything this chief brought to the table and the facts presented, you were putting him on administrative leave. After your glowing review. After corrective measures were quickly implemented. After recognizing the weight of his accomplishments for the department. He still has the potential to do so much more for us.”
The Maui Police Commission is planning to hold extensive closed-door discussions about Police Chief John Pelletier on Wednesday despite the Sunshine Law requiring public boards deal with matters involving top public officials in the open. (Cammy Clark/Civil Beat/2024)
On the other side, a group calling itself The Peace Officers Think-Tank Guild of Hawaiʻi wants Pelletier out. Self-described as “resolute anonymous citizens,” including current and retired state and county cops, the group has written two recent letters to the commission complaining that besides forcing some officers to leave the department Pelletier is working four days a week, 10-hours a day which they say is fine for officers but not for the chief. The 4/10 shift is one of numerous things on the commission’s executive session agenda for next week.
Also on the agenda is an item that should raise concerns for Oʻahu residents. The Maui commission is apparently getting help from the severely understaffed Honolulu Police Commission to investigate Pelletier and other Maui officers’ involvement in a Jan. 1 fireworks incident that caused extensive property damage and also played a role in the federal bribery charges against Vaituulala. Not only is the Honolulu commission struggling to fill investigator and staff positions (including its own executive officer) but no mention of Maui’s request has been made public or acted on by commissioners on Oʻahu. That raises serious questions about Sunshine Law violations by the Honolulu commission, too.
Beyond the obvious broad public interest in the commission’s actions, there’s the very public feud between Pelletier and Bissen that deserves deeper examination. Elements of it appear in the Police Commission’s upcoming executive session agenda and in letters written by the anonymous Peace Officers Think-Tank Guild. The public needs to know if Pelletier is right when he says that Bissen has been working for years to undermine him and orchestrate his ouster.
It is public record that Bissen opposed Pelletier’s hiring and wrote a letter to the commission supporting then-deputy chief Vic Ramos. Pelletier has accused Bissen of foul play in the past five years including trying to get the Police Commission to put him on leave in 2025 — the commission refused. That was after a wild civil suit was filed in California claiming the chief had been an enforcer for hip-hop star Diddy Combs. That crazy case, which included two anonymous plaintiffs and a few celebrity defendants, was eventually tossed by a federal judge after the plaintiffs failed to file basic paperwork supporting their case.
But the defense cost Pelletier thousands of dollars and he was forced to defend himself publicly in the small island community. He’s spoken angrily about it in a couple public forums, blaming Bissen for exacerbating the situation that created problems for him and his family.
Maui Mayor Richard Bissen is in the middle of a dispute between the Maui police chief and the police commission, making it all the more important for the public to know what’s going on.  (Matthew Thayer/Civil Beat/2026)
Besides all that, the Police Commission itself deserves public scrutiny. The nine commissioners should openly discuss their concerns with Pelletier and make it clear they are not just tools of the mayor, as Pelletier has said.
There’s reason to be concerned. Several commissioners have been significant political contributors to Bissen in his last two elections, a review of Campaign Spending Commission records shows. Don Cameron has donated $2,480, Joseph Arias has given $3,000 and Shackley Raffetto has donated $2,000. They are three of the newest appointees. Lahela Aiwohi, who was appointed by the previous mayor, gave Bissen $1,060 in 2026, records show.
Another commissioner, Toni Rojas, is the daughter of Bissen’s director of economic development.
Even Vaituulala, the lieutenant under investigation by the feds for bribery, gave Bissen $250 in 2022. And he’s related to one of the current police commissioners.
All of this argues that Maui is one very small town indeed. And the public deserves to know how connections — whether financial, familial or something else — are affecting their police operation and their public safety.
Mainly, though, it’s the law. The Sunshine Law requires that hiring, firing and job evaluations of our top government officials be done publicly. The argument that “it’s a personnel matter” and has to be confidential went out the window nearly a decade ago when the Hawaiʻi Supreme Court ruled in another police commission case that the public has a significant interest in the performance of high-level government officials. 
That happened after the Honolulu Police Commission secretly gave then-Chief Louis Kealoha a $250,000 payoff while he was under federal investigation for abuse of power for framing his wife’s uncle for stealing a mailbox to gain the advantage in a civil case the family was in the midst of. Two years later, in 2019, the high court made it clear that privacy of the official only outweighs the public interest in very narrow circumstances, such as discussion of someone’s medical issue. Otherwise, discussion, debate and certainly any action must take place in open session.
“This should not be done behind closed doors,” says Brian Black of the Public First Law Center, which brought the Kealoha case to the Supreme Court nearly 10 years ago and has argued these cases time and again — and won. 
In 2025, the law center prevailed again in a case against the Agribusiness Development Corp. and Defenders Council that resulted in the Office of Information Practices essentially retracting an old opinion and notifying state agencies and boards that the Hawaiʻi Supreme Court had clarified this issue.
And yet, here we are. Again.
Black has filed testimony with the commission urging it to reconsider the executive session agenda items and warning that consequences of violating the Sunshine Law include that whatever action it takes can be overturned and members could face misdemeanor charges.
In Pelletier’s case, the Maui County Charter says a police chief can only be fired for cause, malfeasance being the specific offense. And that can only happen after formal charges are filed and a hearing is held. At that point, it’s considered a contested case hearing and should be public.
But Pelletier is not waiting for that to get his day in court, so to speak. He intends to push the Police Commission to operate openly starting with Wednesday’s meeting.
“Apparently they’re getting ready to fire him and we object to it all being done in secret,” says Eric Seitz, Pelletier’s attorney. “We’re going to ask it all be done out in the open.”

title: Beth Fukumoto: Hawaiʻi Makes It Hard For Independents Like Brenton Awa
description:

The post Bet[...]
text:
On election night, following his decisive loss in Congressional District 2, state Sen. Brenton Awa said voters had stuck with their parties. Three days later, he quit his.
Awa was one of the Hawai‘i Republican Party’s most promising candidates. A former KITV anchor and reporter, he unseated Democratic Sen. Gil Riviere in 2022, won reelection in 2024 and became Senate minority leader. Along the way he built a real following, with more than 100,000 followers on Instagram, and a reputation for both candor and controversy.
Awa’s say-it-like-it-is approach plays a little like a Hawai‘i-specific version of the Trump-style that Republicans have adopted nationally. In 2023, he told a Hawaiian cultural leader she would have been hanged for not supporting a Hawaiian and refused to apologize. In his first speech as minority leader, a joke about “mahus” drew criticism from some trans rights advocates.
Yet much of that speech centered on the economic factors causing Hawai‘i residents to move away. Awa said, “our government solution to housing has been for us to move out of state,” and promised his caucus would “resist all decisions that force locals to leave.”
He has kept that focus since his first campaign, and his message resonates because he says what many local families feel. Even a health educator who condemned the mahu line said that he agrees with Awa on many issues affecting Native Hawaiians, and Civil Beat’s Sunshine Blog, which called the speech’s remarks incendiary, said he was trying to make important points about the cost of living.
His frustration with how leaders deliver for local families is what brought Awa to the Republican Party in the first place. When he first ran in 2022, he said he couldn’t bring himself to run as a Democrat because he believed the party had let corruption fester, criticizing deals struck behind closed doors and state agencies that weren’t listening to people in his district.
In October, Pāʻele Kiakona, who is the first Green Party candidate elected to the Hawaiʻi Legislature, expressed a similar frustration. He told me that after the Lahaina fire, legislators signed a Lahaina Strong pledge and took a picture with the group, then voted against what they had pledged to support. “People are going to another party because they don’t see the progress that they would hope to see,” he said.
Pa’ele Kiakona fields emails during a break in his working the land at Kaiaulu Initiatives mala above Lahaina. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Running as an anti-establishment Democrat, a Republican or a third-party candidate are three routes to challenge the status quo. Now, Awa is trying a fourth. On election night, after he lost his race for Congress, he told HPR he was thinking of leaving the GOP because Hawaiʻi voters were reluctant to back anyone with an “R” next to their name and that his push to bring local values to the party hadn’t won it more votes. On Nov. 6, he resigned from the party to become an independent.
Serving as an independent in the Legislature is logistically straightforward. Between leaving the Republican Party and joining the Democratic caucus in 2017, I was a temporary independent, and the system adapted well. I kept my committee assignments and floor vote. The only real inconvenience: without a caucus, I had to use public bathrooms farther from the House floor.
Winning reelection as an independent is another matter entirely. Reaching the ballot is simple, since a legislative candidate needs only 15 signatures. The problem is getting out of the primary. Under state law, a nonpartisan candidate advances only with 10% of all the votes cast for the office, or as many votes as the weakest party nominee received.
When I first ran as a Republican, I gave similar reasons, feeling that the party in power was ignoring the economic struggles facing our community during the Great Recession. I believed the Republican Party might pay attention to my community. Later, I realized there were dissident Democrats who wanted the same changes I did and found my values actually matched theirs more closely.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

That 10% sounds low until you look at our primary ballot. A voter can choose one party’s ballot or the nonpartisan one. If a voter chooses an independent candidate for state Senate and votes in the Democratic race for governor, their ballot isn’t counted. So a vote for an independent costs a voter every partisan race.
For Awa, that means winning roughly 900 votes from people willing to skip the often more competitive partisan primaries in top ticket races. In this year’s primary, only 1.84% of voters chose the nonpartisan ballot, and a nonpartisan legislative candidate hasn’t reached 10% since at least 2010.
No other state works this way. In 44 states, an independent candidate for the Legislature goes straight onto the November ballot, usually by gathering signatures, and five more put every candidate on one primary ballot. Hawaiʻi is the only state that keeps party primaries and still makes independents run in them with a required threshold to advance.
Under these current rules, Awa’s only viable path is a nonpartisan post such as Honolulu City Council or mayor. Honolulu uses a top-two runoff system, which allowed Mayor Rick Blangiardi to win as an independent in 2020.
Awa appears interested. On election night, he said he would likely consider a mayoral run. Beyond City Hall, however, independents have few options, since the Legislature, governor and Congress all run through party primaries.
If Hawaiʻi wanted to change that, the Legislature has two clear models to consider. The first is what most states do: let independents petition onto the November ballot. Even if the signature requirement is higher, it’s still fairer than forcing candidates to choose a party, start a new one, or ask voters to skip other partisan races. And, asking for community support is a great way to vet candidates.
The second is changing the primary itself, so every candidate runs on one ballot. Alaska sends the top four to November, where voters rank them, and five of the 40 members of its House were independents going into this month’s election. Honolulu voters rejected ranked-choice voting this month, but the Legislature could (and should) still take it up.
The Legislature has already looked at a simpler version. Senate Bill 2480, which Awa voted for in committee this year, would send the top two to November and repeal the 10% bar, though it was sent back to committee and died there. In California, the top-two system has elected at least one independent candidate. Chad Mayes won reelection to the Assembly in 2020 with no party preference.
That said, small parties opposed the bill. The Libertarian Party of Hawai‘i testified that “Libertarians and other non-dominant voices would routinely be eliminated in the primary round.” I’d argue that Kiakona is a great example of why a good candidate with community support could benefit from an all-party primary system. While he received 181 votes on the Green primary ballot, he received 3,025 in November. On one ballot where voters can split their tickets, a candidate like him would likely do far better in the primary than our system allows now.
So, when the Legislature seats two members who belong to neither major party in January, we should remember how they got there. One left his party, and the other ran a third-party campaign. Neither got there the way an independent candidate would have to, and that’s worth fixing.

title: The Sunshine Blog: Have The Inmates Taken Over The Asylum?
description:
The Sunshine Blog was surprised and happy to see that last week's meeting of the Hawaiʻi Elections Commission -- the first in five months -- was much less acrimonious and a heck of a lot shorter than in the past. The politically polarized commission even managed to elect a pro tem chair to serve until members can find a permanent one.
The post The Sunshine B[...]
text:
Election resurrection: What a turnaround. People were mostly really nice to each other. No one got kicked out of the meeting. And it lasted just under three hours.
The Sunshine Blog was surprised and happy to see that last week’s meeting of the Hawaiʻi Elections Commission — the first in five months — was much less acrimonious and a heck of a lot shorter than in the past. The politically polarized commission even managed to elect a pro tem chair to serve until members can find a permanent one.
But, alas, all is not hunky-dory. Only five of the eight commissioners tuned into the Zoom meeting and only one of those was a commissioner appointed by Democrats. The other three Dem-appointed members skipped the meeting.
The next meeting is scheduled for Thursday, but commissioner John Sabas — the sole Dem who made it to the Nov. 12 meeting — will be out of town. Good luck reaching quorum, let alone agreeing on new agenda items. The commission has also seen a lot of turnover, and it would not be a surprise to see more commissioners bail.
The commission fell apart in June when it could not reach consensus on a chair, who would also be the ninth member. Two of the candidates at the time, Ralph Cushnie and Tamara McKay, are now running the show, with McKay (pronounced makai) getting the unanimous nod to be the temporary chair.
McKay is clearly a nice and capable person who has boned up on administrative procedure and Robert’s Rules of Order, something a chair must master. But many of the same people who tuned in to testify raised the same gripes that have long slowed the business of the commission.
It includes a lot of personal attacks, especially on commissioners who disagree with Cushnie, who has led investigations into whether Hawaiʻi’s 2024 election was fair and valid. Some of those attacking the commission are also pushing for the abolition of mail-in voting and a  return to election day-only voting. 
They also really really really want to get rid of Chief Election Officer Scott Nago. Some still accuse him of treason and other criminal acts. One testifier said he should be fired and forced to leave the islands. Yikes.
The Hawaiʻi Elections Commission meeting Thursday.  (Screenshot/2026)
But the Elections Commission also has substantive matters before it that Nago may ultimately have to answer for. One of those who is not too happy with him is Rep. Kanani Souza, who ultimately was reelected even though she was knocked out after the primary by the Elections Office’s tiebreaker lottery-like drawing. It took a Supreme Court ruling to get her back on the ballot where voters had the final say.
“The recent controversy surrounding the method used to resolve a tied legislative race is one example,” Rep. Kanani Souza wrote in her testimony. “Questions have also been raised about voters receiving ballots for the wrong district. These are not matters that should be dismissed or left unresolved. They warrant a thorough examination of the procedures, oversight, and leadership responsible for ensuring that elections are conducted properly.”
Cushnie has raised concerns about the quality of advice Nago’s Office of Elections was getting from Deputy Attorney General Jordan Ching when Cushnie and McKay urged the Elections Office to allow the Elections Commission to meet. The two commissioners had to take their case to the Hawaiʻi Supreme Court, which ordered the commission to get back to work with the office’s help. Cushnie now wants the commission to hire its own legal counsel.
The Elections Commission did not meet during the primary and general election. Thus far, it has not been able to review any objections or complaints lodged about both elections, which is actually a core part of their unpaid jobs. At least for now, McKay seems committed to ensuring that they do exactly that.



A Special Commentary Project
Civil Beat is focusing on transparency, accountability and ethics in government and other institutions. Help us by sending ideas and anecdotes to sunshine@civilbeat.org.





Read More

Survival of the unfittest:  And speaking of Democrats who went MIA last week, to use a baseball term: It was a swing and a miss. 
Democrats had the chance to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for high crimes and misdemeanors related to his handling of the Iran War, abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and extrajudicial killings on the high seas. 
But House Republicans successfully blocked the efforts, which was spearheaded by one of their own, U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, because 11 Democrats didn’t show up to vote. Some of them said they were stuck in D.C. traffic. The impeachment effort failed 211 to 204.  
Hawaiʻi Reps. Ed Case and Jill Tokuda both managed to find their way to the vote on time. And both voted to move the impeachment effort along.
Case told Civil Beat’s Nick Grube that while he wished his Democratic colleagues had shown up for the vote he doesn’t see it as an indication of the party’s ability to take charge once they’re in the majority come January. 
Case believes Hegseth still deserves to be impeached. The Defense Secretary has  obstructed congressional oversight by withholding information, including about the cost of the Iran War, and has undermined merit-based military promotions by sidelining or blocking officers for political reasons, such as for their connection to the military’s Covid-19 vaccine policy or the withdrawal from Afghanistan.
Some of the information Hegseth has provided, Case said, has been inaccurate, twisted or misrepresented.
Democrats had a chance to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth last week but too many missed the meeting. It appears they will be taking up the question again next year.  (Andrew Harnik/Pool via AP)
“He completely dismisses and does not fundamentally understand the role of Congress in overseeing the largest portion of our entire federal budget and an area that has life or death consequences,” Case says. “I’m not prepared to accept any longer a secretary that is in charge of a department and leads a culture of basically blowing Congress off.”
Whether that means Hegseth will face impeachment in the new Congress remains to be seen. After the failed vote this week, House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries said: “This is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning.” 
But Case said that he and many of his Democratic colleagues are not in the mood for  “endless impeachment proceedings,” especially given the many other priorities aimed at reducing costs and improving affordability. 
If Democrats do take another swing at ousting Hegseth, he said he’d prefer a more methodical approach, one that includes hearings and gathering evidence, rather than a forced vote by an outgoing Republican during a lame-duck session. This time around he felt that Democrats were pressured into voting for Hegseth’s impeachment before they were ready. 
“This is not how most Democrats want to deal with oversight of this administration,” Case says. “I would welcome a very deliberate analysis of Secretary Hegseth’s conduct in office, and if that led to a proposed impeachment of him, I would be willing to do it.”
Family feud?: Also in the nation’s capital, Congress has been considering a controversial permitting reform bill that’s dividing members and led to a lot of hand-wringing among conservationists, including those in the islands.
Count Hawaiʻi’s two Democratic senators among the delegations who split their votes this week while advancing the proposal.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act seeks to make it easier to build energy and infrastructure projects, such as pipelines, offshore wind farms and data centers, by accelerating environmental and cultural reviews and making it harder for lawsuits to halt progress. 
Proposed national legislation that seeks to make it easier to build major infrastructure while raising environmental concerns has split Hawaiʻi’s two senators. Schatz is for, Hirono against. (AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana/2023)
Proponents of the measures, including U.S. Sen Brian Schatz, have said that this will help get clean energy projects off the ground and lead to cheaper, faster electricity and drive down energy costs for Americans while creating good-paying jobs.  
“This bill is a bipartisan compromise,” he said, “and deals like this are tough.”
Opponents, however, warn that such reforms will also make it easier for polluters in the gas and oil industry to trample over existing environmental protections as well as those that seek to protect Indigenous lands and cultures. 
That’s why U.S. Sen. Mazie Hirono said she couldn’t go along with the bill as currently constituted and voted against it with 24 other senators, including several of her progressive colleagues.  Hirono’s staff told Civil Beat she was particularly concerned about the bill diminishing the voice of Indigenous communities while locking in fossil fuel projects that she said were hastily approved by President Donald Trump’s administration without a chance for amendment or revocation.  
Schatz, who is the ranking member on the Indian Affairs Committee, said that changes had been made to the bill to make sure that federal agencies consults with Native Hawaiian organizations and tribes about the potential impacts future projects might have on historic and cultural resources. 
“I understand these changes won’t be enough for everyone to support the bill,” he said, “but we’ll continue working to ensure Native Hawaiian organizations and Tribes have a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their communities.”
Local environmental and Indigenous rights groups have lined up in opposition to the bill, including the NDN Collective, Sierra Club of Hawaiʻi, Earthjustice and Local Power Hawaiʻi, calling it an “end-run” around bedrock environmental and cultural protections, such as the Endangered Species Act, Clean Water Act and National Environmental Policy Act. They want to pause work on the bill until Democrats are fully in control of Congress which starts in January.
As of now the Senate is expecting its final vote on the bill next week. 
Cabinet maker: Gov. Josh Green continues to make more changes to his second-term Cabinet.
The latest new face, The Blog hears, is Robert Yu as director of the Department of Budget and Finance. He was president and general manager of Oahu Transit Services and a member of the Honolulu Authority for Rapid Transportation board. Yu would succeed Seth Colby, if confirmed by the state Senate.
George “Rick” Bruno, meanwhile, may be named by Green to run the Department of Health, sources tell The Blog. He was formerly president of The Queen’s Medical Center. Bruno, if appointed and if confirmed by the Senate, would succeed Kenny Fink.

name: VTDigger
title: Spend our tax dollars on healthcare, not pricey consultants
description:
Nearly six years after McKinsey settled with Vermont over its role in the opioid crisis, the state is handing the consulting firm $5.1 million meant to shore up rural healthcare.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Spend our tax dollars on healthcare, not pricey consultants.
text:
Dear Editor,
I read with interest the VTDigger article of Nov. 2 about how Vermont is using the $195 million in Rural Health Transformation funding. As someone who uses the services of Brattleboro Memorial Hospital, I am keenly aware of the financial challenges it and other rural hospitals are facing. As access to birthing care has shrunk, I am relieved that Brattleboro Memorial will receive funding to keep birthing care accessible in southeastern Vermont.
I was less pleased, however, to see that $5.1 million is being granted to McKinsey, a high-priced consulting firm notorious for its role in the 2008 subprime mortgage debacle, for consulting with authoritarian governments and for insider trading, among other things. Particularly relevant to healthcare, McKinsey designed a marketing plan to “turbocharge” sales of OxyContin in order to inflate the value of the company, fueling an epidemic that continues to destroy lives, families and communities in Vermont and around the country.  
In 2021, Vermont received $1.5 million in a multistate settlement with McKinsey for its role in fueling the opioid epidemic. Now we are paying over $5 million in precious healthcare dollars to that same company. And if paying high-priced consultants has a familiar ring, look back no farther than 2024, when Vermont paid $1.05 million to Oliver Wyman for a report that told us that healthcare is expensive here — as though we didn’t know that — and recommended regionalizing, whether or not that makes sense given Vermont’s geography and lack of public transportation.
This past January, Becker’s Payer Issues reported on five predictions McKinsey senior partner Adi Kumar made for healthcare in 2026 in a report called “McKinsey Perspectives on Healthcare Industry Trends and the Year Ahead.” In the face of reduced federal subsidies, Kumar encouraged payers  — i.e., insurers — to play the “productivity game,” advising CEOs to figure out “how to do more with less.” We don’t need to spend $5 million to predict the kind of advice the state will get. Unsurprisingly, a firm that consults with corporations on how to maximize profits looks to austerity as the solution and, increasingly, sees artificial intelligence as the magic bullet. 
Though these grants are called Rural Health Transformation funds, they are actually not transforming the system that created the problems in the first place. The thrust of Vermont’s grant spending appears to be on regionalization, shared services and the use of telehealth and AI. While each of these can deliver some benefits when used appropriately, counting on them to solve our healthcare crisis is wishful thinking. 

READ MORE

It is cruelly ironic — and intentional — that the federal government created this grant program at the same time that it has taken health insurance away from people who counted on Affordable Care Act subsidies and from many immigrants and is about to kick more people off Medicaid starting in 2027, with the intention of cutting $1 trillion from Medicaid and the ACA over the next 10 years.
Or maybe it’s not ironic. It seems that the cuts and the grants are two sides of the austerity coin. But while austerity is the name of the game for individuals, families and our community hospitals, there is once again plenty of money for costly consultants who deliver no actual healthcare and who aren’t tasked with transforming the system into one that guarantees access and affordability to all Vermont residents and ensures that our hospitals no longer have unreimbursed care. A universal and unified public system would benefit both patients and hospitals but is nowhere to be found in all this spending.
Ellen Schwartz
Brattleboro, Vt.

name: VTDigger
title: Birders with disabilities are making the hobby more accessible
description:
Birdability volunteer Nick Parker said he would “love to see more hard-of-hearing and deaf people out birding.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Birders with disabilities are making the hobby more accessible.
text:
Bird walk attendees gather to observe chickadees perched along the Universal Access Trail at the North Branch Nature Center in Montpelier on Oct. 24. Photo by Catson Shane/Community News Service

This story by Catson Shane was first published in the Community News Service on Nov. 13, 2026.
MONTPELIER — On a recent Saturday afternoon at the North Branch Nature Center, Community Engagement Coordinator Luis Gonzalez led about a dozen people into the woods on a bird walk.
The group followed the center’s Universal Access Trail, a wide and flat packed gravel path.
“You heard that one?” Gonzalez asked, pausing on the trail. “Can anybody tell me what it is? What does it look like? Use your binoculars.”
As the group shouted out guesses (“A crow or a raven?” “A turkey vulture?”), an American Sign Language interpreter signed along.
The walk was one of several offered throughout the afternoon as part of an inclusive birding event. Nick Parker, a birder from central Vermont who is hard of hearing, organized it.
Parker volunteers with Birdability, a national nonprofit working to make the birding community and the outdoors more welcoming, inclusive, safe and accessible for everybody. Parker said the afternoon was the first Birdability event ever hosted in Vermont.
“I would love to see more hard-of-hearing and deaf people out in birding,” Parker said. “I’m certainly not the only one — I know there are other people that have been working on this sort of thing — but I want to see what I can do.”

Nick Parker poses next to a trail sign at the North Branch Nature Center in Montpelier on Oct. 24. Photo by Catson Shane/Community News Service

Parker started birding relatively recently. Last year, he started his life list, which is a record birders keep of every species they’ve identified.
“My life list right now is at 211,” he said. “That’s all Vermont birds.”
Parker said he got into birding in part because of his disability.
“I sort of was challenging myself like, ‘Okay, I’m gonna be an avid birder. What does that look like for me?’” he said. He started learning to identify birds by their visual characteristics, known as field marks.
About a year ago, he went on his first group bird walk with an ASL interpreter. The increase in language access helped him process what his fellow birders were pointing out.
“I didn’t realize how much I’d been missing,” he said. “I mean, I had a feeling, but (having an interpreter) was just really fantastic, and it did feel like full access.”
Bird walk participant Mary Essex, who is deaf, also appreciates having an ASL interpreter on group bird walks. She said interpreters don’t sign bird calls, but instead help her communicate with the rest of the group.
“When the facilitators are talking and giving some education, I learn something myself, and sometimes I even have something to add,” she said. “I don’t want to keep that information to myself, so if there’s an interpreter present, then I can share the knowledge I have as well.”
Like Parker, Essex identifies birds visually, looking for flight patterns, size, coloration and feeding behaviors. She got into birding through her friend, Jerry Berrier, who is blind and who advocates for inclusive birding with Birdability and Mass Audubon.
When she was starting out, Essex said, she and Berrier would team up to identify birds on bird walks. “He would do the auditory part, and then I would confirm it visually,” she said.

ASL interpreter Joe Loga (left) watches as North Branch Nature Center Community Engagement Coordinator Luis Gonzalez (center) points out a bird in a field book to Mary Essex (right) on Oct. 24. Photo by Catson Shane/Community News Service

Jude Hawthorne, another bird walk participant, started birding during the Covid-19 pandemic. “We put out a bird feeder and got a bird book, and then it was just really fun to collect all the different breeds,” they said.
Hawthorne uses a wheelchair and relies on accessible trails such as this one to get out in the woods.
“Disabled people are left out of so many spaces because we’re not thought of,” they said. “The outdoors is, like, right here, and we’re still left out of it.”
Hawthorne said they appreciate that accessible trails are popping up around Vermont, such as the new trail at the Pratt Refuge in Duxbury that opened this summer. “The extra steps that people do to make it accessible is so massively appreciated,” they said. “Every little bit can make a big difference for folks.”
Parker wants everyone to be included in nature. In addition to advocating for birders with disabilities, he also advocates for queer birders. “As an older trans person, this is not a very friendly world to live in right now,” he said. “But when I’m birding, I feel more myself. I don’t feel like I’m having to put on a face or a mask for anybody.”

Bird walk attendees stop to look for birds along the Universal Access Trail at the North Branch Nature Center in Montpelier on Oct. 24. Photo by Catson Shane/Community News Service

Ultimately, Parker said, his favorite thing about birding isn’t the birds — it’s the people.
“I get most excited about people getting excited about birding,” he said. “It’s always really fascinating if I see something new, but if I’m seeing other people experience that, and getting excited about that, then I feel excited.”
Now, Parker is collaborating with other birding groups across the state to host more accessible events.
“I try to be the change you want to see in the world,” he said. “People are doing fantastic stuff all over the U.S. and the world, so I think I would just love to do more of that.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Birders with disabilities are making the hobby more accessible.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont skier Ben Ogden began the year winning 2 Olympic medals. Then came the twist.
description:
Spring knee surgery and six months of physical rehab have reminded U.S. Nordic’s most decorated man of his priorities: like changing his winter tires first.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont skier Ben Ogden began the year winning 2 Olympic medals. Then came the twist..
text:
Vermont skier Ben Ogden recuperates at home last spring after knee surgery. Instagram photo courtesy of Ben Ogden
Vermonter Ben Ogden can pinpoint the moment when, scoring two silver medals at this year’s Milan-Cortina Winter Olympics, he became the most decorated American man in cross-country ski history.
“Oh, my God,” he recently recalled thinking, “did that really just happen?”
The 26-year-old had a similar reaction when, slushing along a melting local slope this spring, things quickly went downhill.
“I was just having some fun when I came to a dirt patch, had to do a quick stop and tweaked my knee.”
Thinking he had pulled a muscle, Ogden checked with a physical therapist. Then came an MRI, discovery of a major tear in his shock-absorbing meniscus cartilage and a doctor’s recommendation for surgery that would put him on crutches for weeks and in physical rehab for months.
Ogden asked for a few days. It wasn’t to seek a second opinion.
“I had to take the snow tires off my car — stuff like that,” said the favorite son of the tiny southwestern town of Landgrove, population 177. “These things take a little planning.”
Many Olympic medalists return home to appearances on the “Today” show or a box of Wheaties. This is the story of how a fourth-generation Vermonter instead landed on a couch and, staying true to who he was before his wins, launched his own version of a comeback.

Ben Ogden celebrates with fans on Feb. 10 after winning silver in the men’s cross-country sprint at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Italy. Photo by Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP

Ogden began by throwing out the traditional playbook. Take when he was told to hire a top-tier agent, like the one who urged him to ditch his small sponsors for big brands. The new medalist instead has opted for a part-time assistant and his local supporters — Brattleboro’s Vermont Plank Flooring and Richmond’s Bivo water bottles and UnTapped maple sports nutrition.
“They may not be able to offer me the most money, but I want to work with them because they invest in Vermont,” he said.
Ogden headlined NBC’s Olympic prime-time programming that drew more than 10 million nightly viewers, only to save his next broadcast interviews for VTDigger’s “Vermont Conversation with David Goodman,” Vermont Public’s “The Sports Rapport” and WCAX’s 70-year lunch-hour staple “Across the Fence.”
“The more you answer similar questions, the more they become rehearsed, but I hope that doesn’t mean I’ve become less authentic and less me,” he said.

READ MORE

As for public appearances, Ogden has spoken at the Landgrove Meeting House and his two alma maters: Flood Brook elementary school in nearby Londonderry and the University of Vermont in Burlington. His latter speech came at this year’s commencement. There, he recalled how he earned a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering in 2022, then began a master’s program before withdrawing to compete.
“There were so many professors I felt I left hanging,” he said after, “so getting to circle back and hear that they don’t hold it against me took a weight off my shoulders.”
Family and friends are bemused by Ogden’s steadfast response to his success.
“I don’t see any difference in him,” said his mother, Andrea, the town of Landgrove’s treasurer, assistant clerk, delinquent tax collector and trustee of public funds.
“He’s still the same Ben,” added Bill Koch, speaking as a friend, neighbor and, 50 years ago, the first American man to win a Nordic Olympic medal.
Ogden, for example, recently posted an Instagram photo that prodded voters to the polls with a “shoutout to whoever dialed in these cider doughnuts.”
“Skiing fast is terrific,” one commenter responded. “Leading by example — legendary.”

Ben Ogden performs a back flip on Feb. 10 after winning silver in the men’s cross-country sprint at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Italy. Photo by Evgeniy Maloletka/AP

Ogden could have lost his head to the hype. As he prepared for the Olympics at the start of the year, the New York Times noted that the two-time NCAA Nordic champion and 2023’s fastest young male World Cup sprinter “just might be on the verge of taking American cross-country skiing where it hasn’t been before.”
But on Feb. 10, Ogden was happy to simply repeat history when, racing in the individual sprint, he scored the only U.S. men’s Nordic medal since Koch snagged the first at the 1976 Winter Games in Innsbruck, Austria.
Ogden recalls his dry mouth screaming for water and his drained legs shaking as he finished a split second behind Norway’s Johannes Høsflot Klæbo to nab silver. Soon the Vermonter felt the arms of teammates. Heard the throaty roar of the crowd. Saw the teary face of his mother who, like him, was thinking of his father, John, who died of cancer in 2023.
Ogden wrapped himself in an American flag as his friends, under the eye of a live television camera, were shown cheering at a watch party in Richmond. Receiving his medal, the skier then performed a celebratory backflip just like he did the first time he landed a top-three World Cup performance shortly after his father’s death.
“I told my 15-year-old self that if I won an Olympic medal, I’d do a backflip off the podium.”
Ogden won his second silver a week later on Feb. 18 when he and fellow U.S. racer Gus Schumacher finished 1.37 seconds behind Norway in the team relay sprint. 
“I thought it would be different or less intense,” he said of his follow-up victory. “But no, it’s just astonishing.”
Koch, tuning in 3,800 miles away, offered congratulations through a phone call.
“Your life,” the 71-year-old recalls saying, “will never be the same.”

Ben Ogden swims this summer at the University of Vermont’s Forbush Natatorium in Burlington. Instagram photo courtesy of Ben Ogden

Fast-forward to Ogden’s April outing at Cochran’s Ski Area in Richmond, home slope of fellow Olympic medalist Ryan Cochran-Siegle.
“Not exactly the spring update I had hoped,” Ogden went on to post alongside an Instagram photo of him sidelined on a couch. “Unfortunately, I had a slight mishap while corn snow harvesting.”
After surgery at UVM Medical Center in Burlington, Ogden couldn’t stand on his left leg for six weeks.
Enter his cellphone camera.
“I first and foremost want to apologize for how long of a break it’s been since my last video,” he told viewers on his YouTube channel. “But as some of you may have realized, things got pretty busy for me.”
Ogden went on to gripe about his shaky crutches before grabbing a blowtorch to weld aluminum piping into a sturdier pair — no surprise to those who’ve watched him take apart and tinker with a 1973 Land Rover he’s rebuilding in a family barn.
By June, Ogden was swimming at the UVM pool. By July, he was biking. By August, he was roller skiing.
“Now I’m able to train really hard and do 98% of what I would normally do,” he said this month at an event celebrating him and his colleagues on Stratton’s SMS T2 elite cross-country training team.
Ogden is preparing for a set of U.S. Ski Team physical tests later this year. When he passes, he’ll return to the World Cup racing circuit to cap his recovery.
“I’ll maybe have a bit of a slower start,” he said, “but hopefully by January or February, I’ll be just as good as new.”
Some people have told Ogden the timing of his surgery — just after the Olympics and well before coming competitions — was fortuitous.
“It’s never fun to be injured, but I’ve been forced to be thankful that it happened when it happened.”
Others have questioned how it will affect his future.
“Someone asked me, ‘Do you ever think that your best days of skiing are behind you?’ Of course. But what can I do but just keep trying my hardest? Every day is a new challenge. If one day or one week or one month or one year of training is bad, all I can do is try and make the next one better.”

title: New Mexico House Democrats retain leadership
description: The Democratic caucus for the New Mexico House of Representatives kept its leadership in place, according to a news release on Saturday. Among other positions, the caucus retained state Rep. Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque) as speaker, a position he has held since 2022, pending an official vote by the full house on opening day of the 2027 session on Jan. 19.
text:
NM House Speaker Rep. Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque) acknowledges members of the Democratic caucus during a press conference on House Floor following the close of the 30-day legislative session on Feb. 19,  2026. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)The Democratic caucus for the New Mexico House of Representatives will keep its leadership in place for next year’s legislative session, according to a news release on Saturday.
The caucus retained state Rep. Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque) as speaker, a position he has held since 2022, pending an official vote by the full House on opening day of the 2027 session on Jan. 19.
“As the son of hardworking, blue-collar immigrants, I could not be more grateful for the opportunity to continue fighting for New Mexico’s working families from the Speaker’s Chair, alongside the incredible leaders in this caucus,” Martínez said in a statement. “We’re heading into session energized and with an ambitious agenda to continue to deliver real results for New Mexicans, while providing the blueprint for the rest of the nation.”
The caucus also retained Majority Floor Leader Reena Szczepanski (D-Santa Fe), House Majority Whip Dayan Hochman-Vigil and Raymundo “Ray” Lara (D-Chamberino) in their positions.
New Mexico House Democrats have eight newly elected members following the Nov. 3 election, and unseated four incumbent Republicans. As a result, Democrats will hold 47 of 70 House seats when the new legislative session begins on Jan. 19 for a 60-day session. Democrats also kept their 10-seat majority in the state Senate. New Mexico is one of six states whose legislatures have at least 50% women following the midterm elections.
New Mexico House Republicans last week also named their leadership team for the upcoming session, reelecting Rep. Gail Armstrong (R-Magdalena) as minority floor leader.

name: VTDigger
title: Wolk makes Vermont history as first independent elected to state Senate
description:
Dave Wolk returns to the Senate chamber where he served more than three decades ago as a Democrat.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Wolk makes Vermont history as first independent elected to state Senate.
text:
The Senate chamber at the Statehouse in Montpelier on Tuesday, Feb. 26, 2019. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Katy Savage was first published in the Mountain Times on Nov. 11, 2026.
In May, Dave Wolk returned to a workplace he hadn’t seen in over 30 years, and it felt like a homecoming.
He visited the Senate chamber, where he served 34 years ago, after dropping off the signatures needed to get his name on the November ballot at the secretary of state’s office.
Much of the chamber looked as he remembered it, from the furniture and decor to the desk where he once sat. Inside, Wolk found his son’s signature, written there when his son was just 8 years old.
“They allow you to have your kids write their names inside the desk, and my son is now 46, so he was 8 years old then,” Wolk recalled. “I sat there and I felt like I was at home.”
At the time, Wolk didn’t know whether voters would send him back to Montpelier.
Six months later, they did.
Wolk, 73, made Vermont political history on Election Day, becoming the first independent candidate elected to the state Senate. The former Democratic senator, who served from 1988 to 1992, defeated Republican incumbent Terry Williams to claim one of Rutland County’s three Senate seats, finishing second in the four-way race with 14,259 votes.
Williams finished fourth with 11,190 votes. Days before the election, Williams was arrested and charged with domestic assault after allegedly striking a relative in the face during an argument over chores at his Poultney home.
Wolk will serve with Republican Brian Collamore, who led the field with 15,755 votes, and Republican David Weeks, who finished third with 13,319 votes. 
Wolk’s return to the Statehouse will be different this time. He’s heading back without a political party behind him — and that’s exactly how he wants it.
“You don’t want to be beholden to anyone except for voters,” he said.
Wolk ran an unconventional campaign. He refused contributions from political action committees, lobbyists and lawyers who represent lobbyists. He also never directly asked anyone for a donation.
Instead, individuals contributed $23,214 to his campaign.
“I was grateful that a lot of people sent enough money in to run a campaign,” he said.
For Wolk, running as an independent was about more than campaign financing. He said he wanted the freedom to vote according to his constituents’ interests rather than the demands of party leadership.
Wolk said conversations with Republican and Democratic lawmakers reinforced that decision. Some told him they had felt pressured to support legislation favored by party leaders, even when they personally disagreed.
Wolk also said he has grown frustrated with the increasingly confrontational tone of politics.
“I have felt it more acutely in the last few years that I’ve seen more people try to lift themselves up by tearing other people down, and it doesn’t work,” he said.
Running without a party affiliation, he said, has been liberating.
“I know who I’m beholden to, and it’s not a political party, and it’s not a political action committee, it’s not a lobbyist, not a lawyer. It’s for the people I represent,” he said.
Wolk’s election marks another chapter in a public service career spanning more than five decades and all three branches of Vermont government.
Wolk is a Middlebury College graduate. He began his career in education in the 1970s as a teacher and guidance counselor at Mount St. Joseph Academy in Rutland.
He later earned a master’s degree from the University of Vermont and pursued graduate studies at Harvard before returning to Vermont, where he became principal of Barstow Memorial School in Chittenden.
In 1988, he was elected to the Vermont Senate as a Democrat, serving two terms before running for lieutenant governor in 1992. He lost that race to Republican Barbara Snelling.
Wolk then returned to education, serving as principal of Rutland High School and later as superintendent. He went on to become Vermont’s commissioner of education for two years. He then spent 16 years as president of what is now Castleton University.
During his tenure he ushered in a $25.7 million initiative that included the multipurpose Spartan Stadium — now named Dave Wolk Stadium. That investment in athletics increased participation rates fivefold and increased the offerings to 28 varsity programs.
Most recently, he served as an assistant judge in Rutland County.
Even after leaving those positions, Wolk has remained involved in public service. He has operated a leadership coaching business and served as a guardian ad litem, a court-appointed advocate who represents children’s interests in legal proceedings.
He admits that stepping away from work has never been easy.
“I failed retirement,” he joked.
Wolk said he doesn’t have hobbies outside of public service.
“I’m sort of addicted to public service,” he said. “I love it. I feel a kind of sense of purpose.”
During his campaign, Wolk met with local boards and heard concerns about deteriorating roads and bridges and rising education and property taxes.
Wolk said public safety was among the issues that came up most frequently, particularly concerns about repeat offenders who commit property crimes and fail to appear in court.
Wolk wants to change Vermont law to give judges additional tools to address repeat offenders who consistently miss court appearances.
Wolk said the goal is to address what he sees as a revolving door for people repeatedly accused of misdemeanor property crimes, including thefts from stores and break-ins involving homes and vehicles.
He said the issue affects the quality of life in communities.
When Wolk returns to the Senate in January, he’ll be entering a chamber that looks much as it did more than three decades ago. But he’s less certain about how much the political atmosphere has changed.
During his first two terms, Wolk remembers lawmakers from opposing parties working together despite their disagreements. He hopes to find that same spirit of cooperation when he returns.
“The decorum back then was bipartisan or nonpartisan, and it was collegial, friendly, civil,” Wolk said. “I’m not saying it’s not that way now, but I’m going to be curious about that.”

name: VTDigger
title: Saving pennies, saving a planet
description:
The Chittenden Energy Fair celebrated the highlights of the Rutland County town’s Energy Challenge and introduced the next chapter of the community’s energy goals.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Saving pennies, saving a planet.
text:
Maddy Murray, project manager with Green Mountain Power, answers questions at the Chittenden Energy Fair in Chittenden on Thursday, November 12, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell, VTDigger
CHITTENDEN — Sue Priest’s freshly mowed grass has recently found a new purpose: feeding her family’s cattle.
Priest and her husband participated in the Chittenden Energy Challenge, which called on residents of the small town in Rutland County to participate in 500 creative sustainable actions over the past year. 
In addition to sustainability measures they’ve taken in the past, the couple decided to mow their lawn less, repurpose the grass and embrace bike commuting, including on trips to the grocery store.
“We’ll carry back 20 to 40 pounds worth of groceries, and so save a car trip that way,” Priest said.
A fair held Thursday at Mountain Top Resort marked the end of the challenge. But the event wasn’t simply an ending. At a community dinner after the fair, a “Menu of Ideas” placed on dining tables at the resort served up inspiration for future projects.
The challenge and corresponding fair were intended to enhance community awareness and excitement for saving energy and the environment. There were learning opportunities throughout the challenge that incorporated experts in eco-friendly transportation, renewable energy transitions and invasive species, among other things.
But the project was about more than enthusiasm for sustainability. It was designed, as many other energy fairs across Vermont are, to bridge the gap between affordability and green energy investments.
“This isn’t just for the wealthy,” said Melanie Paskevich, chair of the Chittenden Energy and Climate Committee. “This isn’t just for, maybe the low income either. We can all do this.”
The fair featured giveaways of everything from travel mugs to weather-proofing supplies. Energy experts set up tables in an event room at the resort and answered community members’ questions.

Bekah Kuster of Efficiency Vermont, left, speaks with Robert Baird at the Chittenden Energy Fair in Chittenden on Thursday, November 12, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell, VTDigger

Bekah Kuster, community engagement manager at Efficiency Vermont, fielded questions from residents about their personal energy goals and ways to make them happen through rebates and other cost-saving measures. Efficiency Vermont, a statewide energy efficiency utility designed to help Vermonters reduce their energy consumption, provides a variety of rebates, advice and financial assistance for renewable energy projects.
Awareness is a crucial part of the puzzle when encouraging residents to go green, Kuster said. It’s important to help people find economic resources to implement measures like heat pumps and weatherization, Kuster said, and educate them about smaller measures that people can take.
These conversations become increasingly important when households are preparing for worsening winter weather, Kuster said. And people are especially concerned this year, she added, due to rising prices for energy and other everyday essentials. 
“My hope is just to make people aware of the ways that they can save energy this winter and be more comfortable with rising energy costs,” Kuster said.
Priest has taken advantage of rebates in the past when updating appliances to energy-efficient alternatives, she said.
“We always look before we buy something to see if there’s a rebate available to help with the cost,” Priest said.
John and Ellen Bodin, residents of North Chittenden and relatives of Priest, attended the event. They have had a long interest in sustainability, investing in solar panels and heat pumps and replacing their appliances with higher-efficiency models. For this year’s challenge, they decided to carpool more, hang laundry outside to dry and cut their lawn less.
The Chittenden Energy Fair is one of many energy fairs that have sprouted across Vermont to encourage community involvement in conservation. There’s also an annual Waterbury LEAP Fair in April focused on educating residents on saving energy and costs. Another event, the Net Zero Energy Festival in Burlington, centers on electrification and reducing fossil fuel use.The festival was in August this year.

Robert Harness, left, speaks with Paige Prouty of Downvalley Bike and Apparel at the Chittenden Energy Fair in Chittenden on Thursday, November 12, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell, VTDigger

Last week’s event in Chittenden was somewhat unusual because of the series of workshops and community events that spanned a year leading up to it, according to Sean Beatty, a regional planner with the Rutland Regional Planning Commission who worked one of the event tables.
“It’s a real chance to educate people,” Beatty said. “And especially on a smaller scale, where this is really only Chittenden residents, where we can get pretty specific to some of the problems that Chittenden residents might have.”
The challenge’s goal was to record 500 actions taken by community members during the year, Paskevich said. 
Chittenden exceeded expectations and recorded 624 actions.
The “Menu of Ideas” featured different options for energy-saving actions. Options ranged from individual community support, including home energy visits and a community firewood lot for residents in need of heat assistance, to townwide actions such as a rideshare system.
People who attended the event voted on the possible actions to implement. The most popular was safer walking and biking routes. As for community energy support, the favorites were volunteer weatherization/project help and home energy supply kits.
John Bodin said going green is a matter of “individuals coming together to make it happen.” He highlighted the efforts of the energy committee for organizing the project.
“It exposes more people to it,” Bodin said, “so that they’re aware of what opportunities there are and what kind of financial rebates there are, which makes it a little less scary when, if you’re thinking in dollars and cents, which we often are these days.”
