text:
Geebers, a cat, in October 2025. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)His name was Geebers and he was like other cats, at turns greedy or loving, but mostly aloof, and with great lime-colored lantern eyes that hid a secret. He was striped gray, of 12 pounds at his best weight, and the markings on his face gave him a perpetual scowl. The expression was fitting because Geebers approved of precious few things, and chief among those was sunshine and wet food and my wife, Kim.
For a long time he disapproved of me.
And I of him.
He came to us in 2015, carried to our backyard in the mouth of his gray cat mother, who also deposited his white-furred sister along with him. Why the mother picked our house is a mystery, but it probably had to do with Kim being a soft touch.
Cats know these things.
Kim recognized the mother on sight, a cat that may have once belonged to some family but now belonged only to the alley. The mother had Geebers with her near our back door the first time she saw them. Then two days later she spotted both kittens alone in the backyard, near the shed. The story of the kittens’ arrival became part of the lore of life on Constitution Street.
Our house sits on one of those narrow, 50-by-150-foot lots common to small Kansas towns of a century past. The backyard is bounded by a wooden privacy fence installed in recent decades, and the wooden shed that houses the mower and other lawn tools is in one corner. This area is where the kittens lived that first summer, peering warily through the grass and weeds at the back door and deck, and ducking behind or into the shed whenever Kim approached.
Kim could no more ignore stray kittens in the backyard than she could have ignored an ivory-billed woodpecker. She took blurry photos of them, because they wouldn’t let her get too close, and she talked to them in one of her high-pitched animal voices. She has a different voice for each kind of animal. All of the voices are cheerful and some are goofy, especially when she’s addressing dogs. But her cat voice is the voice of recognition, of one traveler upon the earth greeting another in kindness. The kittens ate the dry food she left, but always at a distance, and Kim despaired that they would never let her hold them.
What were we to do with the kittens?
I was not thrilled at the prospect of having cats to take care of. They would have to be outside cats, because I am allergic to cats, and we’d already had one outside cat before. The neighbors had left that cat behind when they moved and Kim took care of her by default. That had been 15 years ago, when we were first married, and that is another story about a fine cat but one that did not rate an elegy by me.
Geebers, however, was another matter.

Stray kittens, later named Geebers and Foxy, in the author’s backyard, about 10 years ago. (Photo by Kim Horner McCoy)

Over the course of the summer the kittens came, Kim began feeding them plastic spoonfuls of turkey baby food she left for them on a dish. She left the spoon so they would get used to it. Then she held the spoon at arm’s length as they cautiously licked it clean. She moved ever closer to the back deck with each feeding, and the kittens followed, daring to leave the safety of the grass and weeds and the oily-smelling shed behind.
The white cat, Foxy (sometimes called The Foxy One or simply Fox) was always the smarter or at least more practical of the two, hanging back while her brother ventured ahead. Geebers (short for the Gray Baby in that silly way people have of naming cats) would never get too far from her, always glancing back to make sure she was there.
But gradually even Foxy began to trust.
In time Kim lured them up onto the back deck, where they took their breakfasts and dinners of dry cat food and lazed in the sunshine and sometimes played the hunting game with butterflies they never killed.
As to me, the cats had a strict rule that I was to come no closer than I could reach. That suited me just fine. Cats make my eyes water and my nose run, even when I’m only a few minutes in the same space. There are few things that are as much trouble in a small package as a cat and there were two of them, but I tolerated them because I loved Kim.
The domain of the cats expanded as they grew, encompassing the sides of the house and the driveway and eventually the front porch with its railing and wooden steps. As a grown cat, Foxy would sometimes stalk and kill the occasional bird, a necessary part of feline competence. But I never saw Geebers pounce on anything besides a tennis ball or a giant toy carrot. Both became used to the routine on Constitution Street, of rising early with Kim for breakfast at the back door, of waiting for her to return from her morning walks, of watching as I walked up the front steps from work. He and his sister had a little house and a heated pad on the deck and spent the nights inside on the back porch during the worst of winter.
Being a responsible cat owner, Kim took them both to the vet when it was time. There would be no additional litters on Constitution Street. We would occasionally spot a cat that resembled Geebers in the neighborhood, and it would make us ponder what had happened to their mother.
In time another cat came to stay, a calico tabby kitten Kim rescued from a hackberry tree in the backyard in which she was crying. She was little trouble and craved the affection of the other cats, even though Foxy couldn’t stand her. The new cat became Newt (a contraction of New Cat) and at some point we agreed, or perhaps I made a pronouncement, that three cats was enough.
And that was how it was for a long time.
Upon returning home we would pull into the driveway at night and the cats would be there, waiting for us, their eyes shining in the headlights of the Jeep. When we were away for more than a day we would have a friend of mine pick up the mail and feed and water the cats. After the longer trips the cats would punish Kim, deigning to eat but then turning their backs, at least until the next morning came and all was forgiven.
As the years passed Geebers relaxed the arm’s length rule, overcome not by trust so much as curiosity. Whenever I was working on something outside, such as fixing the lawn mower or repairing the steps, he would come closer to get a better view of what I was doing. All sawing and hammering and painting was endlessly fascinating to him.
Then, on June 28 of last year, he allowed me to touch him.
Kim noted the date.
It was just a pat on the head at first, or a touch beneath the chin. I would have to wash my hands immediately after, or else my hand would start itching. But it wasn’t long before this became a ritual, that whenever I came up the wooden steps he would rouse from whatever spot he’d been lazing in, amble over, and receive a few pets. Even if I had my hands full, I would have to put my bundle down and scratch his ears and rake my fingers under his chin. If he didn’t get enough pets, he’d reach out with a paw to try to stop me from walking away, or he would spring up and serpentine around my ankles.
It was both annoying and oddly satisfying.
During the hardest days of the past year, when I was worried about the nation and the world, the ritual became a comfort. Things were always a little better with Geebers waiting on the porch because of what it symbolized. Our life on Constitution Street remained, despite trials. As long as the cats were there, so was Kim.
In a column in November of last year, I wrote about how on a sunny afternoon the cats lounged on the porch while I pondered where we were headed as a country. In the piece, I declared that I wasn’t a cat person.
I still am not.
But I did become a Geebers person.
There was a lot of handwashing.
Geebers also came to like the mail carrier, who would pause on the porch and give him a pet. It was unusual behavior. I thought at the time that Geebers must have been confused, that perhaps he had come to regard all men as me. Or perhaps it was something else. In August of this year, Geebers developed a bloody spot on his right cheek. We assumed it was from a scrap with another animal and Kim took him to the vet, who gave him a shot of antibiotic.
But instead of improving, the wound worsened. It seeped blood.
By early September it was back to the vet, who said he feared it was cancer. A biopsy confirmed feline lymphoma. It is the most frequently diagnosed of all types of feline cancer. Chemotherapy treatment would have been expensive and, because the disease involved his head, was unlikely to prolong much of anything except his suffering.
Geebers spent the next three weeks keeping to his routine while the disease steadily ate him alive.
He stayed mostly at his spot at the top of the front steps, waiting for pets from me or a word from the mail carrier, and while his face looked like hell he continued to eat well. But he wouldn’t allow anyone to touch his head, although he still enjoyed a few pets beneath his chin.
Kim made a final appointment with the vet. She was determined to spare him the suffering of the inevitable surrender to cancer.
She spooned his last meal out of a baby food jar. Turkey.
At the vet’s, Kim picked him up out of his carrier and followed the business-like but sympathetic staff back to an exam room, where she placed him on the table. Then the vet administered a lethal sedative, probably sodium pentobarbital, and placed a bandage over the spot. The bandage was for us.
Kim’s hand was on his flank. We said goodbye. In a few minutes those bright eyes went dull, and Geebers the cat was dead.
Kim wept.
“I’ve never seen anything die before,” she said.
She had not witnessed a person, or an animal, die. It was something she had been spared, something I had not known about her in 15 years of marriage. I felt suddenly odd and somehow callous, having assumed that everyone was as familiar with death as I was. I had been present at the deaths of both of my parents. As a journalist, I had been at various crime and accident scenes not long after the passing of many strangers. And I had seen many animals die, some by my own hand while hunting in decades past.
“I’m sorry,” I said.
I told Kim how lucky Geebers and his sister had been that she had lured them out of the weeds. But I was thinking what everyone thinks, the rotten truth that one day each of us will be taken, in ways peaceful or not.
But I knew the secret behind those lantern eyes.
It was love.
If there is any grace in this world, either animal or human, it is to be found reflected in the eyes of those who love us. It is a small epiphany sparked by a small soul, but a real one, and watching Geebers die was an indictment of all the days I’ve wasted in forgetting something I already knew.
There is a trap in becoming desensitized to death, of becoming too comfortable with the idea, of reducing all things to an anecdote. Perhaps it was the pain of watching as my parents died early so long ago, in different but equally horrific hospital rooms, of the delayed shock journalists suffer witnessing the fatal results of war, wickedness or just bad luck.
I have held death at such a reserve that I cannot give a coherent timeline of events leading up to the deaths of my parents, my brother, of close friends. I would have to rely on notes and letters and death certificates. Even with Geebers, Kim had to correct my dates, because in my memory the cancer lasted longer and Geebers had been letting me pet him for three years, and not one.
If there is a lesson in this, an elegy for a cat, perhaps it’s among the most ancient of ones, a lesson reserved for human beings but spared lesser creatures who know nothing of their own mortality. It is a sin to waste — or fail to mark — a single day.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The Holland Tunnel’s centennial year
description: Happy birthday to New York City’s Holland Tunnel, now into its 100th year of operations, carrying cars and trucks between lower Manhattan and New Jersey.
text:
In many ways our region is blessed with a transportation infrastructure built by our forefathers:  our railroads, the Merritt Parkway and, in the case of New York City,  America’s first underwater vehicular tunnel, named after the man who died building it.
Happy birthday to New York City’s Holland Tunnel, now into its 100th year of operations, carrying cars and trucks between lower Manhattan and New Jersey.  Before the tunnel, 19,600 vehicles each day had to cross by ferry.



But in the winter of 1917, the Hudson River iced up and the overloaded boats struggled.  That’s when plans to build a vehicular crossing, discussed since 1906, finally got going.
But this was not to be the first trans-Hudson underwater crossing.  What we know today as the PATH (Port Authority Trans Hudson) train tunnel opened in 1908 and the Pennsylvania Railroad tunnels in 1910.
But should the city’s first vehicular crossing of the Hudson be a bridge or a tunnel?
In 1908 a commission suggested a bridge crossing starting at 57th, 110th or 179th Street in Manhattan.  Then the War Department jumped in saying any such crossing would have to offer ships a 200-foot clearance, so a bridge (estimated in 1913 to cost $42 million, $1.4 billion in today’s inflated dollars) would instead become a tunnel as it could be built for $11 million ($372 million today).  So a tunnel it was.
But the Federal government refused funding (sound familiar?) so New York and New Jersey would have to raise the money themselves, which they did.

One of the Holland Tunnel’s huge ventilation towers. Credit: Wikimedia

Engineers knew the tunnel was possible:  the railroads had proven that.  But those operated with electric trains.  A vehicular tunnel had a different challenge: exhaust fumes.  Without extensive ventilation drivers could be asphyxiated.  And that’s kind of bad for business.  So four huge ventilation towers would be built, their 84 fans changing the air in the tunnel every 90 seconds. 
Construction was to be led by engineer Clifford Holland, for whom the tunnel would be posthumously named.  Holland had already built several subway tunnels under the East River.  Sadly, Holland was never to see this plan to fruition, dying of a heart attack at age 41, reportedly due to the stress of this project.
In 1927 the 1.6 mile tunnel was officially opened with the tap of a telegraph key by President Calvin Coolidge (sitting on his yacht).  In the first day, 20,000 people walked through the tunnel.  From the beginning, horses were banned from the twin tubes.  Judging by today’s rush hour traffic, horses might be faster.
When cars were allowed to cross the next day the toll was 50 cents. Today a crossing costs as much as $23 eastbound from New Jersey.  Adjusting for inflation today’s toll is about the same as in 1927.  The traffic is not.

Opening day at the Holland Tunnel in 1927. Credit: Wikimedia

These days some 30 million vehicles drive the tubes, 97% of them cars (according to 2025 numbers), roughly twice the capacity first estimated by engineers in 1927.  That compares to 100 million crossings each year on the George Washington Bridge and almost 36 million traversing the Lincoln Tunnel.
Maintaining a structure this old isn’t easy.  In 1955 the original road surface of Belgian blocks and concrete was replaced with asphalt.  Repairs after super-storm Sandy flooded the tubes in 2012 cost $364 million. Today the tunnel’s six million white and colored ceiling and wall tiles are scrubbed regularly by overnight crews.  Without that effort the Port Authority says the tiles would blacken within a week.
Had he lived, Clifford Holland would have been proud of what he built and prouder still to know that it’s still meeting its mission, now into its 100th year.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: FAA: US air travel should normalize Sunday after ground stop, cancellations
description: The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
text:
This story has been updated.
Airlines canceled thousands of flights across the U.S. on Saturday as they worked to recover from a nationwide ground stop that left passengers scrambling for seats and disrupted travel around the world.
The U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of Sunday, two days after what was the nation’s longest ground stop in 25 years, Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said, declaring the “worst is behind us.”
The problem began when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing a section of the air traffic control system’s old copper wire with new fiber wire, somehow causing the system to overload, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
The work led to “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, prompting the government to shut down air traffic for more than four hours. Officials were investigating whether contractor “incompetence” or a faulty router was the cause,” he said.
“Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment,” Duffy said.
L3Harris said in a statement that it was supporting the FAA in the investigation to understand what led to the ground stop and the company takes seriously the impact to travelers, airlines and air traffic operations.
The FAA normally consults its own technicians in advance and asks them to assess the risks of any upgrades or repairs but that didn’t happen in this case, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, the union representing the agency’s technicians, said in a Saturday statement.
The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday’s stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day.
“The knock-on effect of that is incredible,” said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. “The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back … and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Thousands of flights delayed and canceled
At airports across the U.S., passengers scrambled Saturday to figure out how to reach their destinations. Some waited out the chaos in hotels while others sprinted to snag rental cars and bus or train tickets. Many camped out in airports.
Others got creative. Video in Seattle’s airport showed a passenger serenading stressed out travelers with classical music. Stranded strangers in Lexington, Kentucky, participated in a cornhole tournament. The singer T-Pain and the band Hoobastank were captured on video singing to passengers as they waited on commercial airplanes.
Dan Russell, 66, learned his connecting flight from Hawaii to California was canceled a half-hour before boarding was scheduled in San Diego Friday night. Hotels were full, so he and his wife waited at the airport.
“There’s nothing you can do,” Russell said.
At the Newark, N.J., airport, Umi Egchi was trying to figure out when he could return home to Japan.
“I’m not sure exactly what happened. I just want to go home,” said Egchi, who had a sleep mask on top of his head.
Sports teams that traveled for games this weekend adjusted game start times, and No. 19 Mississippi’s football game at Oklahoma was delayed to Sunday.
FlightAware, a website that tracks flights, said more than 6,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. had been canceled Saturday.
Officials say no one was in danger during ground stop
Duffy reiterated Saturday that no one was in danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely.
Trump administration officials blamed Congress for failing to approve more money to replace decades-old technology that helps manage air traffic. Duffy said 70% of the system had been replaced, but his agency needs new air traffic control towers and runways.
The FAA has replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year with $12.5 billion in funding. Duffy and the White House want $30 billion more to complete the work.
“We have aging infrastructure throughout the airspace,” Duffy said, while stressing that flying remains safe.
Charlton, the aviation consultant, pointed to the difficulties of updating a system that can never shut down.
“What you’re watching here is trying to change the tires of your car when the car’s going at 80 miles an hour down the expressway, because nothing stops in aviation,” he said.
Although Duffy said he had repeatedly spoken with President Donald Trump since the ground stop began, the president has not spoken publicly on the matter, nor issued statements via social media. He spoke on the phone with a Fox News reporter, but that was not on camera.
Past problems have been linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast. That disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line.
Aging equipment was also blamed for brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference Friday was the scale of the disruption that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.

name: VTDigger
title: Living ‘in the shadows’: Some pro-ICE Vermonters support pathways to citizenship
description:
A demonstration Saturday in Williston showcased Vermonters grappling with the current immigration system and looking for ways to move forward.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Living ‘in the shadows’: Some pro-ICE Vermonters support pathways to citizenship.
text:
ICE supporter Doug, of Waterbury, who did not give a last name, listens to a counterprotester during a gathering in front of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Law Enforcement Support Center in Williston on Saturday, November 14, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

WILLISTON — One ICE supporter showed up to a demonstration Saturday with an American flag and a strong belief in the work that immigration agents do every day.
But that supporter, who introduced himself as Adam Manley, also believes in the American Dream — for undocumented immigrants and U.S. citizens alike.
“By inviting people to come here undocumented and not sending them through the proper channels with documentation, it’s like stabbing them in the back because all these people, they have to live in the shadows,” Manley said.
The planned gathering in support of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement was promoted on social media by a group calling itself Mass ICE Patriots. The event outside the agency’s Law Enforcement Support Center turned into an amalgamation of Vermonters on both sides of the immigration issue. Counterprotesters and observers showed up as the ICE supporters waved flags in the rain.
Some conversations got heated. But some members of both sides said there should be better pathways to citizenship.
For Manley, a resident of Essex Junction, supporting ICE is a matter of preserving law and order in society.
“The laws apply equally to everybody,” Manley said. “And, you know, once you start attacking those, you open up the door to, you know, all kinds of, you know, basically anti-American way of life.”
An ICE supporter who introduced himself as Adam Manley, of Essex Junction, left, debates CJ, who did not give a last name, during a gathering in front of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Law Enforcement Support Center in Williston on Saturday, November 14, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
John Ames, of Winooski, was the first person to turn up on the rainy morning. He carried a sign with a simple message of his own: “ICE Thug Goons Out.”
“They do terrible things, you know, at the behest of Stephen Miller,” Ames said, referring to President Donald Trump’s newly appointed chief of staff. “You know, they want them to do, what, 3,000 arrests a day? So they do these horrible things to people.”
While his views differed strongly from the pro-ICE demonstrators, Ames said he found common ground with one person who agreed that ICE’s enforcement tactics were too harsh.
Manley said he worries about the negative sentiment against ICE officers. But he also worries about the status of undocumented immigrants in the U.S., who are excluded from many rights that citizens are granted.
“There needs to be a one-time program where anybody that isn’t documented can step forward,” Manley said, adding that, in his view, Biden-era policies led to the current situation. “We can vet them and get them on a pathway to either citizenship or at least legal working standards.”
Saturday’s situation was not without conflict. Manley got into a passionate debate about law and order with CJ, a resident of St. Albans, who declined to provide a last name. CJ argued that to solve the immigration issue, America needs to look toward communities like Fairfax County, Virginia. 
Fairfax County decided not to abide by federal immigration policies, instead adopting policies that allow undocumented immigrants to live in the community without fear of discovery.
CJ argued that the policy there has contributed to a thriving education system and a growing tech sector.
“When people are willing to say, ‘Oh, OK, new people are coming in. How can we welcome them so that they can join the community, can follow the laws here,’” CJ said, “we are better for it.”
Hank Poitras, a provocative online presence also known as Planet Hank, turned up to condemn both sides of the demonstration and the media attention it garnered. He directed most of his comments toward the journalists present, arguing that the news was “obsessed” with the immigration debate.
Poitras went on to argue that there were more counterprotesters than ICE supporters present.
“That’s the whole point, man,” Ames called back.
VTDigger counted about 10 pro-ICE protesters and roughly six counterprotesters and observers at the height of the demonstration.
CJ said Poitras was an example of the people who drive immigration debates — people who gain attention by using inflammatory rhetoric. Their voices drown out people on the pro-ICE side who may be trying to express themselves in a reasonable manner, she said.
“These discussions are unavoidably piloted by people like that who ultimately know you, you can make a career, you can find success and public support if you’re loud and hateful,” CJ said.
Manley said he knows many undocumented immigrants in his community and would like them to have a chance at the rights and benefits that citizens enjoy, such as voting.
Reforming the laws is the first step to changing their situations, he said.
“I hope, you know, that they can do well and participate in society right next to the rest of us and, and not have to live in the shadows,” Manley said. 
“But you know, until we change the laws, you can’t just wish it away.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Living ‘in the shadows’: Some pro-ICE Vermonters support pathways to citizenship.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Republicans acknowledge voters rejected them but show little appetite for breaking with Trump
authors: By Steven Sloan, Joey Cappelletti and Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press
description: President Donald Trump gives a thumbs up after his speech during his rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026.
text:
WASHINGTON — Rep. Richard Hudson wanted a triumphant return to Capitol Hill this week after steering Republicans to another majority. Instead, the North Carolina Republican is facing the reality that he and dozens of colleagues will soon clear out their offices.
“It was really people coming out to send a message,” Hudson, the chair of the House GOP’s campaign arm, said in a brief interview. “They, rightly so, felt gas was too high, things were too expensive.”
“The mistake Republicans made,” he said, “is we didn’t convey to them that we cared about that and cared about them.”
Back in Washington this week for the first time since the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses, Republicans were in something of a daze. Even as they acknowledged the depth of their defeat, there was little appetite for a wholesale break from President Donald Trump.
Instead, they met behind closed doors to talk about what went wrong. And they scrutinized the calendar to figure out how to push through as much of their agenda as possible before Democrats assume control of the House and the Senate in January.
‘We collectively failed’
There was widespread frustration that Republicans who were awarded full control of the White House and Congress just two years earlier had lost touch with voters.
“You cut rural healthcare spending, when you abandon pro-lifers, when you abandon the poor, when you abandon the needy, when you abandon working people, you’re gonna get your butt kicked,” said Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., who unsuccessfully sought to delay his party’s leadership elections in the Senate. “And you’re gonna deserve it.”
“We collectively failed,” said Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., who is trailing her Democratic challenger in a district that Republicans carried by more than 18 percentage points in 2024.
“It’s very clear,” she said. “The American people let us know we have failed in this governing experience for this Congress.”
The anger is sharp in part because of the rosy predictions from top Republicans ahead of the election. Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., who is also trailing a Democratic rival, said people kept telling her she couldn’t lose. But she knew otherwise.
“I couldn’t get anybody to listen to me,” she said. “People just didn’t think it could happen, but we knew it could.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson spent the final stretch of the campaign rejecting the historic headwinds that often befall a president’s party during a midterm. He toured the country, insisting the polls were wrong and Republicans would retain their majority even as some incumbents were skeptical.
Back on Capitol Hill this week, Johnson said voters made the “wrong choice” as Democrats flipped more than 40 Republican-held seats. That puts the Democrats on track to hold the most robust majority since the early years of Barack Obama’s presidency.
House, Senate take different approaches
Republicans, meanwhile, are weighing how to proceed, balancing calls for moderation against an impulse for hard-line positions that might reenergize the party’s base. Each chamber took different tracks, previewing divisions that may lie ahead.
In the House, the Republicans who will remain in Washington next year largely represent staunchly conservative districts where Trump remains popular. Their decision to elect Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan as their next leader reflected a fighting stance.
Jordan is a co-founder of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, currently chairs the Judiciary Committee and has previously chaired the Oversight Committee. From those positions, he’s waged heated fights against Democrats and become a top Trump ally.
“The way that Jim fights says a lot about where this conference is,” said Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla.
In the Senate, the desire for combat was less intense.
The question for Republicans there was less about whether they would stick with John Thune of South Dakota as their leader than when they would make that decision. Hawley and a small group of conservatives spent hours huddled with Republicans in the Old Senate Chamber arguing for a delay in leadership elections to allow the party to consider alternative candidates.
But the problem was that no one would come forward to offer themselves as an alternative to Thune, who has faced criticism from Trump at times for his refusal to abandon Senate rules to make it easier to pass conservative legislation.
“It’s a bad job,” Hawley said.
After hours of deliberation, Republicans ultimately backed Thune without so much as a voice vote.
“We’re going to let our leader be the leader,” said Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, who was also elected to lead the party’s effort to regain seats in the 2028 election.
GOP unites to protect Hegseth
Perhaps the biggest question for Republicans going forward is how to manage their relationship with Trump, whose policies on trade and the war in Iran helped contribute to their losses. He’s in the last two years of his second term, and the election defeats have raised stark questions about the durability of his Make America Great Again movement.
But there was no rush to distance themselves from the president as House Republicans, even those who have been critical of his administration, overwhelmingly blocked an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Only Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie, who led the push alongside Democrats, broke ranks.
“What I found out tonight is they still haven’t broken from the spell of Donald Trump,” Massie said after the vote. “He still controls this conference.”
When asked whether the election was a referendum on Trump, Thune said the results stemmed from “a combination of things,” refusing to directly blame the president for contributing to the party’s challenges.
Signs of Trump’s shaky influence
But there were signs that Trump’s influence had limits.
Few echoed his argument in a social media post this week that there were problems with the election. In conceding a closely fought Senate contest in Mississippi, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith said she would “respect the decision” of voters.
Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith waves to supporters during President Donald Trump’s rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Several Republicans, including Sens. Joni Ernst of Iowa, Tim Scott of South Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas and Rep. Mike Lawler of New York, posted pictures of Democrats who will either succeed them or soon represent their states, harkening to an earlier era of postelection unity.
Rep. James Comer of Kentucky pushed back against White House warnings to congressional Democrats that planned probes of the Trump administration could amount to “blatant criminality.” Comer, who oversaw extensive investigations of Democratic President Joe Biden and his family as chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said lawmakers have a role in holding any White House accountable.
“Regardless of who is in the White House, there’s always going to be a strong desire for the Oversight Committee to be a check and balance on the executive branch, regardless of the political scenario,” Comer said.
___
Associated Press writer Kevin Freking contributed.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Senate’s coalition majority shrinks to bare minimum as three Republicans leave
description: The coalition majority in the 20-person Alaska Senate will be a bare-minimum 11 people after the departure of three Republican lawmakers. On Thursday, Sen. Jesse Bjorkman, R-Nikiski and a former member of the majority, said he will be minority leader of a newly expanded nine-person, all-Republican Senate minority. Sen. Robert Yundt, R-Wasilla, will be the […[...]
text:
Sen. Jesse Bjorkman, R-Nikiski, expresses frustration at a March 19, 2024, news conference the day after the legislature failed by one vote to override Gov. Mike Dunleavy's education-funding veto. Next to him is Sen. Bert Stedman, R-Sitka, a co-chair of the finance committee. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The coalition majority in the 20-person Alaska Senate will be a bare-minimum 11 people after the departure of three Republican lawmakers.
On Thursday, Sen. Jesse Bjorkman, R-Nikiski and a former member of the majority, said he will be minority leader of a newly expanded nine-person, all-Republican Senate minority.
Sen. Robert Yundt, R-Wasilla, will be the Minority Whip, effectively the No. 2-ranked member of the minority.
The change means the Senate’s majority will be predominantly Democratic, which could mean an easier working relationship with the predominantly Democratic coalition in the state House and with Democratic Governor-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins. It also means that the absence of a single member — due to illness, travel or family issues — could halt work in the Senate.
From 2025 through this year, the Senate Majority had 14 members — nine Democrats and five Republicans. As well as Bjorkman, its Republican membership included Sens. Kelly Merrick, R-Eagle River; Cathy Giessel, R-Anchorage; Gary Stevens, R-Kodiak; and Bert Stedman, R-Sitka.
Stevens retired and is on course to be replaced by Rep. Louise Stutes, R-Kodiak, who was leading a three-way race as of Friday.
Giessel will replace Stevens as Senate President. Stedman and Merrick are joining Bjorkman in the minority. 
According to a news release from the new Senate minority, Stedman will serve as the lead member of the minority on the Senate Finance Committee. 
Sen. Cathy Tilton, R-Wasilla, is on course to lose her election campaign to fellow Republican Ryan Berry. By phone, Berry said he will take Tilton’s spot in the minority and will not seek to join the majority.

name: WyoFile
title: Pragmatist Republicans tapped to lead Wyoming Legislature following Freedom Caucus’ electoral defeat
description:
Lawmakers nominated Cheyenne Sen. Tara Nethercott and Lander Rep. Lloyd Larsen respectively to serve as Senate President and House Speaker. 
The post Pragmatist Republicans tapped to lead Wyoming Legislature following Freedom Caucus’ electoral defeat appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
When the Wyoming Legislature convenes in January, they’ll likely be led by two Republicans known more for their traditionalist, pragmatic approach than the ideological conservatism of their predecessors.
Senate Republicans selected Cheyenne Sen. Tara Nethercott as the next president while House GOP members chose Lander Rep. Lloyd Larsen as incoming speaker, several legislators told WyoFile. 
Leadership positions hold significant power in both chambers, particularly the speaker and the president. They decide the makeup and head of each committee as well as what legislation goes to which committees, and in what order. Leadership also has the tools to kill legislation before it’s even considered by the larger body. 
While the GOP has controlled both chambers in the Wyoming Legislature for decades, its supermajority split in recent years between more traditional  Republicans and those aligned with the Wyoming Freedom Caucus. For the last two years, Freedom Caucus members have held all of the majority leadership positions in the House. During their tenure, the Legislature did away with most of the state’s gun-free zones, adopted a string of changes to the state’s election system and created a private-school waiver program with no income limits.
However, the caucus lost its House majority in this year’s primary election, and no longer has enough allies to form a voting bloc big enough to do much. Speaker of the House and Freedom Caucus member Chip Neiman, R-Hulette, lost his seat in the August primary, as did House Majority Floor Leader Scott Heiner, R-Green River, and House Majority Whip Ocean Andrew, R-Laramie. The caucus’s allies also backslid in the Senate. 
As a result, most legislative leadership races this weekend came down to contests between traditional Republicans with similar policy positions. 
Nethercott, who is now majority floor leader in the Senate, ran unopposed for president while Larsen competed against Casper Rep. Art Washut for speaker.
Larsen, who voters first elected in 2013, has become one of the House’s healthcare policy wonks and has spent much of his tenure trying to improve public health services. He also has eight years worth of experience serving on the Joint Appropriations Committee — a powerful panel of lawmakers responsible for crafting the initial budget bill. Larsen was also a vocal opponent of many of the budget cuts called for by the Freedom Caucus in the most recent session. 
Nethercott, an attorney, has largely focused her legislative career on economic development, higher education and judicial issues, including a term as chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee. In the most recent term, Nethercott worked as part of a coalition in the Senate to improve decorum and efficiency in the upper chamber.
“Wyoming deserves leadership that is steady in its principles, disciplined in its decisions, and focused on the future,” Nethercott said in a statement. “Our responsibility is to strengthen the foundations of our state, protect the opportunities that make Wyoming exceptional, and ensure the decisions we make today serve generations to come.”
Selections for some positions are only nominations at this point, since the entire body — Democrats included — must vote to affirm them. That includes the position of Senate president and vice president as well as House speaker and speaker pro tempore. However, with just two Democrats in the Senate and seven in the House, the nominations will likely win approval when the session begins in January in Cheyenne. 
If the chamber backs her next year, Nethercott would be just the second woman in Wyoming history to serve as president of the Senate, according to Legislative Service Office records. The first was Sen. April Brimmer-Kunz, also a Laramie County Republican, who served as president from 2003 to 2004. 
Lawmakers chose Evanston Sen. Wendy Schuler, who ran unopposed, to serve as Senate majority floor leader, a position that comes with the responsibility of deciding the order of bills lawmakers work through on the floor, among other things. 
For Senate vice president, Ten Sleep Sen. Ed Cooper bested Lander Sen. Cale Case for the second-in-command post.
In the House, Lusk Rep. JD Williams won majority floor leader over Wheatland Rep. Jeremy Haroldson, one of the few Freedom Caucus members who won their reelection bid. 
Jackson Rep. Andrew Byron beat Cheyenne Rep. Clarence Styvar for speaker pro tempore while Rock Springs Rep. Cody Wylie bested Worland Rep. Martha Lawley for majority whip. 
The Legislature’s democratic members also met Saturday in Casper to decide leadership positions, such as minority floor leader and whip in each chamber. Their meeting had not concluded by publishing time. 
This is a breaking news story and may be updated.

title: Colorado Senate Republicans pick Lisa Frizell as minority leader
description: Colorado Senate Republicans unanimously selected Sen. Lisa Frizell of Castle Rock as their new minority leader on Saturday morning. The vote came after Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, a Democrat, named former Senate Minority Leader Cleave Simpson as his nominee for Commissioner of Agriculture. Frizell arrived to the Senate in 2025 after one term in the House […]
text:
Colorado state Sen. Lisa Frizell, a Castle Rock Republican, listens to opening day proceedings on the first day of the 2025 session of the Colorado Legislature on Jan. 8, 2025, at the Colorado Capitol. (Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Senate Republicans unanimously selected Sen. Lisa Frizell of Castle Rock as their new minority leader on Saturday morning.
The vote came after Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, a Democrat, named former Senate Minority Leader Cleave Simpson as his nominee for Commissioner of Agriculture.
Frizell arrived to the Senate in 2025 after one term in the House of Representatives and a career in the Douglas County Assessor’s Office. Before Saturday, she was the assistant minority leader for the caucus. When the new legislative session starts in January, she will lead the 11 Republicans in the chamber against a 24-member Democratic supermajority.
“It is forever my honor to serve this caucus, serve the people of Colorado and serve with this caucus, because we are a team and we are in this together,” she said. “I look forward to the opportunities in front of us — not the adversity — but the opportunities. They are there and we will make the most of them.”
Senate Republicans also unanimously chose Sen. Byron Pelton of Sterling as assistant minority leader, Sen. Scott Bright of Platteville as caucus chair and Sen. Janice Rich of Grand Junction as caucus whip. Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer of Weld County will continue serving on the Joint Budget Committee.
In the Colorado House, Republicans earlier this month reelected Rep. Jarvis Caldwell as minority leader, a post he has served in since September 2025.
The legislative session will begin on Jan. 11, 2027.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Commentary: Washington needs to keep pushing for youth safety on social media
description: Existing at the forefront of any new technological frontier comes with advantages and drawbacks, and that is especially true for our digital lives. Organizing, connecting, and communicating has never been quite as seamless as it is today, and social media has progressed far beyond just entertainment. It’s granted us an awesome ability to foster community […]
text:
Washington's attorney general will not push a sweeping bill to limit social media for youths following a court settlement with Meta. (Photo Illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Existing at the forefront of any new technological frontier comes with advantages and drawbacks, and that is especially true for our digital lives. Organizing, connecting, and communicating has never been quite as seamless as it is today, and social media has progressed far beyond just entertainment.
It’s granted us an awesome ability to foster community amongst those of us who would otherwise remain disconnected. But at the same time, the power to connect with virtually anyone and anything can be all-consuming. And in an era where it feels like many adults aren’t equipped to engage with social media, how on earth can we expect that of children?
It’s time we stand up to the big-tech giants that design our children’s digital lives who have left parents with little to no say in the matter. I have spoken with families across Washington who do their very best to stay up-to-date with the latest that social media has to offer, both in terms of parental control options and social/educational opportunities for their kids. But in a reality where most kids are juggling multiple apps with multiple profiles, parents simply can’t keep up.
Washington Attorney General Nick Brown took a stand on their behalf. He and other attorneys general across the country secured a settlement deal with Meta that will bring safeguards to its platforms to help parents do their job. These new features will roll out over the next couple of months and include time limits, notification blockers at night/during school hours, and options to switch off auto-play features. These types of settings will help kids manage a healthier relationship with technology so they can best succeed at home and in the classroom. The fight, however, is not over yet.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
I laud AG Brown for his work, as I’m sure most parents do across Washington state, but we know that the movement to keep kids safe does not stop at just Instagram and Facebook. Any form of social media that engages kids the way Meta’s platforms do should be held to the same standard. YouTube and TikTok both offer the same style of short-form, auto-playing content that exists on Instagram, but neither is bound by the agreement. This is meaningful because part of the agreement states that if the other major platforms adopt the same standards, Meta will release more money to states. In Washington, that means jumping from $237 million to nearly $339 million over the next decade. That’s roughly $100 million more that could help fund the youth mental health programs so many students in our communities rely on.
Surveys show that YouTube is the most widely used social media platform amongst American teens, so there is an even greater urgency for the platform to adopt these common-sense standards. YouTube is trying to evade responsibility by claiming it isn’t social media, which won’t fool anyone who has used the app recently.
I’ve seen firsthand how beneficial social media platforms have been for teens in the LGBTQ community. Finding peers and mentors with similar lived experience can be transformative, and in many cases, life-saving. I want to make sure these platforms are being used the right way, and AG Brown deserves great credit for heading that mission. We are so close to a huge breakthrough in the mission to keep kids safe online. I sincerely hope YouTube and TikTok step up so we get to see it through.
Sheila Stickel is a renowned family advocate throughout the Pacific Northwest. She has worked for 20 years advocating for human rights, including managing Washington State’s history making same-sex marriage campaign in 2012.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Massachusetts led twice on health care. It’s time for a third major reform – this one focused on keeping people well.
description: Finding people whose risk is rising, before they become patients, is what makes prevention pay.
text:
GOV. HEALEY won her second term promising, among other things, to lower health care costs and expand access to primary, mental, and maternal health care. She takes up that challenge in the 20th anniversary year of the law that made Massachusetts the national model for health coverage. 
Twice, the Commonwealth has led the country on health care. If Healey wants affordable access to last, it will have to lead a third time, by building a system that pays to keep people well. 
The first wave was coverage. The 2006 reform, signed by a Republican governor, Mitt Romney, and written with a Democratic Legislature, made near-universal insurance a state guarantee and a template for the Affordable Care Act. It worked: 97.9 percent of residents are insured, against about 92 percent nationally. 
The second wave was cost. In 2012, Chapter 224 made Massachusetts the first state to set a target for health care spending growth, and created the Health Policy Commission to monitor it. For a while, it worked. Spending per resident grew an average of 3.5 percent a year from 2012 to 2019. 
Since then, the benchmark has been left behind. Growth has averaged 5.3 percent a year since 2019. In 2024, the state spent $83.3 billion on health care, or $11,663 per resident, an increase of 5.7 percent against a 3.6 percent target, the fourth year in a row it was missed. 
Two in five residents report trouble affording care. Family premiums for employer coverage reached $28,151, the highest in the country, and with out-of-pocket costs, a family’s health care cost $32,469. At recent growth rates, family premiums would reach a staggering $50,000 by 2032, according to Health Policy Commission projections presented last week.  
Coverage is also under strain. Federal Medicaid changes are expected to double the state’s uninsured rate. Expanding access is the right goal. But access built on a cost curve like this one will not hold. 
The benchmark measures what the system spends without changing what it buys. Meanwhile, primary care’s share of spending is shrinking, even though it is where most prevention happens: From 2019 to 2023, primary care spending grew 13.6 percent, against 20.6 percent for other medical care. 
I have seen this problem from the inside. For eight years, I built and scaled an integrated health care platform across the US and Canada under the two basic ways care is paid for. Under global payment contracts, we were responsible for a population’s total cost of care, so a visit that kept a patient out of the hospital saved money.  
Under fee-for-service, we were paid for each service delivered, so the same visit, by the same patient to the same clinician, earned only a modest fee, and keeping that patient out of the hospital earned us nothing at all. The contract, not the medicine, decided what got done. 
Massachusetts sits between those two models. It pioneered global budgets, and MassHealth now pays for 92 percent of members in its accountable care and managed care plans that way.  
But in commercial insurance, only about 35 percent of members’ care was under such arrangements in 2024, down from 39 percent two years earlier; the rest is still paid service by service.  
And even global contracts are settled year by year against spending targets, rewarding savings that appear quickly rather than those that arrive a decade later. For most residents, the system still works the way fee-for-service always has. I call it find it, fix it. Wait for disease to appear, then pay to treat it. Coverage brought more people into that model, and the benchmark tried to make it cheaper, but neither changed it.  
The third wave should finish what global payment began, and build a system to predict illness and prevent it. 
Prevention is not a blank check. Screening everyone for everything costs money. The Congressional Budget Office found that about 80 percent of the preventive services it studied raised total spending.  



What pays is prevention aimed at the right people. In the national Diabetes Prevention Program, an intensive lifestyle program cut new cases of type 2 diabetes by 58 percent among high-risk adults. And the opportunity for big gains with the right targets is huge: Only about one in four Americans with high blood pressure has it under control. That is why prediction comes first. Finding people whose risk is rising, before they become patients, is what makes prevention pay. 
Massachusetts already owns most of the tools. Five moves would lay the foundation for a system built to predict disease and prevent it: 
1. Measure health, not just spending. Alongside the cost growth benchmark, the Health Policy Commission should publish a yearly prevention scorecard for every major insurer and provider system. This should show the share of patients with blood pressure and blood sugar under control, and the hospital admissions that good primary care should have prevented.
2.  Use the data the state already has. The state’s all-payer claims database already tracks claims across most of the state’s insurers. Used with strong privacy protections, it can show where residents’ risk is rising before a diagnosis, so prevention can be targeted. 
3.  Protect primary care’s share. The Legislature is close: the House and Senate have each passed bills requiring at least 15 percent of health care spending to go to primary care, more than double today’s share, and a conference committee is now reconciling them. Lawmakers should finish the job before the year ends, and keep the new primary care payment models both bills include, so that practices are paid for keeping patients well rather than for the number of visits they log. 
4.  Pay for results, starting with the state’s own plans. MassHealth and the Group Insurance Commission, which covers state and municipal employees, should tie a meaningful share of payments to those control rates and avoided admissions. The state is a long-term payer. It should act like one. 
5.  Give prevention time to pay. The same two plans should also offer multiyear global contracts that credit providers for prevention savings measured over five years or more, and the Health Policy Commission should judge prevention investments over the same horizon when it assesses performance against the benchmark. 
None of this requires choosing between Democrats and Republicans. Romney, a Republican, signed the first wave into law with a Democratic Legislature. Gov. Deval Patrick, a Democrat, signed the second. Healey now has the chance to build the third. The Health Policy Commission has urged that Massachusetts “once again be the national leader in reimagining our health care system.” 
Twenty years ago, the question was who would be covered. Fourteen years ago, it was how much the system should cost. The question now is what all that money buys. Massachusetts answered the first two questions for the country. It should answer the third by laying the foundation for a health system that is paid to predict illness and prevent it. 
M. Vaman Rao is a Boston-based scientist, serial entrepreneur, innovator, and investor. He built and scaled an integrated health care platform across the US and Canada.

title: Tower Hill Field Hockey Crowned State Champions for First Time in nearly Two Decades
description: The Tower Hill Hillers defeated the Caravel Buccaneers, 3-1, in the 2026 DIAA Division Two State Championship, earning the program’s 19th state title.   FREDERICA, Del. — Tower Hill junior Molly Gallagher stepped to the penalty spot with her team tied, 1-1, under a minute to play in the third quarter. Gallagher placed the ball down and readied to take ... Re[...]
text:
The 2026 Tower Hill Field Hockey team poses for a picture after winning the 2026 DIAA Division Two Field Hockey State Championship game. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
The Tower Hill Hillers defeated the Caravel Buccaneers, 3-1, in the 2026 DIAA Division Two State Championship, earning the program’s 19th state title.
 
FREDERICA, Del. — Tower Hill junior Molly Gallagher stepped to the penalty spot with her team tied, 1-1, under a minute to play in the third quarter. Gallagher placed the ball down and readied to take her shot. The whistle blew and Gallagher didn’t waste a second. 
Gallagher fired a quick shot toward the right of the cage. Caravel goalkeeper, Hartley Haynes, moved quickly and got in front of the shot. Haynes seemed to have stopped the shot with the pad on her left hand, but the ball deflected off the pad backwards and right behind her to the back of the cage.
Gallagher scored on a second penalty stroke opportunity in the fourth quarter helping Tower Hill defeat Caravel, 3-1, and earn the 2026 DIAA Division Two State title.
“It’s just such an amazing feeling. We’ve been working so hard all season,” Gallagher said postgame. “This was such like a team effort, it wasn’t just one person. We like, we passed so well, we moved the ball, we stuck to the gameplan. This is just like an unreal feeling.”   
The Hillers and Buccaneers played a close game through frigid temperatures and strong winds, Friday night. The two teams battled for possession through most of the first quarter with only a pair of Caravel penalty corners presenting possible scoring chances. Midway through the second quarter the Hillers broke through.
The game’s opening goal was scored by Tower Hill senior Hailey Allen on the right of the cage. The play was initiated by Gallagher who dribbled through a pair of Buccaneer defenders at the top of the circle to create a bit of space for a pass to Charlotte Vanni a few yards away from the goal. Vanni quickly fired a backhand shot that was deflected by a Caravel defender, but landed right in front of Allen to knock in.    
Tower Hill’s defense withstood three Caravel penalty corner attempts in the final five minutes of the quarter and closed out the half with a 1-0 lead.
The midfield battle continued into the second half until Caravel worked the ball into its offensive zone with just under six minutes to play in the third quarter. The Buccaneers breached the circle and fired a pair of shots at the goal to no avail. One of the shot attempts drew a foul call on the Hiller defense and resulted in a penalty stroke opportunity for Buccaneer sophomore, Allie Sweeney. Sweeney fired a low shot to the left of the cage to tie the game, 1-1.
Gallagher’s first penalty stroke followed about four minutes later and her success returned the advantage back to the Hillers before the fourth quarter. 
Caravel’s offense put together a couple strong attempts at an equalizer, but the Hillers’ defense stood strong and didn’t allow another score. Gallagher added a second goal to her ledger with a score on a second penalty stroke opportunity and Tower Hill protected the lead until the final buzzer rang out. Gallagher finished the game with two goals on two successful penalty stroke attempts.
“It’s such an honor, like, it’s so much pressure but I know they believe in me and that just gives me the strength to keep going,” Gallagher said about being the one to take the penalty shots while a group of Tower Hill fans shouted MVP chants in the background. 
The 2026 Hiller team finished the season with a 17-1 overall record and the program’s first state championship since 2008. Tower Hill head coach Lindsay Goeller graduated from the school a year before that title but won three before that as a player under former Hiller head coach Robin Adair. Adair led the Hillers to ten state championship victories over her career, winning four straight titles multiple times.
Goeller said her staff is filled with alumni that span across three decades of Hiller field hockey and that passion and investment for the school and program make this state championship special.
“As a staff we’re so invested in this program, in Tower Hill, in the culture of field hockey and its so special to bring a state championship back to Tower Hill,” Goeller said. “We’re so proud and you can feel the tradition, you can feel what it means to our program to have the trophy back.” 
Caravel finished the season with a 13-5 overall record and the program’s first state championship appearance since 2020.

title: State librarian seeks funding, Capitol campus return amid budget cuts
description: This article was first published by TVW. On Thursday, the Joint State Capitol Committee and Capitol Campus Design Advisory Committee vot[...]
text:
This article was first published by TVW.
Washington’s new state librarian wants $4.2 million to stabilize services and restore public access to historic collections while advancing a long-delayed plan to return the State Library and Archives to the Capitol campus.
On Thursday, the Joint State Capitol Committee and Capitol Campus Design Advisory Committee voted to recommend a new library and archives building to the Legislature to be built on the site of the former General Administration building on the campus.
Melody Sky Weaver told Inside Olympia host Austin Jenkins that persistent budget cuts have left the state’s oldest cultural institution struggling to maintain services.
State Librarian Melody Sky Weaver appears on TVW’s “Inside Olympia.” (Photo courtesy of TVW)
Twelve employees received layoff notices in 2025 after revenue from real estate recording fees fell short of projections. The state library in Tumwater is now open by appointment only, on Thursdays from 1 to 4 p.m.
“The level of access they had before has been crippled by these budget cuts,” Weaver said.
The library’s approximately $12.7 million biennial budget supports historic collections, institutional libraries in prisons and other facilities, and the Washington Talking Book and Braille Library.
Even before Weaver began as state librarian on October 1, she made news by advocating for the return of the library to the Capitol campus, which it left following the 2001 Nisqually earthquake.
The proposed Library and Archives Building (LAB) would replace aging and inadequate facilities with collection storage, exhibition space, meeting rooms and other public amenities.
Weaver sees the project as an opportunity to make the library more accessible to lawmakers, researchers and visitors. A self-described “extroverted loud librarian,” Weaver says advocacy is essential to reversing years of cuts and raising the institution’s profile.
Her larger goal is to make the State Library indispensable, rather than one of Washington’s best-kept secrets. “I feel like libraries are very sexy, but of course I’m biased,” she said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ‘The auditor owns a used car dealership. His landlord is a friend he signed deeds for.’
description: The relationship that led to calls for investigation and resignation by state lawmakers between state Auditor Mark Hunt and Charleston attorney Robert L. Johns goes beyond property deeds and state office work.
text:
After Hours Used Auto was a by-appointment car dealership owned and operated by state Auditor Mark Hunt and high ranking officials in his administration. The owner of the property is Robert L. Johns, an attorney Hunt signed tax deeds for in a move some lawmakers say may have violated the law. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)The relationship that led to calls for investigation and resignation by state lawmakers between state Auditor Mark Hunt and Charleston attorney Robert L. Johns goes beyond property deeds and state office work. 
During Hunt’s term as auditor he has sold cars at After Hours Used Auto, a by-appointment car dealership less than a mile from the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia, that sits on land owned by Johns. 
The lot holds five cars — including a black 2013 Ford Expedition, with dents in the hatch door and a silver sedan with a flat tire — and a small shack with a sign telling customers to call to book an appointment to see a car. 
A silver sedan with a flat tire sits on the lot of After Hours Used Auto, a dealership owned and operated by the state Auditor and high ranking officials in his administration. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)
Hunt established the business in July 2024, roughly four months before he would be elected state auditor. When reached by phone Friday at his private law practice, Hunt stressed that no cars were sold during state government working hours.  
“It was a hobby. That’s the reason, you know it’s kind of funny, the name was After Hours,” he said. 
The owner of the property is NAJ, a limited liability company owned by Johns, who has accumulated $38 million in tax delinquent land across the state. A West Virginia Watch investigation revealed that Hunt, as auditor, has signed nine tax deeds for Johns, even though state law says that’s a duty of the deputy land commissioner. 
Hunt acknowledged Johns had been a “friend for years.” Johns, a bankruptcy attorney, was also hired by the Auditor’s Office after Hunt took office to act as a receiver in the event that McDowell County declared insolvency. 
Johns was paid $14,000 for his work in 2025, according to the State Checkbook, an online repository detailing West Virginia’s finances. 
Hunt said the fact that Johns owns the land the lot sits on is a coincidence. 
“(There’s) not a ghost behind every door. It’s just coincidental,” Hunt said. “He happens to have all of these vacant lots, and most of this property is scrub property. It’s hillsides, it’s vacant lots, it’s right-of-ways, and he just happened to own this.” 
The revelations about the tax deeds led to outcry from public officials, both Republican and Democrat. The Democratic caucuses in the House of Delegates and the state Senate also sent letters to Attorney General JB McCuskey to request an opinion on the legality of the situation. 
Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanawha, has been a leading Republican voice in the tax deed controversy, taking to social media to call for the auditor’s resignation. The car dealership has added fuel to that fire, he said. 
“This new information raises significant additional questions about Hunt’s relationship with Johns,” he said. “Is Hunt’s car dealership paying market price for rent on the lot owned by Johns’ company, or did Hunt illegally sign his landlord’s deeds as payback for a sweetheart lease? Regardless, this business relationship further underscores Hunt’s cronyism and why he should resign as auditor immediately for signing those deeds.” 
Hunt said that he paid fair market rent to Johns for the lot. But he doesn’t know how much. 
“I’m not saying that like I’m hiding it,” Hunt said. “I don’t know how much we were paying. I didn’t do that part of it. OK. So all I did was cut the grass.” 
The “we” Hunt referred to are people he calls “the boys” — his co-deputy chiefs of staff Caleb Hanna and David Cole. 
Hanna is a former state delegate who ran for auditor during the 2024 Republican Primary. Cole worked at Hunt’s law office for 17 years as an operations and marketing manager. 
Hanna sold a 2012 Lincoln MKZ Hybrid to Amber Blankenship, of Huntington, on a Saturday in October 2025. 
“It was for my then-19-year-old son,” she said. 
Blankeship said she did not visit the lot on a Friday evening in October. Instead, Blankenship met the state auditor at his private law office, she recalled. 
“The main office that I walked in was, they asked what I was there for, and I said, ‘Well, I’m supposed to be meeting somebody here about a car,’ and they called him (Hunt) and told him to bring it over,” Blankenship said.
The sign on the door at After Hours Auto Sales explains that it is appointment only, and includes a phone number to call. (Photo by Henry Culvyhouse/West Virginia Watch)
Blankenship said after taking it for a test drive, she was ready to buy. Hanna filled out the paperwork and Cole helped handle the payment. Cole asked her to send the money via an app, but the sale price was over the limit allowed by the app. Instead, she came back the following day and paid for it with her savings from the bank. 
Hunt said he never sold cars personally on the lot, but in this case the Lincoln was his personal, daily driver. 
“Yeah, I sold my car like anybody else does. I bought another car and I sold that one. I mean that that’s all it was,” Hunt said. “A deal between two parties is a deal.” 
Blankenship sued Hanna and After Hours Used Auto after the car broke down just nine days after purchase, according to Kanawha County court records. 
She accused the dealership of selling a lemon, court records show. 
Hunt himself entered an appearance in the case on a Tuesday in February 2026. A magistrate court judge dismissed the case after finding Blankenship had agreed to buy the car “as is.” 
Blankenship said she later sold the car for “basically scrap.” 
Hunt said the dealership from the beginning was a money losing proposition and in recent months has shuttered its doors. He said he, Cole and Hanna haven’t gotten around to clearing the cars off the lot. 
“After we lost about $40,000, I convinced the boys that we need to quit doing this. There’s no more to it or less to it than that,” Hunt said. 
Lori Kersey contributed to this report.
